people.n: Luis de Carvajal y de la Cueva

s.d: Born in 1537 in Mogadouro, Portugal, Carvajal grew up in a New Christian family marked by the tensions of forced conversion. Mogadouro symbolizes the roots of many conversos who would later venture into the Atlantic world, carrying both ambition and vulnerability.

Seville was Carvajal’s base during his early career as a merchant and seafarer. As the main port to the Americas, Seville offered opportunities for New Christians despite inquisitorial scrutiny. Carvajal’s networks here paved the way for his colonial ambitions.

In Madrid, Carvajal negotiated with the Spanish Crown to secure his colonial enterprise. His time at court reflects the precarious balance for New Christians: access to royal patronage but constant vulnerability to suspicion.

s.t: Colonial Power and Trial in Mexico City (1580s–1591)
s.d: Mexico City was the stage for Carvajal’s rise as a colonial leader and his fall into disgrace. As governor and royal official, he became entangled in the Inquisition’s investigations into Judaizing among his relatives, leading to his arrest and death in 1591.

Carvajal founded Nuevo León under a royal grant to settle Spain’s northern frontiers. His vision was ambitious, but controversies over slave raids and his family’s crypto-Jewish practices led to his downfall. Nuevo León embodies both his colonial achievements and the complexities of converso life. He died in 1596, in Mexico City.

s.t: Probable Birth and Youth in Salonika (Late 19th Century)
s.d: Moise B. Soulam was likely born in Ottoman Salonika, a city teeming with Ladino-speaking Jews, newspapers, and intellectual ferment. The city’s multilingual atmosphere nurtured his future role as a cultural mediator and satirist.

s.t: Migration to New York City (Early 20th Century)
s.d: Soulam emigrated to New York City during the great wave of Ottoman Sephardic migration. He joined an immigrant milieu grappling with language barriers and Americanization, setting the stage for his journalistic career.

s.loc: Lower East Side, New York, USA
s.d: Early in New York, Soulam entered the Ladino press world. This multilingual press was central to immigrant identity and communication, and Soulam quickly became one of its brightest voices.
Soulam contributed articles and commentary to La America, one of the earliest and most influential Ladino newspapers in the U.S., engaging in debates over identity, modernization, and communal life.

s.t: Editorial Work at La Vara Newspaper (1920s–1940s)
s.d: Soulam worked extensively at La Vara, the leading Ladino weekly in America, shaping the paper’s voice on social, political, and cultural issues. His writing was witty, critical, and deeply tied to Sephardic communal affairs.

s.t: Creating the Persona “Bula Satula” for Advice Columns
s.d: Under the pseudonym “Bula Satula,” Soulam penned the Ladino advice column Postemas de Mujer, tackling love, marriage, and gender tensions in a humorous, sometimes biting tone. This persona became legendary in Ladino press circles.
Another of Soulam’s pseudonyms was “Ham Moshón,” under which he wrote satirical, ironic pieces on community politics, assimilation, and the “Americanization” pressures facing Sephardic immigrants.

Soulam’s columns often addressed the tense relations between Sephardim and Ashkenazim, and between Sephardim and other immigrant groups, revealing complex interethnic dynamics in New York’s Jewish life.

s.t: Documenting Women’s Voices and Gender Roles
s.d: Through Postemas de Mujer and other writings, Soulam explored issues like arranged marriage, romantic love, spousal disputes, and shifting gender norms. His columns provide unique insights into Sephardic women’s experiences in America.

s.t: Chronicling Decline of the Ladino Press (1940s)
s.d: As Ladino readership declined post-WWII, Soulam remained active, lamenting the loss of communal cohesion and linguistic heritage. His later writings reflect nostalgia and efforts to preserve cultural memory.

Tudela is the city where Benjamin of Tudela was born and raised, in the medieval Kingdom of Navarre. This is the starting point of his journey, before he set out across the Mediterranean world and recorded Jewish communities, trade routes, rulers, scholars, and sacred places.
Benjamin’s itinerary became one of the most important Jewish travel accounts of the Middle Ages. From Tudela, his writing follows a wide network of cities and communities, showing how Jewish life connected Spain, France, Italy, Greece, the Levant, Mesopotamia, Persia, and Egypt.

First stop. Zaragoza, in the Aragón region of northeastern Spain, was the first stop on Benjamin of Tudela’s journey. From here, he followed routes shaped by the Ebro River, regional trade, and movement between Christian and Muslim-ruled lands.
For Benjamin, Zaragoza marked the beginning of a larger project: observing communities not only as places on a map, but as living networks of scholars, merchants, and religious institutions. The city introduces the pattern of his travel writing, where geography and Jewish communal life are always connected.

Second stop. Tarragona stood near the third and fourth stops, but Benjamin treated it as a distinct place with its own history and Jewish presence. He described it as an ancient city and noted its unusual remains, connecting the city’s physical landscape to its long past.
This stop helps show how Benjamin of Tudela moved through places with layered identities: Roman, medieval, Christian, and Jewish. His notes distinguish Tarragona from nearby cities while still placing it within the broader route from the Ebro corridor toward the Mediterranean coast.

Third stop. Barcelona appears in Benjamin’s account as a major city with a documented Jewish community. He wrote that after traveling from Zaragoza toward Tortosa and Tarragona, “two days thence is Barcelona,” where he found a congregation of wise, learned, and princely men.
Benjamin’s description gives Barcelona special importance because it emphasizes scholarship, leadership, and social standing. The city was not only a travel point but a center of Jewish learning and Mediterranean connection, linking Iberian Jewish life to wider networks of commerce and knowledge.

Fourth stop. Girona was recorded as a smaller Jewish community, but Benjamin still marked it carefully in his itinerary. He wrote that “a day’s journey and a half brings you to Gerona,” and noted that the city contained a small congregation of Jews.
Across the Spanish stops, Benjamin’s travel writing records the size of communities, their social status, and their scholars. From Girona, he continued toward northern France, expanding his account from Iberian Jewish life into the wider Jewish geography of medieval Europe.

Fifth stop. Marseilles represented a major Mediterranean port and a place of high levels of trade and travel. Benjamin of Tudela noted the wider region of France, called Tsarphat in Jewish tradition, and placed the city within a network that reached toward Paris and other centers.
The importance of Marseilles came from movement: ships, merchants, pilgrims, and scholars passed through its harbor. For Benjamin, the city showed how Jewish communities were connected to maritime commerce and how Mediterranean ports helped ideas, people, and goods move between Europe and the East.

Sixth stop. Genoa, in Liguria, was another important maritime city. Benjamin noted smaller traces of Jewish community here, but the city’s significance came from its role in trade, shipping, and commercial networking across the Mediterranean.
Correcting the name: the traveler is Benjamin of Tudela, spelled with one “i” in Benjamin. In Genoa, his account continues to show that even where Jewish communities were smaller, their presence mattered within larger systems of travel, exchange, and regional connection.

Seventh stop. Lucca was a brief but carefully noted visit. Benjamin described it as a large city and recorded a small Jewish community of about forty Jews, naming leading figures such as R. David, R. Samuel, and R. Jacob.
This entry is typical of Benjamin’s method: even when a place had a small community, he preserved names, numbers, and status. Lucca therefore becomes part of a larger map of Jewish continuity, showing how small congregations maintained leadership and identity across medieval Italy.

Eighth stop. Pisa was less prominent in Benjamin’s account for its Jewish community, but it stood out as a powerful and fortified city. He described it as a place of great extent, with many fortified houses and a strong connection to conflict, defense, and trade.
Benjamin’s note about Pisa shows that his travel writing was not only a list of Jewish communities. He also recorded political and urban conditions, helping readers understand the environments in which Jewish merchants, travelers, and residents lived and moved.

Ninth stop. Rome was remarkable for its historical and religious significance. Benjamin called it the metropolis of all Christendom and noted that about two hundred Jews lived there, respected and exempt from ordinary tribute in his account.
Rome’s Jewish community carried special meaning because it lived under the authority of the Pope while preserving its own communal identity. Benjamin’s description highlights dignity, political status, and the deep historical layers of Jewish life in Rome.

Tenth stop. In Greece, Benjamin mentioned cities such as Arta, Corinth, Corfu, Thebes, and Thessaloniki, also known as Salonika. Some places had larger Jewish communities than others, but all formed part of his eastern Mediterranean route.
His descriptions emphasize commercial skills, local crafts, and regional movement. Greece helped Benjamin show the diversity of Byzantine Jewish life, where Jewish communities lived among Greek-speaking, Christian, and mercantile worlds while maintaining their own institutions.

Eleventh stop. Istanbul, then Constantinople, was one of the largest and wealthiest cities Benjamin encountered. He described a major urban center marked by imperial power, trade, religious diversity, and a large Jewish presence.
For Benjamin, Constantinople revealed the scale of the eastern Mediterranean world. Its Jewish community lived within a city of immense wealth and political importance, where merchants, officials, craftspeople, and travelers moved through the capital of the Byzantine Empire.

Twelfth stop. Syria received more attention in Benjamin’s account because of its layered religious and political landscape. He observed Jewish communities living under different forms of Christian and Muslim rule and noted their economic activity.
This stop shows how Benjamin’s journey followed both sacred geography and trade geography. In Syria, Jewish communities were part of regional markets, pilgrimage routes, and urban centers, making the area a key bridge between Anatolia, the Levant, Mesopotamia, and Egypt.

Thirteenth stop. Lebanon appeared in Benjamin’s account through biblical memory, local geography, and trade. He connected the region to places mentioned in Scripture, including Baalath in the valley of Lebanon, and described impressive stone construction.
Although the Jewish communities he described here were smaller, they were involved in trade and commerce. Benjamin’s writing links Lebanon to a landscape of memory and movement, where biblical associations and everyday mercantile life existed side by side.

Fourteenth stop. The Land of Israel held deep religious significance in Benjamin’s journey. His writings emphasize Jewish continuity through spiritual, cultural, and political memory, especially in places connected to Jerusalem and biblical history.
Benjamin described sacred sites, monumental remains, and Jewish presence as evidence of enduring connection. His account of Jerusalem and the surrounding land turns the travel narrative into more than geography: it becomes a record of Jewish memory, longing, and continuity.

Fifteenth stop. Northern Mesopotamia, also linked with Shinar, brought Benjamin into one of the great centers of eastern Jewish life. He found thriving communities, especially around Baghdad, where Jews enjoyed peace, comfort, honor, and prosperity under local rule.
This stop is central because Mesopotamia connected Benjamin’s route to the historic heartland of the Babylonian Jewish world. His description points to scholars, communal organization, economic success, and the prestige of Jewish institutions in the East.

Seventeenth stop. Persia was described as a frontier region with Jewish communities integrated into the societies around them. Benjamin noted communities of significant size, including a place he described as containing about fifteen hundred Jews.
Although this sheet moves from the fifteenth to the seventeenth stop, the description keeps the original numbering. In Persia, Benjamin’s account expands the map of Jewish diaspora life beyond the Mediterranean, showing communities connected to eastern trade routes and older centers of Jewish settlement.

Eighteenth stop. Egypt held a central role in Benjamin’s account because of its wealth, religious tolerance, scholars, and important sites. He described large and beautiful cities where merchants from many regions gathered because of Egypt’s strategic location.
This final stop also suggests the closing movement of Benjamin’s travels, after which he likely retraced parts of his route back toward Spain. Egypt brings together many of the themes of the journey: commerce, scholarship, sacred memory, political power, and the resilience of Jewish communities across the medieval world.

Victor Perera’s family traced its origins to Jerusalem, but departed the city in defiance of his great-grandfather’s solemn injunction to remain in the Holy Land “from now to eternity,” unless given divine consent. In the generations that followed, this act of departure was regarded as a transgression, and many family members believed they were cursed as a result. This sense of spiritual rupture and ancestral disobedience would later echo in Perera’s explorations of exile, identity, and the burdens of historical memory.

One of Victor Perera’s ancestors, Nunes Pereira, was executed by burning at the stake in Mexico City in 1595 during the New World Inquisition—a stark testament to the persecution faced by crypto-Jews in the Spanish colonies. This ancestral history of religious violence and displacement became a resonant theme in Perera’s later work, informing his exploration of Sephardic identity, historical memory, and the enduring legacies of exile.

Perera’s grandparents lived in Salonika, a vibrant center of Sephardic Jewish life following the Spanish Inquisition, which forced Jews from Spain and Portugal. His writings often reflect on this inherited legacy—exploring themes of exile, the preservation of Ladino language and customs, and the trauma of displacement that profoundly affected Salonika’s Jewish community, particularly during and after World War II. In the 1920s, his parents migrated from Salonika to Guatemala, bringing with them the cultural memory of a diasporic past that would later shape Perera’s literary and intellectual preoccupations.

Victor was born in 1934 in Guatemala City, where he lived with his parents throughout the 1940s. In a deliberate act of secularism, his father arranged for a non-Jewish doctor to perform his circumcision, signaling a desire to distance the family from religious tradition. However, during his youth, Victor underwent a second circumcision—a physically painful experience that also served as a formative assertion of Jewish identity within a predominantly Catholic society. His early years were marked by tensions between assimilation and tradition, contributing to a persistent sense of cultural dislocation and unbelonging.

Following their relocation to New York, Victor enrolled at Brooklyn College, a move that marked a significant turning point in his personal and intellectual development. In Rites: A Guatemalan Boyhood, he reflects on his sense of alienation both within Guatemalan society and the Jewish community—experiences that deeply informed his evolving worldview. New York, in contrast, provided a space for cultural reinvention and creative autonomy, allowing him to forge a more self-defined identity.

Victor pursued graduate studies in English literature at the University of Michigan, where he earned his master’s degree. In 1960, he met Padma Hejmadi, an Indian writer and artist, whom he later married; the couple had one daughter before their marriage ended in 1972. During this period, Victor produced a variety of early drafts and research materials that revealed his developing interests in subjects as diverse as the Guatemalan conflicts, Sephardic Jewish genealogy, and cultural myths surrounding whales and the Loch Ness Monster.

From 1960 to 1971, Perera taught at the University of California, Berkeley, where he engaged with leftist and liberationist thought that significantly shaped his intellectual orientation. These influences are evident in his later critiques of colonialism, particularly in works such as Unfinished Conquest, which interrogates the historical and ongoing effects of imperialism in Latin America.

Between 1972 and 1979, Perera taught journalism and creative writing at the University of California, Santa Cruz, a period during which his writing increasingly combined personal memoir, historical inquiry, and cultural commentary. This stylistic evolution reflected his growing interest in the intersections of identity, politics, and memory. Perera continued writing and teaching into the following decades until his death in 2003 at the age of 69.
s.cr: The Regents of the University of California

s.d:
Isaac Monsanto was born in Lisbon, the capital of Portugal and the heart of the Portuguese Inquisition. His family lived as Crypto-Jews, outwardly practicing Catholicism but secretly preserving Sephardic Jewish traditions passed down over generations. Lisbon’s inquisitorial courts, autos-da-fé (public punishments), and religious surveillance made Judaism a faith of secrecy and resistance.
Jewish life in Lisbon was defined by covert ritual: Shabbat candles hidden from view and prayers whispered. Monsanto’s family eventually fled to escape the reach of the Inquisition.

Arriving in Amsterdam, Isaac Monsanto and his family rejoined Jewish communal life in the open for the first time. The Dutch Republic was known for its religious tolerance, and Amsterdam had become a major hub for Sephardic Jews who had escaped the Iberian Peninsula. The city’s Portuguese Jewish community built a strong cultural and religious infrastructure centered around education, charity, and trade.
Life here was vibrant and public. The community preserved Iberian customs — Ladino-speaking prayers, Spanish-Portuguese melodies, and elegant, formal dress. Shabbat and holiday meals featured puchero, almodrote, and egg breads soaked in honey. This was where Monsanto entered global trade

Isaac Monsanto moved to Willemstad, the capital of Dutch Curaçao, which by the 1700s was the economic and spiritual capital of Sephardic life in the Caribbean. The island’s Jewish community, descended from Spanish-Portuguese exiles, enjoyed full rights and operated as merchants, civic leaders, and religious figures.
The community was centered around Mikvé Israel, the oldest functioning synagogue in the Western Hemisphere. Here, Jewish life blended Iberian ritual with Caribbean culture. Shabbat meals combined kosher meats with tropical fruits, plantains, and local fish. Services were held with Spanish-Portuguese melodies, and the sand-covered floors of the synagogue symbolized the Marrano…

By the mid-1700s, Monsanto arrived in New Orleans, then a colonial frontier under French rule (later Spanish). Although Catholic law banned Jews from settling, Monsanto’s commercial value gave him leeway. He became one of the city’s most successful merchants, dealing in indigo, textiles, and household goods.
There was no formal synagogue, but Monsanto quietly upheld Jewish life in the French Quarter, likely hosting Shabbat gatherings and holidays in private homes. Meals might include kosher gumbo, Creole vegetables, and spiced red wine in place of traditional Kiddush wine.
Though he died in 1778, Monsanto helped lay the foundation for Southern Jewish life. His legacy shaped the eventual…

Susana Behar's maternal grandparents were Sephardic Jews who emigrated from Turkey to Cuba in the early 20th century. They brought with them the Judeo-Spanish language, also known as Ladino, and traditional Sephardic songs. These cultural elements were integral to Susana's early exposure to her heritage.

Susana Behar was born and raised in Havana, Cuba, in a Sephardic Jewish family with Turkish roots. Her early years were shaped by the cultural diversity of mid-20th century Havana, where she was first introduced to Ladino songs and the traditions of the Sephardic diaspora.

In 1965, Susana and her family emigrated to Caracas, Venezuela, where she lived for 17 years. During this period, she explored and performed the music of her adopted country, as well as that of Latin America and Jewish folklore. This experience expanded her musical repertoire and allowed her to connect with a broader range of cultural traditions. ​

In 1983, Susana relocated to Miami, Florida, where she has resided ever since. In Miami, she has dedicated herself to preserving and promoting Sephardic music. In 2007, she founded The Sephardic Music Ensemble, developing an extensive repertoire to help preserve this integral part of Jewish culture. Susana has performed at festivals and concerts across the United States and internationally, and has released two albums, "La Galana y El Mar" (2010) and "TAPIZ" (2018). She continues to perform regularly throughout South Florida. ​

Benguiat was born in Izmir (formerly Smyrna), Turkey, a thriving port city within the Ottoman Empire known for its diverse population and vibrant Jewish community. Izmir was a significant hub for Sephardic Jews, many of whom had resettled there after the 1492 expulsion from Spain. The city nurtured a rich tradition of Ladino language, Jewish scholarship, and artisan crafts — an environment that deeply influenced Benguiat. Raised in this culturally fertile atmosphere, Benguiat developed his skills in Hebrew calligraphy, bookbinding, and printing, laying the foundation for his future contributions to Sephardic literature and religious life.

In the mid-19th century, Benguiat relocated to Alexandria, Egypt — a cosmopolitan city experiencing rapid growth and modernization under Ottoman rule. Alexandria had become a magnet for Sephardic Jews seeking economic opportunity and religious freedom, and Benguiat quickly found a place within its flourishing Jewish community. There, he continued his work as a printer and calligrapher, producing religious texts, prayer books, and ketubbot (marriage contracts) that were admired for both their spiritual value and artistic beauty. His presence helped reinforce the cultural identity of Sephardic Jews in Egypt, and his work served as a bridge between tradition and innovation during a period of…

Hadji Ephraim Benguiat spent his final decades in New York City, where he left a lasting legacy through his dedication to preserving Sephardic traditions in a rapidly changing world. Through his art, publishing, and communal leadership, he ensured that the voices and values of Sephardic Jews, many of whom were new immigrants navigating life in America, remained visible and vibrant. His contributions laid a foundation for future generations of Sephardic Jews in the United States, blending the cultural richness of the Ottoman Empire with the evolving identity of Jewish life in the American diaspora.

Benguiat supplied custom prayer books and religious texts for newly established congregations in Boston. His works helped unify Sephardic immigrants arriving from different parts of the Ottoman Empire with familiar texts and liturgical customs.

In San Francisco, Benguiat was instrumental in providing religious materials and guidance to Sephardic Jews who had settled there during westward expansion and the Gold Rush era. Though smaller in number, this community relied on figures like Benguiat for authentic Sephardic religious texts.

April 27, 1855 Manissa, Ottoman Empire - September 10, 1928 New York, NY. 
Morris Schinasi was a Sephardic Jew from the Ottoman Empire. Schinasi started an incredibly successful tobacco business in New York City in the early 1900's with his brother, Solomon. His business provided work for many Sephardic immigrants in the US and left a lasting legacy in New York and his birthplace Manisa, Turkey.

Schinasi had a difficult childhood during which he contracted Dipthyeria at nine years old. The nurse who treated him was named Schinassi, and his parents gave him her surname as a gesture of gratitude for saving their sons life. In Manisa, Schinasi was forced to leave school in order to work as a guard at a Jewish cemetery. Although the cemetery was destroyed in 1878 after the Turko-Russian War and it is difficult to determine the exact cemetery Schinasi worked at. 
 Schinasi was illiterate and was fired at age 15 when he failed to direct a family to their relatives grave. Later in his life, at a convention in Athens, Greece he asked someone to read for him because he was illiterate. The…

s.d: At fifteen years old, Morris and his brother Solomon moved to Alexandria with just two Mecidye (Imperial gold coins) to their names. For twenty years the brothers worked as tobacco merchants under the mentorship of a man named Garofollo. In 1883, the Otttoman Public Debt Assocaition established a state monopoly over the tobacco industry in the form of state company called the Regie. British-occupied Egypt was outside of the jurisdiction of the Regie, making Alexandria a crucial port for tobacco growers in the Ottoman Empire. This move served to enrich the Schinasi's and provide them with connections with tobacco farms throughout Turkey.
s.cr: Source: By Marsupium - Own work, CC BY 4.0

s.d: In 1890, at 35 years old Morris Schinasi immigrates to New York City. With fifteen years of experience in the industry under the tutelage of of Garofollo, the Morris Schinassi et out for America. He was given a $25,000 loan from his boss and set out for Ellis Island. After a few years in New York, with business thriving Morris paid back his lone to Garroflo and arranged for his brother Solomon to immigrate to the United States.

s.t: 1893: The Chicago World's Fair and a New Factory
s.d: 1893 was a watershed year for the Schasi Brothers Tobacco Company. The pair opened up their first small factory at 48 Broad Street in New York City, and displayed their innovative cigarette rolling machin at a manufacturing exhibition at the Chicago's World Fair. The international symposium showing off the advances of the Industrial Revolution attracted 27 million visitors. Their presence at the fair put the Schassi Brothers brand on the map as the leading innovators in the tobacco industry.

s.t: Schinasi Brother's Cigarette Manufactory: 120th Street & Broadway, New York City, USA (1903)
s.loc: 120th Street & Broadway, New York City, USA
s.d:
Morris Schinasi and his brother Solomon, founded Schinasi Brothers in New York City. Together, they produced ready made cigarettes under the brand name "Natural" at their factory on 120th Street and Broadway. 
 The brothers only used Turkish grown tobacco rather than Virginia grown tobacco.
 The business grew rapidly and the brothers were millionaires by 1900. They employed 100s of Sephardic Jews from the Ottoman Empire in their factories, helping to establish the flourishing Sephardic community in the city.
Business trip to Salonica, modern-day Thessaloniki, then part of the Ottoman Empire.
s.cr: Source: Devin Naar, University of Washington

s.d: On the business trip to Salonica Morris Schinasi met Laurette Schinasi (née Ben Rubi), the 16-year-old granddaughter of his business partner Joseph Ben Rubi. They married in 1903 and had three daughters: Victoria, Juliette, and Altina. Their daughter Altina Schinasi would go on to become a renowned American sculptor, filmmaker, entrepreneur, inventor, and designer—best known for creating the iconic Harlequin cat-eye glasses frame popularized in the 1950s and 1960s.

In 1904, the Natural, Prettiest and Royal blends of tobacco proved to be incredibly popular. With then state of the art Ludington machines, and blends that called for 20,000 pounds of tobacco for each mix, the Schinasi brothers needed to expand.

They moved from 48 Broad street to a six story building on West 120th Street in Harlem. Seeking to give back to the Sephardic Jewish Community, the Schinasi brothers employed large numbers of immigrants from Turkey and Ionnaia, Greece. For their first years in business a majority of their workers came from Ionnaia; however, after the Balkan War in 1912, the Schinassis' workforce came primarily from Manisa and Smyrna.

Morris Schinassi took annual trips to the brothers' tobacco warehouse in Kavala, Greece where he oversaw the selection of tobacco plants for their Ottoman blends in high demand. Each block of tobacco mixture weighed roughly 20,000 pounds.

s.loc: West 107th Street & 351 Riverside, New York City, United States of America
s.d:
In 1907 Morris Schinasi comissioned a 12,000 square foot, 35 room, marble mansion on 351 Riverside Drive on the Upper West Side of Manhattan. It is now the largest un-attached family residence in Manhattan 
 Morris Schinasi lived in the home with his wife Laurette, and three daughters, Victoria, Juliette, and Altina Schinasi until he died in 1928. The family then sold the home for 200,000 in 1928 after his death. The Schinasi house has been home to many organizations including Columbia University, a girls finishing school, and is now owned by Mark Schwartz, vice chairman at Goldman Sachs. The mansion was designed by the architect of Carnegie Hall, William Tuthill.

s.loc: West 107th Street & 351 Riverside, New York City, United States of America
s.d: The mansion is designed in the French Renaissance style- but in a nod to his Middle Eastern roots-features Egyptian marble and Turkish glass.
Today the mansion is on featured on the National Register of Historic Landmarks.

s.t: Morris Schinasi elected President of the Federation of Oriental Jews (1914)
s.loc: 91st Forsythe Street, New York City, United States of America
s.d:
Morris Schinasi worked with many Jewish organizations throughout his successfull career. His tobacco business provided work for many Jewish immigrants in the 1900's and he continued to support the community until his death and through his legacy. 
 The brothers were members of the Anatolian Sephardim Union and Peace Society as well as the Shearith Israel Synagogue in New York. On June 7th, 1914 the Federation of Oriental Jews, elected Morris Schinasi Honorary President at an event with over 1,000 Sephardic Jews on Forsythe Street.

s.t: 1915-16: A Lawsuit and a Company Sale
s.d: In 1915, the Schinasi brothers took a Russian Jewish cigarette company- owned by Louis, Michael, & Abraham Schinasi- to court for using their last name to give the impression that they were selling the same product as the already established Turkish Schnasis. Given that the Schnasi Brothers had done acts of charity for the Ashkenazi Jewish community and did not want that relatioship to be meddled with. Further illustrating the tensions between the two communities, the Russian Schinasis said that only they could have customers in the Russian Jewish community because of their shared heritage. A year after the dispute was settled, the Schinasi brothers sold their tobacco company to the American…

s.t: Schinasi brothers sell the cigarette factory & company (1916)
s.loc: 120th Street & Broadway, New York City, USA
s.d: In 1916, the brother sold the business for $3.5 million dollars and retired from business life.

s.d: Morris Schinasi died in 1928 leaving the estate of over $5 million dollars to his wife and three daughters. He is buried at the Fresh Pond Crematory and Columbarium.

Schinasi was well known for his committment to hiring Sephardic Jewish immigrants from the Ottoman Empire and for his philanthropy. His most most legacy can be seen in the form of the Morris Schinasi Children's hospital in Manisa, Turkey. Schinasi bequeathed one million dollars to construct the hospital in his will.

Doña Gracia Nasi was born Beatriz de Luna in 1510 in Lisbon, into a converso family descended from Spanish exiles. Her early life unfolded in the shadow of forced conversion, after Portugal’s coerced baptisms of 1497 reshaped Jewish life and pushed many families into public Christianity and private Jewish memory.
Although raised outwardly as a Christian, Gracia inherited the networks, loyalties, and hidden solidarities of Iberian crypto-Jewish society. Those foundations later shaped her public return to Judaism, her protection of persecuted conversos, and her emergence as one of the most influential Sephardic women of the sixteenth century.

In 1528, Gracia married Francisco Mendes, also known by the Jewish name Meir, a leading figure in the Benveniste banking dynasty. Through this marriage she entered the world of Iberian and Atlantic commerce, including spices, textiles, precious stones, credit, and long-distance finance.
After Francisco’s death in 1535, Gracia became guardian of her daughter’s inheritance and a central actor in the family business. Her command of converso mercantile networks made her both a formidable strategist and a protector of relatives, clients, and refugees navigating the dangers of Inquisition-era Europe.
s.cr: Local media file / Lisbon commemoration image

s.d:
With the Portuguese Inquisition looming, Gracia relocated in 1536 to Antwerp, one of Europe’s great commercial centers. Working with her brother-in-law Diogo Mendes, she helped coordinate international banking operations across ports, courts, and family houses.
Antwerp became both an economic headquarters and a strategic refuge. From there, Gracia quietly supported escape routes for persecuted conversos, using commerce, credit, and kinship to move people and assets through hostile territory. Yet Spanish imperial power made the city only a temporary sanctuary.

Seeking greater security, Gracia moved to Venice in the 1540s, entering a city where trade, diplomacy, and suspicion closely overlapped. There she faced arrest amid political and financial rivalries, revealing the precarious position of wealthy conversos in Catholic territories.
Venice marked a turning point in her life. The tension between public Catholic identity and private Jewish loyalty intensified, pushing Gracia toward a decisive break with Iberian concealment. Her experience there sharpened her determination to seek a setting where she could live openly as a Jew.

In Ferrara, under the more tolerant Este dukes, Gracia could live more openly as a Jew. She supported Hebrew printing and the Ferrara Bible of 1553, a Spanish translation that helped conversos reconnect with Jewish scripture and learning.
Ferrara represents Gracia’s transition from crypto-Jewish financier to public Jewish patron and communal leader. Her later institutions in Constantinople, including traditions associated with the Academy of the Giveret and the Synagogue of the Señora, continued this wider program of supporting refugees and rebuilding Sephardic life.

By 1552, Gracia arranged the storage of merchandise in Ragusa, now Dubrovnik, using the city’s Adriatic neutrality and trading privileges. The maritime republic offered a practical waystation between Catholic Europe and the expanding Ottoman sphere.
Ragusa symbolized Gracia’s mastery of Mediterranean logistics. Goods, documents, credit, and people could be shifted through its commercial networks as she moved eastward. The city became a bridge toward the Ottoman world she increasingly saw as a haven for Jewish renewal.

Arriving in Constantinople, now Istanbul, under Sultan Suleiman I, Gracia entered the Ottoman Empire with remarkable prestige. Freed from Inquisitorial threat, she openly embraced Judaism and used her wealth, household, and diplomatic reach to support Sephardic refugees.
Her household became a center of Sephardic influence, linking Iberian exiles across the Mediterranean. In Constantinople, Gracia patronized scholars, communal institutions, and relief efforts, helping shape Ottoman-Jewish political life and the memory of the Mendes-Nasi family.

In 1558, Gracia secured a firman to rebuild Tiberias as a semi-autonomous Jewish settlement in Ottoman Palestine. She envisioned agricultural production and textile manufacture that could sustain Sephardic refugees and create a durable communal base.
Although only partly realized, the Tiberias project stands as one of the earliest modern attempts at organized Jewish territorial restoration. It reflected Gracia’s unusual blend of pragmatism, political access, philanthropy, and messianic aspiration.

s.t: Origins in Spain and Expulsion Hesca (Huesca), Spain
s.d:
The Pariente family is believed to have originated in Spain, with the earliest recorded ancestor being Samuel Pariente, who appeared in documents from Hesca in 1489 facing the Inquisition. After the expulsion of Jews from Spain in 1492, records show a Rabi Yaakov Pariente settling in Fez, Morocco, marking the family's initial relocation due to persecution. Using censuses, legal records, notarial deeds, and family petitions, the talk reconstructs a network built on trade, diplomacy, and kinship.
Jacob Marache is an admin of NAJMA, the Moroccan-Jewish group, and a Geni.com curator. His work includes publishing on Tetuan's Jewish history, transcribing Tangier cemetery and Mogador's Beth Din…

Fez was a site of both opportunity and crisis for the Pariente family. While some family members lived there briefly, they ultimately left the city due to episodes of instability and rising tensions. Fez’s long-standing Jewish scholarly tradition may have shaped the family’s outlook, but economic hardship and social unrest pushed them to relocate to safer and more prosperous cities like Meknes.

s.t: Settlement in Larache under Spanish Protection
s.d: In 1610, during a period of shifting Spanish-Moroccan relations, Solomon Pariente played a diplomatic role by aiding in peace treaty negotiations between the two powers. For his contributions, he was granted permission to settle in the Spanish-controlled enclave of Larache. His influence allowed him to live outside the Jewish quarter, indicating his exceptional status within both communities.

The Pariente family rose to prominence in Tangier in the 19th century. Moses Pariente established what is considered the first modern bank in Morocco in 1840. This institution became a cornerstone of Moroccan Jewish economic life and functioned for over a century, ceasing operations shortly before Moroccan independence in 1956. This period cemented the family’s reputation for wealth and influence.

Tetouan was a regional hub where members of the Pariente family maintained trade links and extended kin networks. Although not a primary place of settlement, the city played a role in the family’s mobility between inland centers like Meknes and Mediterranean ports. Tetouan’s strong Judeo-Spanish heritage and mercantile culture resonated with the family’s linguistic and commercial background.

Fidala, a coastal town later renamed Mohammedia, was a temporary stop for members of the Pariente family during their transition from Meknes to Casablanca. Its strategic location near the Atlantic and growing industrial port made it a practical waypoint. While they did not settle there permanently, Fidala served as a logistical bridge in the family's migration toward urban centers with greater economic opportunity.

Saul Pariente, later known as Saul De Leo, and her two sisters are believed to have moved from Tetouan or Tangier to Gibraltar around 1839. Their migration was part of a broader pattern of Moroccan Jews moving to British Gibraltar for economic and social stability. Despite local traditions that claimed their origin was in Livorno, records indicate Moroccan birthplaces, possibly reflecting efforts to Europeanize their identity post-migration.

Amid the siege of Gibraltar in 1779, many Jewish families fled to France. Abraham and Yona Pariente settled in Nice, where they established businesses and integrated into local Jewish society. Records show the family remained in Nice for decades, marrying into other Sephardic families, owning property, and conducting commercial activities. Their time in Nice marked a phase of relative prosperity and adaptation to European norms.

s.t: Later Generations in Oran and Return to Gibraltar
s.d: By the early 19th century, some descendants of the Pariente family moved to Oran, Algeria, while others returned to Gibraltar. This return migration saw the reintegration of the family into the Jewish community there. Census records and grave inscriptions document their presence and suggest a continued engagement in trade and communal life, particularly in the tobacco industry.

s.t: Pisa, Italy - Sidur Printing and Claims to Lineage
s.d: In 1815, a siddur was printed in Pisa under the sponsorship of Abraham Pariente and his sons. The introductory texts proclaimed their descent from King David and the exiles of Jerusalem, likely to assert noble lineage and religious authority. This publication reflects both a desire for prestige and a strategic self-representation common among Sephardic elites of the time.

The Pariente family established itself in Livorno after leaving North Africa or Iberia, drawn by the city’s status as a free port and haven for Sephardi Jews. They integrated into Livorno’s commercial networks and maintained religious practices in one of Europe’s most vibrant Sephardi communities.
s.cr: Source: Samuel Gruber's Jewish Art & Monuments

s.d: Pariente family members passed through Menorca during a transitional phase in their migration. While they did not settle there permanently, Menorca offered temporary refuge—likely under British control—during the family's movement across the western Mediterranean.

A branch of the Pariente family reached London in the 18th or early 19th century. There, they became part of the growing Sephardi community, engaging in trade and maintaining connections with relatives in Livorno, Gibraltar, and the Caribbean. London's relative openness to Jews offered the family legal protections and new opportunities.

Marseilles served as a critical point of transit for the Pariente family in the 19th and 20th centuries. On journeys between Morocco and Europe, family members stopped in Marseilles, sometimes for extended stays, navigating both the Jewish communal structures and the challenges of migration bureaucracy.

While there is no definitive evidence that the Pariente family lived in Amsterdam, family correspondence and naming patterns suggest intellectual influence and religious alignment with Amsterdam’s Sephardi traditions. The city’s prominence shaped the family's diasporic identity and legal thinking.

Meknes was one of the early and stable homes of the Pariente family. Several generations lived there as merchants, scholars, and community members. The family contributed to the city’s rich Jewish cultural and economic life before relocating due to shifting political and economic conditions.
s.cr: Old Jewish School in Meknes. Source: Wikipedia Commons

s.d: In the early 20th century, the Pariente family moved to Casablanca, seeking urban opportunities and the relative stability offered by French colonial rule. Casablanca became the family’s final home in Morocco before later migrations to Europe and the Americas.

s.t: Roots in Porto: The Birthplace of the Teixeira-Fernandes Family
s.loc: New Christian neighborhood and mercantile center.
s.d: Porto was the family’s ancestral home and a hub for New Christians after the forced conversions of 1497. It was home to key figures like Bento Teixeira and Miguel Fernandes, embedded in mercantile networks but also subject to constant suspicion. The Rua de São Miguel was a New Christian stronghold. Porto symbolizes the family’s Iberian roots and the tensions of hidden faith under watchful eyes.

s.t: Lisbon: Crossroads of Empire and Inquisition
s.d: Lisbon was central to the family’s trials and destinies. It hosted the Tribunal of the Portuguese Inquisition that judged Bento Teixeira, and it served as the gateway between Portugal and the Atlantic colonies. Lisbon embodied both opportunity for New Christians seeking fortune overseas and danger as the seat of religious persecution.

s.t: Espírito Santo: First Steps in Brazil
s.d: Espírito Santo was where Bento Teixeira initially settled after arriving in Brazil as a child. It was an early site of Portuguese colonial presence and New Christian activity. The region symbolizes the family’s first encounter with Brazil’s colonial society, its opportunities, and emerging religious tensions.

s.t: Tapera: A Quiet Corner of Colonial Brazil
s.d: Tapera, while less documented, is listed as a location where Bento Teixeira resided during his early years in Brazil. It marks part of his trajectory through Brazilian colonial settlements and the formation of his identity in the new world.

s.t: Rio de Janeiro: A Colonial Metropolis in the Making
s.d: Bento Teixeira spent part of his youth in Rio de Janeiro, absorbing colonial culture and Jesuit teaching. The city was a burgeoning colonial center crucial to trade and New Christian communities, providing both cultural formation and exposure to inquisitorial suspicion.

s.t: Ilhéus: Marriage and Life in the Sugar Economy
s.d: Ilhéus was one of Bento Teixeira’s residences in Brazil, where he married Felipa Raposa, an Old Christian woman. It was also a sugar-producing region with a significant colonial population, embedding New Christians in local society while exposing them to scrutiny.

s.loc: Colonial town, site of Latin school.
s.d: Igarassu was where Bento Teixeira opened a Latin grammar school. It’s significant for showing how New Christians like Teixeira engaged publicly in teaching and cultural life, even while privately facing suspicions of Judaizing.

s.t: Olinda: Center of New Christian Life and Peril
s.d: Olinda, with a large New Christian community, was where Bento Teixeira became entangled in a scandal that ended with him killing his wife. It was also a major location during the Inquisition’s visitation in the late 16th century, highlighting the dangers New Christians faced in colonial Brazil.

s.t: Recife: Gateway to Trial and Exile
s.loc: Port city, trade hub, Inquisition departure point.
s.d: Recife was a key port in colonial Brazil. It was the port from which Bento Teixeira was shipped back to Lisbon as a prisoner of the Inquisition. It reflects the connection between Atlantic commerce and inquisitorial surveillance.

s.loc: Refuge city under Livornine privileges, mercantile activity.
s.d: Pisa became a place of refuge for Miguel Fernandes and his family after leaving Portugal. Under the Livornine, New Christians could settle there with greater freedom. Pisa reflects the shifting opportunities and continued dangers faced by Iberian converts in the Mediterranean.

s.t: Venice: A Mediterranean Crossroads for Marranos
s.d: Venice offered Iberian converts the possibility to openly practice Judaism and join the new Sephardic community. Though none of the immediate Teixeira-Fernandes family settled there permanently, members were tried in Venice’s Inquisition courts, showing the complex intersections of religion and identity.

s.t: Milan: Trials and Testimonies in the North
s.d: Milan was the site of inquisitorial proceedings against Beatriz Dias, a descendant of the family. It reveals how family networks extended into the Spanish territories of Italy and how inquisitorial reach followed them.

s.t: Livorno: The Tuscan Haven for New Christians
s.loc: Trade port, refuge for New Christians.
s.d: Livorno, near Pisa, became a crucial settlement for Iberian New Christians under the Livornine edicts. Though the family mainly settled in Pisa, the entire region symbolized new horizons for mercantile and religious freedom.
s.cr: Source: Samuel Gruber's Jewish Art & Monuments

s.loc: Sephardic community center, religious and intellectual crossroads.
s.d: Amsterdam stands as a symbolic endpoint for this diaspora story, where relatives like Uriel da Costa ultimately embraced Judaism. It illustrates the final step of religious reinvention, albeit fraught with tension even within Jewish communities.

s.t: Birthplace of the Cohen de Azevedo Line
s.d: Lisbon was the point of origin for the Cohen de Azevedo (or D'Azevedo) family before their migration in the 17th century. Many members were born here, including Isaac and Moses, prior to fleeing persecution during the Portuguese Inquisition. Though Lisbon’s Jewish archives were largely destroyed in the 1755 earthquake, it remains central to the family's Sephardic heritage. This site marks their forced conversion context and the beginning of their diasporic journey, later shaping their communal roles in Western Europe and the Atlantic.
s.cr: Engraving or painting of 17th-century Lisbon, ideally the Alfama district. Source: Wikipedia Commons

s.t: Formation of a Sephardic Pillar in Amsterdam
s.d: Amsterdam served as a safe haven and center of communal rebirth for the Cohen de Azevedo family. After fleeing Iberian persecution, Isaac Cohen de Azevedo joined the Portuguese Jewish community in 1640. He became a key figure, serving in roles such as treasurer and member of Dotar. This city marks the family's establishment within the Western Sephardic elite, from which they later migrated to Hamburg, London, and the Americas.
s.cr: Interior of the Portuguese Synagogue (Esnoga) in Amsterdam

s.t: Final Resting Place of Isaac Cohen de Azevedo
s.d: Hamburg became the unexpected final destination of Isaac Cohen de Azevedo, a key patriarch of the family. In 1675, he was buried in the Sephardic cemetery in Altona, with his gravestone noting his lineage as 'Isaac Daniel Azevedo'. Though most migration trends moved westward, his move reflects the fluidity and interconnectedness of Jewish trade routes. Hamburg’s Jewish cemetery retains historical value as a witness to this migration turn and burial tradition.
s.cr: Photograph of the Jewish Cemetery in Altona, Hamburg

s.t: Birthplace of the Cohen de Azevedo Line
s.d: Lisbon was the birthplace of many Cohen de Azevedo ancestors before they fled during the Portuguese Inquisition. It represents the family's forced conversion and underground Jewish life, prior to their emergence in the Western Sephardic diaspora.
s.cr: Engraving of 17th-century Lisbon, ideally Alfama district

s.t: Formation of a Sephardic Pillar in Amsterdam
s.d: Amsterdam provided sanctuary and opportunity. Isaac Cohen de Azevedo joined the Portuguese Jewish community in 1640. He held posts in charity, administration, and trade. Amsterdam became the family's principal European base for generations.

s.t: Final Resting Place of Isaac Cohen de Azevedo
s.d: Isaac died in Hamburg and was buried in its Sephardic cemetery in 1675. This reflects the fluidity of Western Sephardic trade routes, even against dominant migration patterns.
s.cr: Photograph of Jewish Cemetery in Altona, Hamburg

s.d: In London, members of the Cohen de Azevedo family held religious and communal leadership at Bevis Marks. This includes Joseph, Moses, and Daniel, who served as hazanim and elders in the 18th and 19th centuries.
Moses Cohen de Azevedo served as Dutch consul and specialist in freeing Christian slaves in Salé, Morocco, demonstrating diplomatic and economic influence in North Africa.
s.cr: Hiloula for Saint Rabbi Raphael Encaoua in Salé

s.d: In 1802, Daniel Cohen de Azevedo emigrated to Jamaica to serve as hazan, joining a thriving Sephardic community. This marked the family's Caribbean establishment, with descendants spreading into the Americas.
Moses, son of Benjamin, kept a business diary noting travel through Suriname. This entry highlights the Caribbean trading activity of the family as part of wider Atlantic networks.
s.cr: Historic Jewish quarter in Paramaribo, Suriname

s.d: Barbados was one of several Caribbean islands where the Cohen de Azevedo descendants engaged in trade. This location served as a hub for sugar and Atlantic commerce.
Martinique is noted as a stop in the business diary of Moses (Benjamin’s son), reflecting the broader French-Caribbean circuit traveled by Sephardic Jewish traders in the 18th century.
Moses, son of Benjamin Cohen de Azevedo, died in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, after traveling through the Caribbean. This marks the family’s eventual move to North America and permanent settlement.
s.cr: Rebecca Gratz educator and philanthropist, member of congregation Mikveh Israel. Source: Wikipedia commons

s.d:
The Danino family traces its origins to a distinguished rabbinic lineage that begins with the renowned medieval philosopher and jurist, Moses Maimonides (Rambam). According to the family’s genealogical manuscript, Maimonides’ descendants continued the rabbinic tradition across generations, including figures such as Rabbi David, Rabbi Abraham, and Rabbi Yeshua. This lineage was rooted in Andalusia, especially Córdoba, and later moved to Salamanca, maintaining religious authority and intellectual leadership.
By the early 15th century, the Danino family—known at the time as n’Daninos—was already established in Salamanca. The manuscript notes that Rabbi Yeshua n’Daninos was captured and later…
Rabbi Yeshua Daninos, Rabbi David n’Daninos, Rabbi Isaac n’Daninos. Prosperous Jewish life in Córdoba and later in Salamanca. Rabbi Yeshua Daninos was ransomed from captivity in Salamanca.

s.t: 1458: Rabbi Isaac n’Daninos - Migration to Fez, Morocco
s.d:
Reason: Rising anti-Jewish violence in Spain, including attacks like those in Toledo (1449), led the Danino family to leave before the 1492 expulsion.
Activity: In Fez, they integrated into the emerging megurashim (expelled Jews) community. They contributed to communal governance and rabbinic leadership, including Rabbi Shlomo Danino signing foundational takkanot (communal decrees).
s.cr: Souce: Slat El Fassiyine Synagogue, Wikipedia

s.t: 1526–1537: Shaul Danino, Eliahu Shlomo Danino - Communal Integration
s.d: Participation in agreements and controversies between Spanish megurashim and local toshavim (Jewish residents)

Rabbi Moshe Danino, Isaac Danino, David Danino
Fez ↔ Jerusalem ↔ Dimnat (Morocco)
Reason: Religious pilgrimage, rabbinic missions, and perhaps a desire to return to the Land of Israel.
Activity: The Daninos served as emissaries and scholars. Some descendants were involved in rabbinic correspondence and supported the Jewish community in Jerusalem.

s.t: 1679: Moved from Jerusalem to Dimnat, Morocco
s.d:
Reason: Possibly part of religious outreach or emissary work; the exact trigger is unclear but may include political instability.
Activity: Rabbi David Danino was sent from Jerusalem and died in Dimnat. His presence helped maintain Sephardic rabbinic influence in the Moroccan periphery.
Nehamia Danino was appointed head rabbi of Hebron

In Meknes (Micnasa), the Danino family held prominent rabbinic and communal roles, continuing their Sephardic scholarly tradition. However, in 1792, violent persecution under Sultan Yazid—marked by attacks, looting, and repression of the Jewish population—forced the family to flee. Rabbi Shmuel Danino and his relatives sought refuge in the remote village of Tissint in the Atlas Mountains, marking a significant shift from urban leadership to spiritual guidance in a rural setting, where they continued to preserve their heritage and assist both Jewish and Berber communities.

1792: The Danino´s moved to Tissint due to the persecutions. Jews flee from urban centers to remote mountain areas.
Rabbi Shmuel Danino and his descendants took refuge in Tissint, where they continued rabbinic leadership, educated Jews and Berbers, and documented genealogy.
1932: Birth of Rachel Danino
31 March 1948 (20 Adar 5708): Marriage Rachel Danino & Israel Kadosh

Aït Bou Oulli, a remote village in the High Atlas Mountains, was the birthplace of Israel Kadosh and the home of Rachel Danino after their marriage in 1948. The couple lived there until their migration to Casablanca in 1954. Israel worked as a skin merchant, often walking long distances to Marrakesh to sell his goods, reflecting both the economic hardships and the resilience of Jewish life in the region. Their time in Aït Bou Oulli represents the last generation of the family rooted in the traditional Jewish-Berber rural world before aliyah to Israel.

Reason: Zionist aliyah movement and Moroccan Jewish emigration amid uncertainty before independence.
Activity: The Kadosh-Danino family waited in royal housing in Casablanca before making aliyah. They preserved family documents and traditions in preparation for resettlement.
Rachel Kadosh Danino, and her husband Israel Kadosh moved to Israel

Born in Avignon around 1451, Abraham Farissol emerged from a vibrant Jewish community deeply influenced by the intellectual currents of Provence. This formative environment laid the groundwork for his later engagement with classical texts, biblical exegesis, and humanist inquiry. Though later associated with Italy, Avignon represents the origin of his cultural and religious identity.

s.t: Residence / site of authorship: Ferrara, Italy (Main Residence and Scholarly Activity)
s.d: Ferrara was the center of Farissol's intellectual life. As a court intellectual and communal figure, he flourished in this Este-ruled city known for its tolerance and cultural patronage. Here, Farissol wrote extensively, culminating in Iggeret Orhot Olam—a groundbreaking geographic work that blended Jewish eschatology, contemporary exploration, and classical science.

s.t: Publication site: Venice, Italy (Publication of Orhot Olam – 1586 edition)
s.d: Though Farissol had died decades earlier, the 1586 Venice edition of Iggeret Orhot Olam, printed by Giovanni di Gara, ensured the lasting transmission of his work. Venice, as a hub of Jewish printing, played a pivotal role in disseminating Jewish Renaissance scholarship across Europe and the Mediterranean.

s.t: Intellectual reference point: Lisbon, Portugal (Geographic Knowledge Source)
s.d: While Farissol may never have visited Lisbon, his geographic treatise draws significantly on Portuguese maritime discoveries and cosmographic reports. Lisbon was a critical node in the knowledge networks that fed into Jewish Renaissance thought, making it a symbolic location in his intellectual cartography.

s.t: Jerusalem: Farissol's Cosmic and Spiritual Axis of the World
s.d: Jerusalem occupies a central spiritual and geographic position in Farissol’s worldview. It serves as a theological and cosmographic axis in his text, reflecting both biblical centrality and the longing for redemption.

s.t: Mecca: Acknowledged by Farissol as the Heart of Muslim Pilgrimage
s.d: Mecca is mentioned by Farissol as part of his engagement with Islamic geography, illustrating his broader awareness of the sacred geographies of other monotheistic traditions.

s.t: India: Described by Farissol as a Land of Riches, Wonders, and Wisdom
s.d: India is described in Farissol's text as a distant land filled with wealth, marvels, and wisdom traditions. His reference reflects contemporary interest in the East as shaped by Portuguese discoveries.

s.t: Ethiopia: Cited by Farissol as Home to Jews of Ancient Lineage
s.d: Ethiopia is portrayed as a land of ancient lineage and mysterious Jewish connections. Farissol repeats legends of Jewish kingdoms or priestly descendants, reflecting long-standing rabbinic fascination.

s.t: China: Farissol Recognizes Its Grandeur and Distant Eastern Power
s.d: China appears in Farissol’s text as a distant and wealthy empire, mentioned within his global survey. His awareness reflects an expanding intellectual horizon among Jewish thinkers of the Renaissance.

s.t: Portugal: Source of Farissol’s Knowledge on Oceanic Exploration
s.d: Portugal is a critical reference point in Farissol’s cosmography due to its leading role in maritime exploration. He relies on Portuguese discoveries to inform his descriptions of distant lands.

s.t: Spain: Remembered by Farissol for Its Jewish Past and Expulsion
s.d: Spain is noted both for its role in Jewish exile and for the geographical knowledge arising from Iberian exploration. Farissol refers to it with layered historical and intellectual significance.

s.t: America: Farissol Describes It as a Newly Discovered and Mysterious Land
s.d: Farissol mentions newly discovered lands west of the Atlantic, speculating on their inhabitants. This demonstrates Jewish intellectual response to the discovery of the Americas.

s.t: Turkey: Identified by Farissol as a Center of Jewish Survival Under Ottomans
s.d: Turkey (the Ottoman Empire) is frequently referenced in Jewish writing as both a political reality and a haven for Jews post-1492. Farissol’s inclusion reflects geographic and communal awareness.

s.t: Persia: Farissol Acknowledges Its Ancient Wisdom and Jewish Diaspora
s.d: Persia is mentioned in Farissol’s account as a land of ancient Jewish diaspora and Eastern wisdom. He draws on rabbinic and classical traditions to describe its peoples and customs.

s.t: Syria: Farissol Includes It as a Key Biblical Territory
s.d: Farissol includes Syria in his geographic writings as a key biblical and historical region. Its cities and terrain are associated with both ancient Jewish history and Christian pilgrimage.

s.t: Babylon: Farissol Reflects on It as a Symbol of Exile and Jewish Learning
s.d: Babylon, located in present-day Iraq, figures in Farissol's writing as the locus of Jewish exile and diaspora. He treats it as both a historical memory and a cultural site.

s.t: Egypt: Noted by Farissol for Its Biblical Significance and Continued Presence
s.d: Egypt appears throughout Farissol’s text as a site of biblical memory, diasporic settlement, and neighboring influence. It is considered both a historical and contemporary reference point.

s.t: Medina: Cited by Farissol in the Context of Muslim Sacred Geography
s.d: Medina, alongside Mecca, appears in Farissol’s awareness of Muslim sacred geography. It is treated with respect and integrated into his broader cosmological mapping.

s.t: Rome: Farissol Recognizes It as the Seat of Christian Power
s.d: Rome is mentioned as both the seat of Christian power and a historical point of Jewish diaspora. Farissol recognizes its significance in theological and political terms.

s.t: Greece: Farissol Credits It with Philosophical Foundations of the West
s.d: Greece is cited in Farissol’s cosmography for its philosophical heritage and historical Jewish presence. He sees it as part of the intellectual genealogy of the West.

s.t: Canary Islands: Farissol Mentions Them as Edge of the Known Atlantic World
s.d: The Canary Islands are described in Farissol’s survey of the Atlantic. Their mention reflects Portuguese exploration and speculation on distant Jewish settlements or exotic peoples.

s.t: Sambation: Farissol Describes the Mythical River That Guards the Lost Tribes
s.d: The Sambation River, which ceases to flow on Shabbat, represents one of the most enduring Jewish mythical geographies. Farissol’s inclusion connects cosmography to rabbinic imagination.

s.t: Childhood Migration from Jewish Plovdiv to Ottoman Istanbul (Father’s Early Years).
s.d:
Salomón Karmona, Moscona’s father, was born in Plovdiv, a Bulgarian city with a deep Sephardic Jewish presence. His childhood movement from Plovdiv to Ottoman Istanbul reflects the mobility of Balkan Jews whose families crossed borders while preserving household languages, kinship ties, and communal memory.
In Tela de sevoya, this migration is remembered through Ladino phrases, family warnings, and the texture of spoken inheritance. The move from Plovdiv to Istanbul marks an early passage in a wider Sephardic itinerary, where language becomes both shelter and proof of belonging.

s.t: Return to Plovdiv from Istanbul Before WWII and Rising Anti-Jewish Laws. Istanbul return to Plovdiv (Pre-WWII)
s.d:
After growing up in Istanbul, Salomón returned to Plovdiv before the Second World War. The route between the Bosphorus and Bulgaria captures a world in transition: Ottoman Sephardic networks still shaped family life, even as nationalism and antisemitic laws narrowed the possibilities of Jewish belonging.
Moscona’s phrase “Kada suvida tiene su abashada” gives this passage its emotional form: every rise has its descent. The return to Plovdiv is therefore not simply geographic; it foreshadows rupture, danger, and the fragile uncertainty of Balkan Jewish life before World War II.

s.t: Attempted Deportation of Bulgarian Jews During WWII – Saved at the Last Minute (1944)
s.d:
During World War II, Bulgarian Jews faced antisemitic laws, arrests, and the threat of deportation. Moscona’s father was detained for deportation with other Jews, but the convoy was stopped before departure, placing his survival inside the larger history of the contested rescue of Bulgarian Jewry.
This episode gives the map one of its most charged points: Sofia becomes a site of state violence, suspended catastrophe, and reprieve. In the family narrative, survival is not abstract history; it is the narrow hinge on which later migration, memory, and Moscona’s own life depend.

s.t: Post-Holocaust Migration to Mexico and Cultural Adaptation in Ladino
s.d:
After the devastation of war, Moscona’s family migrated to Mexico City, where Esther Benaroya and other relatives had to build a new life in an unfamiliar country. Spanish sounded close to Ladino, yet also strange, altered, and sometimes comic in the ears of Sephardic immigrants from Bulgaria and Turkey.
The grandmother’s reflections on Mexican speech turn migration into a linguistic encounter. Mexico becomes both refuge and translation: a place where Sephardic memory survives by adapting, where old words meet new accents, foods, streets, and forms of Jewish communal life.
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons / Historic Synagogue Justo Sierra 71 image

s.t: Return to Sofia Synagogue: A Poetic Pilgrimage to Jewish Memory in Bulgaria. (2000s)
s.d:
Moscona’s return to the Sofia Synagogue becomes a pilgrimage into the layered memory of Bulgarian Jewish life. The building stands as an architectural and communal witness: a place where prayer, rescue, loss, and postwar disappearance all press against the present.
The saying “Konoshe frente a ken estas parado” frames the visit as an ethical encounter with the past. To stand inside Sofia’s Jewish space is to face ancestors, absences, and the responsibility of listening to what remains after migration and silence.

s.t: Encounter with the Gendered Sacred: Visit to the Rila Monastery in Bulgaria
s.d:
At the Rila Monastery, Moscona encounters a sacred space shaped by Orthodox Christian monastic tradition and by rules of gendered separation. The visit opens a meditation on women, exclusion, curiosity, and the limits placed on bodies and voices inside religious worlds.
Her grandmother’s Ladino warning about Mount Athos, monks, and forbidden questions turns the monastery into a mirror for Sephardic women’s memory. The scene links Bulgaria, family storytelling, and female spiritual alienation, making sacred geography part of Moscona’s search for inheritance.

s.t: Family Reconnections and Ladino Heritage Archives: Meeting León Karmona in Sofia
s.d:
In Sofia, Moscona meets her cousin León Karmona, whose family archive preserves thousands of Ladino proverbs. The encounter transforms genealogy into a living archive: kinship is not only bloodline, but also phrases, sayings, jokes, and forms of recognition passed from mouth to mouth.
The phrase “Dos personas ke se buscan siempre sabran rekonoserse” gives the meeting its emotional logic. In this chapter, Sofia becomes a place of reconnection, where personal search meets communal memory and where endangered language briefly regains a social home.

s.t: First Burial in Sephardic Cemetery, Mexico (1942)
s.d:
The first burial in Mexico’s new Sephardic cemetery marks the establishment of a communal landscape for immigrants who had carried memory across continents. In Moscona’s family story, death becomes one of the ways a displaced community takes root in Mexico City.
The blessing “Ke mos veamos en alegriyas” holds grief and future hope together. Around the cemetery, Sephardic language, ritual, and kinship create a new geography of belonging, where mourning also becomes a promise that the community will meet again in joy.

s.t: From Sarajevo to Trieste: Echoes of a Shared Language (20th Century)
s.d: Sarajevo, the origin of Clarisse's parents, represents a core of oral transmission of Judeo-Spanish and a crossroads of Balkan and Sephardic traditions.

s.t: Trieste: Crossroads of Clarisse’s Maternal Lineage
s.d: The mother’s childhood city. A port crucial to 20th-century migratory routes, representing pre-war displacement before Clarisse's father entered the picture.

s.t: Meeting in Barcelona: Love and Memory (1986)
s.d: In 1986, Clarisse's parents reunited in Barcelona, a symbolic city with a deep Jewish history, once vibrant before the 1492 expulsion.
Clarisse was born in Lyon, France, where she grew up surrounded by French, Judeo-Spanish, Serbo-Croatian, and Italian. It marked her linguistic and literary formation.

s.t: Yugoslavia: A Land Without Persecution Memory (Pre-WWII)
s.d: Yugoslavia is described as a land where Judeo-Spanish survived without memory of persecution—until the traumas of WWII and the Ustasha-Nazi alliance.

s.t: Ottoman Turkey: Ancestral Refuge after the Expulsion (1492)
s.d: Clarisse's grandparents arrived in the 'Ottoman Turkish' lands after 1492. Turkey served as a critical safe haven in Sephardic history.

s.t: Spain 1492: Origin of Exile and the Lost Language
s.d: Spain represents both the cultural origin and the historical wound of expulsion. Judeo-Spanish emerged as a diasporic language from this rupture.

Itzhak Ben Rubí was born in Serres, Greece, on March 25, 1903, into a family with rabbinical and medical heritage. His early upbringing reflected a blend of traditional and liberal Jewish values, shaped in part by his father's pharmaceutical profession and his mother's lineage from a banking family in Istanbul.

s.t: Relocation after Balkan Wars and 1913 Fire
s.d: After the 1913 fire that destroyed parts of Serres and as a result of the Balkan Wars, Ben Rubí's family relocated to Thessaloniki, where he pursued studies at the Mission Laïque Française. This period was key to his intellectual development and his early exposure to Sephardic cultural currents.

Ben Rubí continued his studies in Paris, forming a meaningful relationship with the playwright Henry Marx. He participated in literary and philosophical circles and contributed to French publications. This period deepened his cultural synthesis between Judeo-Spanish and European modernity.

Upon returning to Thessaloniki, Ben Rubí married Dora Camhi and managed the Austro-Hellénique Tobacco Co., employing mostly Jewish workers. He became deeply involved in Zionist and communal work, building leadership skills that would later define his literary and activist roles.

After fighting in the Greek army during WWII, Ben Rubí evaded Nazi persecution by hiding in Athens with the help of righteous Greek allies. The period of clandestinity solidified his connection to Jewish resistance and identity, later influencing his novels and dramatic works.

s.t: Post-war Aliyah and integration in Israel
s.d: In 1945, Ben Rubí immigrated to Tel Aviv as a Youth Aliyah leader, bringing 250 Greek-Jewish youth to Palestine. He integrated into Israeli society, contributing to the cultural integration of Sephardic immigrants and building a Judeo-Spanish literary presence in the new state.

s.t: Cultural hub of his later years
s.d: Ben Rubí's home on Arlozorov Street became a cultural salon for Sephardic intellectuals, actors, and writers. He led radio shows like “Aki vos Avla Chimon-Chimon,” edited El Tiempo, and translated Hebrew and French poetry into Ladino, establishing himself as a pivotal figure of Sephardic cultural revival.

During the late 1950s, Ben Rubí toured Cuba and Mexico as a representative of Keren Hayesod. His 'Impresiones de Viaje' reflect his engagement with diaspora communities and helped build bridges between Sephardic Jews of the Americas and Israel.

Ben Rubí passed away in 1977 and was buried at Nahalat Itzhak, a historic cemetery in Tel Aviv. His grave marks the resting place of a prolific figure in Sephardic cultural preservation. Posthumously honored by the city and international communities, his voice continues through archives and re-editions.

Moïse S. Gadol was born in 1874 in Rostchuck, today Ruse, Bulgaria, into a modest Sephardic Jewish family. Educated at the local Alliance Israélite Universelle school, he developed early ties to Jewish communal life, language learning, and Zionist organizing.
Ruse, a Danube port shaped by Ottoman, Balkan, and European exchange, gave Gadol the multilingual and commercial world that later defined his work. Before leaving for America, he worked as a clerk, salesman, and soldier while helping found the city’s first Zionist society, joining practical self-education with a lifelong commitment to Sephardic public life.

In May 1910, at age 36, Moïse Gadol came to New York City to visit his mother. What began as a family visit became a turning point when he encountered a Ladino-speaking Sephardic immigrant community that felt isolated from larger Jewish institutions.
Gadol recognized that these immigrants needed more than charity: they needed a shared language, practical guidance, and a public voice. His response was to remain in New York and use the Ladino press as a tool for advocacy, education, and communal belonging, turning a personal trip into the beginning of a public mission.

On November 11, 1910, Moïse Gadol launched La América at 190 Chrystie Street in New York. The weekly newspaper became the first enduring Ladino newspaper in the United States and a national forum for Sephardic readers.
La América published news, literature, commentary, and practical lessons for immigrants. Gadol used its pages to promote Zionism, workers’ rights, English and Yiddish learning, and a modern sense of Sephardic identity in America, giving readers a place to see their language and concerns treated as central.

s.t: Founder of La America, the first Ladino newspaper in the US
s.d:
By April 1911, La América had moved to 250 Eldridge Street, reflecting its growing readership and stronger place within the Lower East Side’s Sephardic world. The newspaper gave Ladino-speaking immigrants a rare public space of their own.
Gadol’s publishing work linked journalism with community service. His paper addressed immigration, work, language, civic life, and culture, helping Sephardic newcomers navigate America without losing the memory and dignity of their own Ladino heritage.

Around July 1913, La América operated from 197 Eldridge Street, another address in the dense immigrant landscape of New York’s Lower East Side. From there, Gadol continued to turn the newspaper into a civic platform.
Through La América, he promoted workers’ advancement, individual initiative, and women’s rights. Articles by a writer known as “Miss A” pushed gender equality into public conversation, showing how Ladino journalism could carry progressive ideas into Sephardic homes and reshape expectations within the community.

s.t: Livro de Embezar las linguas Ingleza i Yudish
s.d:
In 1916, Moïse S. Gadol published Livro de Embezar las linguas Ingleza i Yudish, a Ladino-language guide for learning English and Yiddish. The booklet was designed for Sephardic Jewish immigrants trying to understand American life.
More than a language manual, it offered translations of U.S. immigration laws, citizenship-study material, and descriptions of “la vida Amerikana”, from public parks and skyscrapers to subways and daily customs. It transformed language learning into a practical survival guide and showed how Ladino could explain the new world without abandoning the old one.
s.cr: Stroum Center for Jewish Studies - University of Washington

s.d:
Gadol also advocated beyond the newspaper. He pushed the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society to recognize the needs of Sephardic Jews, who were often overlooked by organizations built around Ashkenazi immigrant experience.
As secretary of the Oriental Bureau, first as a volunteer, he helped newcomers with immigration procedures, employment, legal aid, and translation. His work made Sephardic immigrants more visible within American Jewish relief networks and connected journalism to direct community service.

Despite its influence, La América faced mounting financial pressure and ceased publication in 1925. Gadol tried to support himself through private business, including supplying leather to shoe stores, but his fortunes declined.
The loss of the newspaper was followed by personal sorrow. In 1933, the death of his wife devastated him emotionally, marking a painful final chapter for a man who had spent much of his life building institutions for others and defending the place of Sephardic voices in American Jewish life.

s.t: Joseph Pardo I – From Solona to Venice to Amsterdam (pre-1589 to 1618)
s.d: Joseph Pardo I, the patriarch of the Amsterdam Pardo lineage, was born in Solona (likely Salonika), a major center of Sephardic resettlement in the Ottoman Empire. Before 1589, he relocated to Venice, then a flourishing node of Sephardic Jewish life. In Venice, Pardo became a khakham (rabbi) of the Letin synagogue, which catered to Levantine and Iberian Jews. Around 1608, Joseph Pardo moved to Amsterdam, a newly tolerant city that attracted Marranos and former conversos seeking to rejoin Judaism. There, he was appointed khakham of the Beth Jacob congregation, and later of Beth Israel. He played a foundational role in educating early Portuguese Jewish arrivals and organizing the institutions…
s.cr: Source: Devin Naar, University of Washington

s.t: David Pardo – Continuation in Amsterdam and Service in Charities (1619–1657)
s.d: David Pardo, the son of Joseph Pardo I, was born in Solona before 1589 and followed in his father's rabbinic footsteps. He served as khakham of Beth Israel and was later included among the famous 'Four Rabbis' of Amsterdam following the merger of the three Sephardic congregations in 1639. While less published than his contemporaries, David Pardo was integral to the spiritual and communal life of early Amsterdam Sephardim. Notably, he also held the role of cantor and acted as khakham for the Chevra Kadisha (Bigger Holand), overseeing rituals for the dead. His signature appears in Dotar archives, signifying his continued leadership in charitable initiatives. He was buried alongside his father…

s.t: Joseph Pardo II – Rotterdam, Frankfurt, and the Birth of a New Generation (1652–1670)
s.d: Joseph Pardo II, son of David Pardo, continued the family’s leadership role by serving the small Portuguese Jewish community in Rotterdam. In 1654, he made headlines by seeking a declaration to defend Rebecca Haman’s honor after rumors of an out-of-wedlock pregnancy in Frankfurt, where she had worked.
