s.t: Resettlement and Kin Networks – Tel Aviv/Ramat Gan
s.d:
Arrival in Israel reconfigured displacement into a new form of belonging, mediated by extended family networks and the state’s absorption frameworks. For Iraqi Jews, the Tel Aviv–Ramat Gan area became a major node of settlement, producing dense Iraqi‑Jewish social geographies and a distinctive urban memoryscape. This chapter situates Bassoon’s Israeli phase as both refuge and transition—an intermediate horizon that shaped subsequent migration choices to North America.
• Initial resettlement in the Tel Aviv metropolitan area, where many Iraqi Jewish families clustered.
• Rebuilding family life through kin networks and community institutions in Israel.

s.t: North American Rebuilding – Montreal to Toronto
s.d:
Bassoon’s later life in Canada reflects a broader Iraqi‑Jewish pattern of rebuilding through education, professional retraining, and synagogue‑centered community formation. Montreal and Toronto offered different linguistic and institutional contexts, but both supported durable Iraqi‑Sephardi communal infrastructures. In Canada, minority status was re‑negotiated through citizenship, public safety, and religious continuity, enabling the transformation of refugee experience into multi‑generational stability.
• Immigration to Canada and integration into established Sephardi communal networks.
• Community life articulated through synagogue affiliation and family‑centered social reproduction.

• Born in Fez (8 Nov 1954) into a long-established Jewish family whose parents and earlier generations were deeply rooted in the city’s mellah and communal institutions.
• Family memory emphasizes dense kin networks—many aunts, uncles, and cousins—typical of mid‑20th‑century Moroccan Jewish life, even as emigration accelerated in the 1950s.
• Fez remains a symbolic point of origin: later returns to the cemetery and mellah streets became acts of historical retrieval and reflection on Sephardi continuity.

• Moved to Rabat around age 3–4 (1957/58), where most childhood memories formed in the modern neighborhood of L’Agdal amid a multilingual Mediterranean cityscape.
• Weekly Shabbat meals—structured by preparation, prayer, and hospitality—served as the household’s central ritual framework and a key site of intergenerational transmission.
• Everyday coexistence with Muslims and Europeans was routine in public space (schools, markets, streets), while home visits across communal lines were comparatively limited.
• Experiences of subtle minority surveillance (e.g., being counted in classrooms) and the norm of discretion about Israel shaped a careful public Jewishness.

• Immediately before leaving Morocco, the family gathered in Meknes with close relatives, highlighting how kin households functioned as logistical and emotional hubs during migration.
• A bar mitzvah celebration—held in the midst of departure preparations—condensed family continuity, ritual obligation, and impending rupture into a single moment of passage.
• This stop underscores how mobility in North Africa often moved through extended-family nodes before crossing international borders.

• The departure from Casablanca dramatized the practical constraints of emigration: limited baggage, restricted funds, and reliance on informal facilitation to ensure smooth passage.
• Family recollection foregrounds the role of trusted relatives in navigating bureaucratic thresholds, a common feature of Jewish departures from Morocco in the 1960s.
• Casablanca functions here less as ‘home’ than as a transit infrastructure linking Moroccan Jewish lives to European and North American destinations.

• A short stop in Paris (July 1965) marked entry into a Francophone metropolitan world long idealized through schooling, media, and cultural aspiration.
• The stopover also highlights how migration routes often combined symbolic centers (France) with onward movement to North America rather than permanent settlement.
• Paris served as an immediate linguistic refuge even as it remained a waypoint rather than the family’s final destination.

• Arriving in Montreal (July 1965) through immigrant-aid networks, the family encountered rapid reorientation: new housing, new consumption patterns, and immediate schooling transitions.
• Cohen’s narrative emphasizes ‘freedom’ as a felt contrast—especially in classrooms where corporal punishment was absent and speech felt less constrained.
• Early summer camp and accelerated English acquisition became key mechanisms of integration into Canadian Jewish and civic life.

• A subsequent move to Quebec City placed the family within a small, largely Ashkenazi Jewish community where Moroccan Sephardi presence was rare and highly visible.
• His father’s public role in Judeo‑Christian dialogue and media commentary during the Six‑Day War reflects a distinctive francophone Jewish voice in Quebec’s public sphere.
• Cohen recalls episodic, low-level antisemitism rooted more in ignorance than institutional exclusion, alongside strong attachments to Canadian pluralism.

• Postsecondary study in Ottawa (journalism and later social work) extended the migration narrative into professional formation and North American civic participation.
• These years illustrate the second-generation arc of upward mobility enabled by Canadian higher education and public institutions.
• Ottawa also served as an interprovincial bridge, linking francophone upbringing, anglophone schooling, and emergent academic identity.

• Doctoral training at the University of California, Berkeley in the mid‑1980s positioned Cohen within transnational scholarly circuits in sociology, public health, and social work.
• This chapter underscores how Sephardi diasporic trajectories often moved from migration-for-safety to migration-for-education and professional specialization.
• The U.S. West Coast period became part of a broader intellectual biography grounded in questions of displacement, identity, and social institutions.

s.t: Later Life & Present Context – Miami Beach
s.d:
• By 2001 Cohen relocated to Miami, where the 2011 Sephardi Voices interview reflects on a life structured by repeated moves and the long afterlife of departure from Morocco.
• He frames ‘leaving’ as a defining biographical event shaping memory, identity, and professional commitments, even decades later.
• Miami becomes the contemporary vantage point from which earlier North African, Canadian, and academic chapters are narrated and reinterpreted.

• Born 8 June 1939 in Ouazzane (Wazzan), a small northern Moroccan town positioned between the Spanish and French zones, shaping a borderland Sephardi sensibility attentive to language, authority, and mobility.
• Family memory situates the Elhadad name within Iberian-Sephardi continuities and craft lineages (Hadad as “blacksmith/forgeron”), linking occupational identity to communal prestige and ritual responsibility.
• Early childhood unfolded in a prosperous mercantile household; his father Joseph was a prominent merchant and communal figure, and the family produced multiple leaders of the local Jewish community.

• Asjen, a village about 9 km from Ouazzane, functioned as the Jewish cemetery site because Ouazzane’s status as a Muslim holy city constrained Jewish burial within the town.
• Elhadad recalls grand communal pilgrimages (hillulot) to the tomb of Rabbi Amram ben Diwan, intertwining sacred geography with regional travel, collective memory, and intercommunal negotiation.
• These gatherings also sustained local welfare economies: candle sales and pilgrimage commerce helped support poorer households across the year.

• At 14, Elhadad left Ouazzane for Casablanca, entering Alliance-linked training pathways that professionalized Jewish education in Morocco and produced teachers for a broad North African network.
• He studied five years at the École normale hébraïque (Alliance Israélite Universelle system), a highly competitive, scholarship-supported program that exchanged tuition for post-graduation teaching service.
• This period deepened his engagement with Hebrew pedagogy, scouting formations (pré‑routiers), and clandestine Zionist youth activity under Moroccan restrictions.

• In 1963 he transferred from Casablanca to Tangier, teaching there for nearly two decades and navigating a multilingual port city marked by Spanish, French, Arabic, and Jewish communal institutions. 
• He describes cross-confessional friendships (Catholics, Muslims, Jews) that could coexist in everyday leisure, yet were periodically strained by regional politics—especially during the 1967 war.
• His long tenure illustrates how Moroccan Jewish educators sustained Sephardi liturgy, piyyut traditions, and communal cohesion amid demographic decline and emigration.

• Arriving in Montreal on 10 September 1981, Elhadad entered the North American Sephardi institutional landscape as a Jewish-studies educator, carrying Moroccan pedagogical and liturgical repertoires into a new diasporic setting.
• His narrative highlights transmission work: sustaining Hebrew learning, synagogue soundscapes of Andalusi-inflected piyyutim, and the social ethics of respect embodied in household and communal ritual.
• Through teaching and memory-work, he reframes Moroccan Sephardi life as both locally rooted (Ouazzane/Asjen) and transnational (Casablanca–Tangier–Montreal).

Born in 1945 in Heliopolis, a cosmopolitan district of Cairo, David Roy Shama grew up within Egypt’s affluent Levantine Jewish milieu, shaped by multilingual education and trans-Mediterranean commerce. His family’s position—linked to grain and flour enterprises and to networks spanning Syria, Egypt, and Europe—situated him in an elite yet increasingly precarious minority as Egyptian politics radicalized after 1952. Together, these experiences illuminate the shifting boundaries of belonging for Levantine Jews in mid‑century Egypt.

Although born in Cairo, Shama’s formative years were largely spent in Alexandria, a port city known for Greeks, Armenians, and other Mediterranean communities. He recalls a household staffed by several Muslim employees and a social world organized through extended-family gatherings, beach houses, and club life, reflecting the integration of many Egyptian Jews into upper‑middle-class society. Together, these experiences illuminate the shifting boundaries of belonging for Levantine Jews in mid‑century Egypt.

The family maintained residence in Cairo’s Zamalek, partly for health reasons within the family, while political change intensified after the Free Officers’ coup and the rise of Nasser. Shama describes new constraints—greater public Islamic influence, nationalization, and the sense of living under surveillance—alongside informal protections mediated through personal connections. Together, these experiences illuminate the shifting boundaries of belonging for Levantine Jews in mid‑century Egypt. His recollections connect household life, language, and commerce to the political transformations that produced displacement.

s.t: Arrest, Trial, and Escape – Alexandria Coast (1956)
s.d:
During the 1956 Suez Crisis, Shama’s father was arrested, accused of espionage, and subjected to a coercive trial process that culminated in a death sentence. Family survival depended on rapid improvisation: clandestine contacts, bribery with dismantled jewelry, and a sudden window to flee after his father was released under warning of imminent re-arrest. Together, these experiences illuminate the shifting boundaries of belonging for Levantine Jews in mid‑century Egypt. His recollections connect household life, language, and commerce to the political transformations that produced displacement.

The family reached Marseille with little beyond the clothes they wore, encountering humanitarian relief and the practical realities of refugee resettlement. Shama recalls being directed to clothing depots and temporary lodging, while his father experienced the disorienting reversal from employer and provider to recipient of aid. Together, these experiences illuminate the shifting boundaries of belonging for Levantine Jews in mid‑century Egypt. His recollections connect household life, language, and commerce to the political transformations that produced displacement.

Shama recounts the psychological toll of displacement on children—schooling disruptions, health crises, and the fear of family separation under welfare scrutiny. He describes pressures to conceal Jewish identity, participation in Christian institutions, and social barriers that limited education and belonging. Together, these experiences illuminate the shifting boundaries of belonging for Levantine Jews in mid‑century Egypt. Shama frames Canada as a pragmatic refuge: closer to U.S. networks, politically stable, and capable of supporting long-term family rebuilding after repeated uprooting. Together, these experiences illuminate the shifting boundaries of belonging for Levantine Jews in mid‑century Egypt. His recollections connect household life, language, and commerce to the political transformations that produced displacement.

His narrative emphasizes memory-work: the ethics of aid, the fragility of minority security under nationalist regimes, and the resilience of kinship networks across continents. Edmond Elbaz was born in Safi during the Second World War, at a moment when Morocco’s Jewish communities lived under the shadow of Vichy rule and Nazi influence. His testimony links local Jewish experience to global wartime dynamics: surveillance, exclusion from civil posts, and the fear that Nazi camp-building projects would be realized if Allied forces had not landed in November 1942. Safi thus functions as both birthplace and historical lens—where everyday family life was shaped by geopolitics, rumor, and communal strategies of protection.
• Born 19 December 1942 in Safi under the Vichy-aligned Protectorate administration, amid restrictions on Jewish mobility and employment.

s.t: Education & Communal Formation – Alliance Israélite Universelle, Safi
s.d:
Elbaz’s early schooling at the Alliance Israélite Universelle in Safi illustrates the educational infrastructure through which many North African Jews entered modern Francophone worlds. He emphasizes teachers’ commitment and the classroom’s material austerity—shared tables, inkwells, and reused textbooks—alongside the intellectual ambition of the curriculum. The school anchored a generation’s mobility: producing graduates prepared for further study in Casablanca and, later, for migration to Montreal’s bilingual environment. 
• Attended the Alliance Israélite Universelle (Charles Netter school), remembered for rigorous pedagogy despite large classes.
• Alliance schooling oriented students…

Moving to Casablanca for secondary education placed Elbaz within Morocco’s largest urban center and its shifting post-independence institutions. His narrative highlights the coexistence of French educational models with accelerating arabization in the 1960s. Teaching in Safi’s transitional collège, he witnessed the replacement of French administrative authority and the social scrutiny applied to Muslims educated in Europe—an everyday index of how national identity, language, and religion were renegotiated in public life.
• Continued studies in Casablanca at a French lycée (Mission culturelle française), extending a Francophone trajectory.
• Taught for two years in Safi (Collège El-Idrissi),…

s.t: Crisis & Decision to Leave – Safi and Rabat (1967)
s.d:
The Six-Day War catalyzed a sharp rupture in Elbaz’s Moroccan life. He recounts the arrest of Jewish teenagers—including his siblings—on allegations of espionage, and his futile search in Rabat for legal representation in a climate of fear. These events condensed longer experiences of vulnerability in a small city where Jewishness could be publicly policed. The episode serves as a decisive turning point: a move from enduring ambivalence to planning departure through official channels and, ultimately, bribery networks.
• After the 1967 war, siblings were arrested in Safi following public celebrations; they and other Jewish youths were pressured to sign false confessions.

Elbaz arrived in Montreal in September 1968, leaving Morocco with strict currency limits and the sense that departure required both bureaucratic navigation and informal patronage. He describes the Jewish Immigrant Aid Services as pivotal for first settlement—securing housing and bridging the first months of economic uncertainty. Montreal becomes the site where Moroccan Sephardi experience is reconfigured within Quebec’s linguistic landscape, as immigrant families build livelihoods while negotiating new civic expectations.
• Departed Morocco in September 1968 with limited funds permitted by the state; family reunified in Montreal by late 1969.
• JIAS assistance (housing and initial support)…

s.t: Educational Leadership & Francophone Advocacy – Montreal Jewish Schools
s.d:
In Montreal, Elbaz’s career centers on Jewish education and institutional development. He narrates a trajectory from classroom teaching to administrative leadership, supported by university studies in education and school management. His work intersected with Quebec’s broader language reorientation: Jewish schools expanded French instruction and adopted curricular standards that enabled students to remain socially and economically rooted in the province. Education becomes both livelihood and communal strategy for long-term continuity.
• Worked in Jewish day school education (including JPPS/Bialik), moving from teaching into administration.
• Advanced university training in Montreal…

s.t: Communal Stewardship – Spanish & Portuguese Synagogue, Montreal
s.d:
By the 2010s, Elbaz’s public role extends into communal stewardship at Montreal’s Spanish & Portuguese Synagogue, a historic Western Sephardi institution that became a key meeting point for diverse Sephardi migrations. His reflections emphasize heritage work as civic duty: recording testimony, strengthening institutions, and cultivating a Judaism characterized by openness and inclusion. The synagogue site thus marks not only arrival and integration but also leadership—where personal biography becomes communal narrative.
• Served in senior lay leadership at the Spanish & Portuguese Synagogue (Shearith Israel), linking Moroccan Sephardi trajectories to an older Western Sephardi institution.

Edna Garah Mashaal was born in Haifa during the final years of the British Mandate, in a city defined by mixed Jewish–Arab neighborhoods and by the rapid political transformations that culminated in Israeli statehood. Her early memories foreground everyday security practices—air‑raid shelters, family cohesion, and the mobilization of civic celebration—alongside the textures of Haifa life: schooling, seaside Shabbat outings, and multilingual contact shaped by her father’s work and the city’s diverse populations. Haifa thus appears as both a home and a formative “borderland,” where Iraqi-Jewish family histories were reframed through Israeli institutions and wartime experience.
• Born 26…

Although Edna herself was Israeli-born, the family’s narrative is anchored in Baghdad, the historic center of Iraqi Jewish life. In the interview, Iraq functions less as a remembered place than as an inherited horizon of loss and refusal: parents and elders avoided speaking about the country, while migration decisions were framed as necessary exits toward safety, education, and communal continuity. Baghdad therefore enters the storymap as an origin-point that explains later commitments—Zionism, family responsibility, and the pursuit of stable futures across borders.
• Family origins in Baghdad within the broader Iraqi-Jewish milieu.
• Parents and elders largely avoided recounting Iraqi life,…

s.t: Maternal Family Migration – Tel Aviv (Neve Tzedek area), 1926–1927
s.d:
Edna’s maternal grandparents migrated from Iraq to Palestine in the mid‑1920s, settling in early Tel Aviv near Neve Tzedek and the Alliance milieu. Their move reflects a pre‑state Iraqi Jewish mobility that combined religious imagination with pragmatic assessment of future security. In Edna’s recollections, this Tel Aviv household becomes a ritual center: holiday journeys from Haifa, collective preparation for Passover (including kashering by boiling utensils), and multigenerational transmission of Iraqi foodways and Hebrew song culture during travel.
• Maternal grandparents arrived 1926–27 and settled near Neve Tzedek in early Tel Aviv.
• Holiday visits (Pesach, Rosh Hashanah) from Haifa…

On her father’s side, migration unfolded in staged steps: his mother (Esther) and a brother arrived first, followed by Edna’s father around 1931, and later additional siblings. The interview emphasizes his sense of obligation and agency—bringing relatives, securing work, and sustaining family coherence under conditions of limited means. This Tel Aviv chapter highlights the social history of early Iraqi Jewish settlement: crowded living arrangements, mutual aid, and the forging of new identities through Hebrew names and public life in the Yishuv.
• Paternal grandmother (Esther) arrived first (c. 1930), followed by Edna’s father (c. 1931).
• Family lived initially in very constrained housing,…

Family excursions to Jaffa offered Edna an early lens on Arabic-speaking urban life within the Tel Aviv region. She recalls Jaffa as ‘very Arab’ in character, a remembered geography of markets, streets, and difference that still existed as a distinct city-space rather than today’s contiguous metropolitan landscape. These visits sit alongside Edna’s later acquisition of Arabic—learned through family interaction and schooling—illustrating how language and place intertwined in her formation as an Iraqi-Israeli subject in a mixed society.
• Jaffa remembered as an Arabic urban environment distinct from Tel Aviv.
• Visits were typically organized by younger relatives during holiday trips.

Edna recalls at least one overland family trip to Beirut, likely before 1948, associated with her father’s professional networks connected to the Iraq Petroleum Company. This movement underscores the porousness of Levantine borders before the consolidation of post‑1948 geopolitical divides. Beirut appears here not as a long-term residence but as evidence of a regional Mediterranean economy in which Jewish professionals and families circulated—an itinerary later rendered impossible by war and state formation.
• Overland trip by car to Beirut recalled as occurring before 1948.
• Linked to her father’s work-related travel and business connections.
• Signals earlier regional mobility later…

As the family’s situation improved, they moved from lower Haifa neighborhoods to Mount Carmel, where Edna remembers a larger home, entertaining English colleagues, and a sense of material stability. Her father’s work at the Iraq Petroleum Company placed the household within transnational corporate circuits, shaping language exposure and social life. This chapter foregrounds the everyday infrastructures of middle‑class Israeli life in the 1950s—schooling, sports, scouting, and Shabbat beach outings—through which Iraqi Jewish migrants negotiated belonging in a largely Ashkenazi public culture.
• Relocation from Hadar to Mount Carmel marked upward mobility and larger domestic space.

The closure of the Haifa pipeline and the contraction of the Iraq Petroleum Company precipitated a decisive family migration to Montreal in September 1959. Edna describes the move as emotionally difficult yet initially underestimated: English schooling, harsh winters, and early experiences of exclusion in housing markets reshaped family expectations. Over time, Montreal became a new Iraqi-Jewish social landscape through institutions such as Young Judaea and the Iraqi Club, enabling renewed community formation while sustaining Hebrew as the household language.
• Arrived in Montreal in September 1959 following employment disruption tied to IPC/pipeline closure.
• Early schooling in English…

In Montreal, Iraqi Jews organized spaces of sociability and mutual recognition; Edna’s narrative highlights the Iraqi Club on Île‑Bizard as a locus of leisure, matchmaking, and cultural continuity. The club’s gatherings—often centered on boating, parties, and interfamily ties—helped translate Iraqi communal forms into a Canadian setting while also mediating generational differences between Israeli‑Iraqis and Iraq‑born migrants. For Edna, these networks mitigated isolation and anchored a durable sense of Iraqi-Sephardi identity within Montreal’s wider Jewish landscape.

• Born 2 September 1940 in Beirut (maiden name Esther Shams), Esther Diwan’s early life unfolded within the multilingual, multi-confessional fabric of Lebanon’s capital and its Jewish quarter networks.
• Her family memory connects Beirut Jewry to wider Mediterranean lineages, including maternal roots associated with Damascus and a paternal grandmother born in Greece, underscoring Beirut’s role as a node in Levantine and Aegean Sephardi mobility.
• Raised in a household marked by French and Arabic usage, she describes everyday coexistence with friends across confessional lines, even as political shocks increasingly reshaped the horizon of Jewish security.

s.t: Communal Landscape – Wadi Abu Jamil & Magen Abraham
s.d:
• Diwan situates her family within Beirut’s Jewish geography, including the Wadi Abu Jamil quarter and communal institutions anchored by the Magen Abraham synagogue.
• She recalls gendered religious practice—men below, women above—and the seasonal movement of families to the mountains during summer holidays, when synagogue attendance and seat rentals structured communal rhythms.
• Her testimony records both belonging and vulnerability: a 1948 bombing destroyed the Alliance school building at night, narrowly averting mass casualties that would have occurred had it detonated at the intended morning hour.

s.t: Education & Francophone Formation – Alliance Israélite & Besançon
s.d:
• Diwan’s schooling reflects Beirut’s Francophone educational infrastructure: primary studies at the Alliance Israélite Universelle, followed by secondary education at the Sisters of Besançon alongside Jewish and non-Jewish classmates.
• She emphasizes durable friendships that persisted into later life in Montreal, illustrating how shared schooling created transnational social continuities after displacement.
• Her subsequent university study (including an initial year of law) signals both aspiration and constraint, as marriage and pregnancy reshaped the possibilities of professional formation.

s.t: Household, Gender, and Professional Life – A Medical Family
s.d:
• Diwan portrays a household organized around medical service: her father Nissim (a general practitioner and obstetrician) maintained a clinic on the ground floor of the family building, with the family apartment above.
• Her mother Alègra (née Matalon) is remembered as unusually mobile and capable—described as among the first women to drive in Lebanon—and as an active assistant in her husband’s rounds and clinical labor.
• Siblings’ professional trajectories (notably medicine) underscore how education and caregiving formed a family ethos, even as political instability progressively narrowed Jewish civic opportunity.

• A modern family house in Hamdun, the mountain resort zone near Beirut, appears in Diwan’s account as both a site of leisure and a symbol of precarity under deteriorating political conditions.
• After her father’s death and amid rising pressure on Jews, she recounts how a Muslim acquaintance occupied the property after a partial payment and used threats to prevent the family from reclaiming it.
• In retrospect, she reads the later destruction of the house during Israel’s Lebanon invasion as a bitter turn in the property’s afterlife—an emblem of how war converts private space into contested terrain.

s.t: Crisis, Targeting, and Exit – Beirut to Paris
s.d:
• Diwan links departure to converging crises: her father’s death in 1969, shrinking Jewish presence, intimidation in employment and bureaucracy, and emblematic incidents of violence and kidnapping that circulated as community warnings.
• Assisted by Jewish Immigrant Aid (JIAS), the family left Lebanon for France, initially housed in a hotel and then in an apartment obtained through informal mutual aid with local acquaintances.
• Paris functioned as an administrative and emotional threshold, where applications for North American resettlement were processed while the family recalibrated its future after the collapse of Lebanese stability.

• Arriving in Montreal around age 30 (c. 1970), Diwan describes the city first through summer abundance—flowers and warmth—contrasting sharply with the grey rain of Paris at departure.
• She narrates post-migration professional adaptation: her husband Benjamin redirected from agricultural engineering toward commerce and accounting, mobilizing kin networks to enter Montreal’s garment-related business sector.
• Over time she pursued education in Canada (Concordia, then McGill) and re-established communal life, framing Montreal less as refuge than as a new home formed through work, schooling, and dense social ties.

s.t: Transnational Afterlives – Family Networks and the United States
s.d:
• Diwan’s later family geography extends beyond Canada: brothers settled in the United States (Chicago and Boston), while American permanent-residency pathways (green cards) shaped mobility options for her children.
• She notes that one son leveraged U.S. status to work in the Washington area for a decade when employment was not immediately available in Montreal, illustrating how legal regimes and kin sponsorship created multi-sited livelihoods.
• These layered North American trajectories highlight a late-20th-century Sephardi pattern: dispersal across urban nodes while maintaining family coherence through frequent contact, visits, and shared ritual life.

By narrating family longevity, work, and neighborhood life, she offers a textured portrait of Iraqi Jewish continuity on the eve of mid‑century political rupture and emigration.

s.d:

Her description highlights disciplined school space (multiple locked entrances, a Muslim guard) alongside civic rituals such as flag ceremonies for the Iraqi state. These memories illuminate how Jewish schooling combined French cultural capital with Iraqi public culture, producing a bilingual and civically literate generation.

s.t: Violence, Fear, and Communal Defense – Farhud Memory (1941)
s.d:
• Her account of the Farhud period underscores how political crisis translated into Jewish vulnerability: when Rashid Ali’s government collapsed and Baghdad briefly lacked effective authority, anti-Jewish violence erupted in central districts. Although her family’s immediate area was safer, the atmosphere of rumor, search for relatives, and subsequent clandestine self‑defense initiatives left a lasting imprint. She situates these events within broader Nazi propaganda and regional instability, helping explain why later generations interpreted emigration as a matter of safety and dignity.

s.t: Marriage under Crisis – Baghdad during the Suez Era (1956)
s.d:
• Shahin recounts marrying in the midst of the 1956 Suez crisis, when curfews and public hostility forced families to scale down celebrations and shutter windows. The episode conveys how regional conflict reverberated into Iraqi Jewish domestic life, constricting public sociability and amplifying insecurity even before mass departures. Her narrative contrasts the curtailed wedding with a later celebratory gathering for her son’s first birthday, capturing the rapid oscillation between normalcy and crisis that characterized the period. 
• Highlights wartime curfew and fear shaping lifecycle ritual.

• After the 1958 revolution and shifting restrictions, Shahin describes leaving Iraq in 1960 and reaching Israel, where she reunited with an elderly grandmother who had emigrated earlier. This stopover is narrated as both familial recovery and strategic recalibration: Israel offered refuge and kin, yet economic constraints and the desire for mobility pushed the family to seek alternatives. Her testimony reflects the layered geography of Iraqi Jewish displacement, in which Israel functioned as an interim home and a site of reunion.
• Recounts reunion with grandmother in Israel after a long separation.

s.t: British Passport Mobility – London and European Transit (1961–1962)
s.d:
• Shahin notes that her husband obtained travel documents through British-embassy connections, enabling European movement at a time when options for Middle Eastern Jews were narrowing. She describes touring and temporary stays in Europe before final resettlement, underscoring how consular networks, visas, and maritime routes shaped refugee-adjacent mobility. This chapter highlights the bureaucratic and diplomatic infrastructures that mediated Iraqi Jewish departure after the monarchy’s fall.
• Mentions British-embassy links that facilitated passports and mobility.
• Emphasizes Europe as a transit corridor rather than an intended permanent home.

She contrasts the comfort of Canadian civic safety with the anxiety of Baghdad, describing adaptation to domestic labor without maids as the price of peace. Her account also foregrounds synagogue life as an anchor of continuity and a key mechanism for Iraqi Jewish integration into Montreal’s broader Sephardi landscape.

s.t: Community & Continuity – Iraqi Congregation and Spanish & Portuguese Synagogue
s.d:
• In Montreal, Shahin describes early participation in an Iraqi congregation (Van Horne area) and later affiliation with the Spanish & Portuguese Synagogue as Iraqi families joined and revitalized an older institution. This movement illustrates intra-Sephardi coalition-building: Iraqi newcomers preserved liturgy, language, and foodways while adapting to established communal frameworks. Her narrative emphasizes gratitude for Canada and a commitment to transmitting Iraqi-Jewish identity to children and grandchildren through ritual, cuisine, and communal belonging.
• Tracks a shift from a specifically Iraqi prayer space to a larger Sephardi institutional home.
• Highlights food, language, and…

• This chapter situates Yvette Mashaal’s Sephardi‑Mizrahi life history within the social worlds of the places she inhabited, foregrounding how migration reworked family networks, ritual practice, language, and economic life. Across these sites, her testimony traces a passage from Baghdadi Jewish community structures to interim European transit and, ultimately, to long-term resettlement in North America, where Iraqi Jewish identity persisted through synagogue life, foodways, and communal association.
• Yvette Mashaal (née Yvette Shaheen) was born in Baghdad in 1939, within the longstanding Baghdadi Jewish community shaped by Judaeo‑Arabic language, commerce, and dense kinship networks.
• Her…

• Mashaal attended the Alliance Israélite school system, where French and Arabic instruction intersected with Jewish communal education and civic rituals such as flag ceremonies.c\
• She recalls childhood sociability through clubs, cousin networks, and holiday visits, alongside gendered forms of protection that limited girls’ movement in public space.

• In 1952, the family departed Iraq by passport amid the wider exodus of Iraqi Jews, entering a precarious interim in Paris while seeking durable resettlement options.
• Her account highlights the uncertainty of temporary status, crowded living conditions, and the emotional labor of parents trying to secure visas and medical clearances for migration.
• Paris functions here as a liminal waypoint—neither origin nor destination—where Iraqi Jewish families clustered, shared information, and improvised support.

• A brief passage through London completed the final administrative steps toward emigration, underscoring how European capitals became bureaucratic gateways for Middle Eastern Jewish migrants.
• The stopover encapsulates the fragility of mobility—entry limits, deadlines, and the pressure to secure onward travel before documentation expired.

• Arriving in Montreal in 1952, Mashaal’s family joined a small but rapidly growing Iraqi Jewish nucleus, where mutual hospitality, synagogue affiliation, and shared language eased early adjustment.
• Her narrative foregrounds the reconfiguration of family roles—children’s schooling and language acquisition, parents’ economic rebuilding, and the consolidation of Iraqi-Sephardi networks in the city.
• Montreal becomes a new anchor site where Iraqi Jewish religious practice and culinary memory continued, even as everyday life adapted to North American institutions and climate.

s.t: Later Life & Memory Work – Fort Lauderdale (2016 interview)
s.d:
• By the 2010s, Mashaal’s testimony was recorded in Fort Lauderdale, reflecting later-life geographies of family dispersion and retirement within the broader North American Sephardi diaspora.
• The interview frames Baghdad as a remembered homeland and Montreal as the principal site of rebuilding, emphasizing the intergenerational transmission of Iraqi Jewish identity through story, food, and ritual.

• Flo Urbach (born Farah Dahoud) entered life in 1937 in Baghdad, within the long-established Judeo-Arabic–speaking Jewish community of Iraq. Her recollections foreground domestic architecture (courtyard houses), everyday foodways, and the layered social hierarchies that shaped Jewish life in the late Mandate and early national period.
• Family life centered on an extended household economy: daily market shopping, same-day cooking, and Shabbat dishes such as t’bit (slow-cooked rice-and-chicken with eggs).
• She describes linguistic ‘ear-training’ in Baghdad—recognizing and shifting between Jewish, Christian, and Muslim Arabic registers—alongside a persistent awareness of minority…

• During the upheavals surrounding the 1941 Farhud and wartime instability, Flo’s British-subject status enabled the family’s evacuation from Iraq to Bombay. This brief displacement placed Baghdadi Jews in contact with a South Asian Jewish world remembered as comparatively secure and socially open.
• In Bombay she encountered relatives and heard family comparisons between Bombay’s civic life and Baghdad’s atmosphere of fear and restriction.
• The stopover functioned as both refuge and contrast, sharpening later memories of insecurity in Iraq and the urgency of emigration.

• In April 1948, weeks before the formal outbreak of regional war, the family left Baghdad for Britain, arriving in London without firm lodging arrangements. The transition from Middle Eastern urban life to a rationed, postwar British city marked a profound shift in language, schooling, and household labor.
• Early days included unstable housing and the search for community networks; Jewish institutions helped relocate the children into more supportive educational environments.
• Flo recalls London as materially difficult yet politically safer, replacing existential fear with the challenges of immigrant adaptation.

• Seeking kin and affordable stability, the family briefly relocated from London to Manchester. Flo remembers the city as dark and fog-laden—an affective landscape that underscored postwar austerity and the emotional costs of exile.
• The move illustrates how migrant decisions were shaped as much by climate and daily livability as by employment prospects.
• Manchester ultimately served as a short-lived experiment before the family returned to London’s larger Jewish infrastructure.

• Back in London, the family gravitated toward Hendon, accessing established Jewish communal networks and schooling that normalized immigrant life. Flo emphasizes how Hebrew/Jewish schooling mitigated isolation and reduced the stigma of foreignness she first experienced in public school.
• Household roles shifted: women’s wage labor and sewing supported family survival, while older children navigated English acquisition and new social norms.
• Hendon became a stabilizing node that enabled educational and professional trajectories that were later portable to other Anglophone destinations.

• Following family dispersion through marriage and transnational opportunities, Flo migrated onward to Australia, spending several years there as part of a broader postwar movement of British-linked migrants. Australia functioned as both refuge for aging parents and a site of renewed independence.
• She describes repeated reinvention across countries—new names, social roles, and expectations—while relying on local Jewish communities for orientation and support.
• This stage highlights how Baghdadi Jewish mobility extended well beyond a single ‘Iraq-to-Canada’ arc, unfolding across multiple Commonwealth spaces.

• Flo’s eventual settlement in Toronto emerged through pragmatic opportunity: professional recognition and immediate employment prospects contrasted with barriers she encountered elsewhere. Toronto became the long-term anchor for a life shaped by serial migrations and adaptive identity work.
• She links belonging to work (pharmacy/hospital employment) and to Jewish communal life, describing consistent mutual aid across diasporic settings.
• Her narrative reframes ‘arrival’ as a process—Toronto representing not a single endpoint but the consolidation of skills, networks, and memory across continents.

Born as Fuad (“Fred”) Mashaal in Baghdad (6 Jan 1936), Fred’s early years unfolded within an Iraqi-Jewish milieu marked by long-standing communal continuity and the pressures of late-Ottoman and post-Ottoman governance. His family narrative preserves an older pattern of mobility between Iraq and Iran, shaped first by wartime conscription fears and later by the Farhud-era rupture. Although he recalls limited detail about grandparents due to generational distance, he emphasizes matrilineal memory of the Mashaal surname’s adoption and the household’s proximity to synagogue life and the Tigris corridor.
• Born in Baghdad in 1936, the youngest child in a family already spanning Iraq–Iran…

s.t: Departure Corridor – Basra and the Border Crossing
s.d:
The move out of Iraq in 1942 is remembered less as a single dramatic moment than as a logistical corridor: Baghdad to Basra, then onward by boat across the frontier. This corridor situates the Mashaal family within a wider pattern of Iraqi Jewish displacement and re-siting during the Second World War period, when mobility often depended on informal transport networks, border knowledge, and the resources to traverse multiple modes of travel. Basra, Iraq’s southern port city, anchors this transitional geography between river, rail, and maritime passage.
• Family traveled by car from Baghdad toward Basra, then continued via boat across the border.
• Basra functioned as a southern hinge linking…

s.t: Refuge and Reconstitution – Tehran (Iraqi Community School)
s.d:
Tehran became the first durable site of reconstitution after departure from Iraq. Fred recalls beginning in an Iraqi Jewish communal school that also served as a synagogue, a hybrid institution typical of migrant communities rebuilding religious and educational life with limited resources. This setting preserved Judeo-Arabic speech and Baghdadi social norms, while positioning children within a diasporic Iraqi network that would expand significantly through the mid-20th century. Tehran thus operates here as both refuge and a staging ground for onward mobility.
• Entered an Iraqi community school/synagogue that maintained Judeo-Arabic language and communal routines.
• Tehran’s Iraqi-Jewish…

After two years, Fred moved into Tehran’s American Community School, run by Presbyterian missionaries yet valued locally for English-language instruction and international curricula. He frames this education as formative—producing fluent English and a familiarity with Euro-American norms—while also noting that missionary aims did not erode Jewish identity or communal endogamy. This chapter highlights Tehran as a cosmopolitan contact zone where Iraqi Jews accessed global education systems while maintaining distinct social boundaries in domestic life and marriage networks.
• Learned English rapidly through an American missionary-run school that served diplomatic and expatriate circles.
•…

s.t: Higher Education and U.S. Transition – Easton (Lafayette College)
s.d:
Fred’s 1955 departure to the United States for university study marks a decisive re-scaling from regional migration to transatlantic academic mobility. Accepted to Lafayette College, he describes the transition as emotionally difficult at first—his first sustained separation from family—yet academically smooth due to strong English preparation. Campus life also produced new forms of Jewish sociality: he gravitated toward Jewish students as an “instant family,” illustrating how collegiate environments offered both integration and ethnoreligious clustering for newcomers.
• Left Tehran in 1955 to pursue higher education at Lafayette College in Easton, Pennsylvania.
• Initial dormitory life felt…

s.t: Graduate Training and Metropolitan Networks – Teaneck (Fairleigh Dickinson)
s.d:
Following undergraduate study, Fred pursued additional training at Fairleigh Dickinson University, extending his U.S. educational trajectory and embedding him within the New York–New Jersey metropolitan orbit. This period strengthened cross-border family ties: he began visiting Montreal from 1960 onward and maintained connections with Iraqi communal networks across multiple North American nodes. The chapter underscores how mid-century Sephardi/Mizrahi mobility often braided education, business apprenticeship, and kin-based travel into a single pathway.
• Continued studies at Fairleigh Dickinson, deepening ties to the New York–New Jersey corridor.
• Began frequent visits to Montreal, where…

s.t: Work and Business Apprenticeship – New York City
s.d:
In New York, Fred entered commission-based business work connected to family and co-ethnic networks, reflecting the role of trade and brokerage as portable skills among Iraqi Jewish migrants. This phase also anchors his long-term “wandering” identity—Baghdad-born, Tehran-formed, and professionally shaped in American urban capitalism. New York provided access to Iraqi Jewish social worlds while offering pathways into broader American economic life, setting the stage for later investments and property development in Canada.
• Worked in commission business linked to family and Iraqi-Jewish commercial networks.
• New York functioned as a key node connecting Tehran-based relatives, U.S.…

s.t: Property Development and Communal Leadership – Montreal
s.d:
Fred’s move to Montreal in 1971 pivoted his trajectory from student and metropolitan worker to long-term investor and community participant. He focused on developing a large tract of land, navigating municipal assessments, court processes, and fluctuating demand—an example of immigrant entrepreneurship shaped by local political economy. Socially, he describes the Mashaal family as an “instant family” that structured daily life and reinforced endogamous community cohesion. He also became a trustee at the Spanish & Portuguese synagogue, linking Iraqi newcomers to older institutional Sephardi frameworks.
• Settled in Montreal in 1971 to pursue property development and manage land-based…

s.t: Family and Medical Travel – Tel Aviv (Israel visit)
s.d:
Although his father imagined Israel as an eventual destination, Fred’s connection to Israel appears primarily through episodic visits rather than permanent settlement. In 1975, he traveled from Montreal to Israel in the context of family medical care, when his mother underwent treatment and surgery arrangements linked to kin support. This episode illustrates how Israel often functioned as a medical, familial, and symbolic center for Iraqi Jews dispersed across the Atlantic world, even when economic life remained rooted elsewhere.
• Visited Israel in 1975 in connection with family medical care and kin coordination.
• Israel appears as a family-support node rather than the primary site of…

s.t: Transatlantic Work and Iraqi Networks – London
s.d:
From 1981 through 2012, Fred’s life oscillated between Montreal and London, where he engaged in work and maintained ties with a substantial Iraqi Jewish community. He locates himself within a web of London-based Baghdadi families—some with direct Iraq-to-UK trajectories and others shaped by the Iraq→Tehran pathway—showing how shared foodways, language, and family networks knit together distinct migration histories. London also reinforced his sense of layered belonging: steeped in American culture, shaped by Tehran, anchored in Montreal, and aesthetically attached to British social life.
• Lived and worked in London intermittently from 1981–2012 while retaining Montreal as a core base.
•…

After 2012, Montreal re-emerges as Fred’s primary base, consolidating decades of movement into a stable locus for family, synagogue affiliation, and memory work. His narrative frames Iraqi Jewish culture as something that “creeps on you” through food, social proximity, and inherited caution shaped by earlier insecurity. In this later phase, Montreal stands as the site where multiple itineraries—Baghdad, Tehran, American education, London work—are held together and transmitted as an intergenerational account of mobility, adaptation, and communal continuity.
• Montreal becomes the later-life center after the conclusion of regular London residence in 2012.
• Describes cultural preservation as…

This chapter situates Freddie James within the historical geography of Iraqi Jewish displacement and resettlement, connecting local Baghdad lifeways to post-1948 migration circuits that reshaped Sephardi/Mizrahi communities across Israel, Europe, and Canada.
• Born in Baghdad in 1936 into an Iraqi Jewish family rooted in local commercial and religious life.
• Recalls a comparatively secure household environment, shaped by family observance and a strong domestic economy.
• Describes early experiences of harassment in public space, underscoring the precarity that marked minority life even before mass emigration.

s.t: Neighborhood Institutions – Synagogue Building & Communal Ties (Baghdad)
s.d:
• Remembers his father as deeply observant, teaching Torah and preparing boys for bar mitzvah without remuneration.
• Links family prestige to the building of a neighborhood synagogue shortly before the family’s departure, signaling both rootedness and impending rupture.
• Frames Jewish life as organized through kinship, holiday gatherings, and local institutions rather than broad intercommunal socialization.

s.t: Aliyah & Dispossession – From Baghdad to Israel (Ma‘abarot)
s.d:
• Left Iraq for Israel in 1948 amid large-scale Iraqi Jewish registration for departure and state confiscation of property and frozen assets.
• Recalls surrendering house and synagogue keys to authorities and departing with only minimal luggage—an enforced compression of an established life.
• Initial absorption occurred through temporary immigrant accommodations before the family secured housing and rebuilt routines in Israel.

• Completed schooling in Ramat Gan, a space he depicts as socially safer than Iraq despite regional wars.
• Describes peer life organized around school friendships, sport (tennis, ping-pong), and neighborhood networks.
• Emphasizes linguistic transition from Arabic at home toward Hebrew as integration progressed.

• Trained in Germany in sewing-machine work and industrial techniques, expanding practical expertise beyond the Israeli market.
• This European interval functioned as a bridge between post-aliyah rebuilding and later North American professional opportunities.
• Highlights skill acquisition as a pathway from refugee-like displacement toward specialized employment and entrepreneurship.

• Arrived in Canada in 1956, first working in Montreal after being recruited to help shift a domestic sewing-machine business toward industrial systems.
• Recounts a one-year period of training and technology transfer, positioning him as a key intermediary for modernization.
• This stage marks the consolidation of immigrant expertise into a recognizable professional niche in Canada.

• Relocated to Toronto after initial Montreal work, undertook short-term employment, then opened his own company in the sewing-machine sector.
• Identifies Canada as the setting of long-term stability, civic belonging, and economic opportunity, culminating in Canadian citizenship.
• Maintains Iraqi-Jewish cultural memory through language, music, and community gatherings while articulating a forward-looking ethic of reconciliation.

This chapter interprets Gabrielle Elia Tawfik’s life through the lens of Levantine Sephardi history and mid‑20th‑century displacement, tracing how education, language, and communal institutions structured mobility from East Asia to Beirut and onward to Canada.
• Born in 1944 in Kobe while her Lebanese-Syrian Jewish parents were immobilized in Japan by the Second World War.
• Her father’s import–export work placed the family within a broader Middle Eastern Jewish mercantile diaspora in East Asia.
• Early childhood was shaped by displacement and linguistic plurality (Japanese and English) before return to the Levant.

• Returned to Beirut in 1948, encountering the shock of re-entry as grandparents could not initially communicate with children who spoke Japanese and English.
• Family origins connected Damascus, Deir al-Qamar, and wider Syrian–Lebanese Jewish networks, including Ladino-speaking Jerusalem lineage on the maternal line.
• Beirut’s Jewish life is recalled as socially vibrant yet politically precarious, with 1948-era violence and later communal anxieties shaping everyday preparedness.

s.t: Schooling & Communal Memory – Alliance and Lycee
s.d:
• Educated through French-language institutions (Alliance and the Lycee), reflecting Lebanon’s Francophone cultural infrastructure.
• Remembers bomb attacks that targeted Jewish educational spaces, underscoring how regional politics seeped into local life.
• Childhood sociability included Jewish, Christian, and Muslim classmates, while community life remained anchored in family and neighborhood networks.

• Studied in Paris (1962–1963) for a teaching diploma connected to Alliance educational pathways.
• Paris functioned as a Francophone hinge between Levantine Jewish schooling and North American migration trajectories.
• Her training and credentials enabled employment mobility, reducing reliance on immigrant aid networks upon arrival to Canada.

• Relocated to Canada in 1965 with employment already arranged in education, entering through family networks (a brother already in Montreal).
• Early adaptation centered on winter hardship and public transport, offset by rapid professional integration into Protestant school systems.
• Connects to Sephardi communal life through marriage and synagogue networks (Spanish & Portuguese), while teaching across linguistic communities.

• Lived approximately a decade in Toronto, where her three daughters were born and raised in largely anglophone social worlds.
• Maintained Levantine Jewish traditions through holiday gatherings and intergenerational storytelling rather than strict synagogue routine.
• This stage reflects the balancing of professional life, family building, and shifting community composition as Lebanese Jews arrived after 1967.

s.t: A Brief Southern Hemisphere Interlude – Melbourne
s.d:
• Spent a period living in Melbourne, reflecting a wider pattern of Lebanese Jewish mobility across Commonwealth and diaspora nodes.
• This relocation underscores how careers and family strategies shaped multi-sited belonging beyond a single national narrative.
• Her account frames ‘home’ less as a fixed territory than as a network sustained through language, education, and kinship.

• Returned to Montreal and identifies it as her primary home despite repeated migrations and long-term winter adjustment.
• Positions storytelling and documentation—especially her book on Lebanese Jewish history—as a form of communal preservation against erasure.
• Her later life is marked by transnational family ties (U.S. West Coast and Ontario) and ongoing efforts to transmit Jewish memory and practice to grandchildren.

This chapter situates Gila Morat Aslan within the intertwined histories of Iraqi Jewish persecution, clandestine escape routes, and post‑1948 Israeli absorption, tracing how family strategies, institutional placement, and later migration reshaped identity and belonging.
• Born 21 March 1940 in Baghdad, in the Bab al‑Sheikh area, within a dense Jewish neighborhood of extended kin and mixed (Jewish, Muslim, Christian) neighbors.
• Remembers a large multi-level courtyard house and rooftop childhood play, even as public space became more dangerous for visibly Jewish children after 1947–48.
• Describes her father’s clandestine ties to the Haganah, requiring secrecy, the destruction of…

s.t: Exit Under Constraint – Baghdad to Basra
s.d:
• In 1949, the family’s escape began through internal travel to Basra under cover stories and strict behavioral discipline.
• Recalls disguises (abaya/face covering) used to conceal their children’s light features during checkpoints and transit.
• This stage marks the transformation from local belonging to precarious mobility as the family prepared for clandestine border crossing.

s.t: Border Crossing – Shatt al‑Arab to Iran
s.d:
• Crossed the Shatt al‑Arab by small boat with no luggage, presenting the outing as a ‘picnic’ to avoid suspicion.
• Describes the loss of property as total: the family closed the Baghdad home ‘as if returning,’ yet left everything behind.
• Arrival in Iran reframed displacement as both refuge and staging ground for onward movement toward Israel.

• In Iran, the family reorganized under uncertainty; her father had fled earlier through dangerous routes and then arranged extraction for relatives.
• As a child nearing ten, she sought to go to Israel; this decision led to family separation and a childhood defined by institutional frameworks of migration.
• Iran appears as a liminal space: safer than Iraq, yet unstable, with later family departures tied to the revolutionary period and anti-Jewish pressures.

s.t: Child Migration & Absorption – Kibbutz in Northern Israel
s.d:
• Sent from Iran to Israel with a younger sister, she was placed in a northern kibbutz near the Syrian border, part of state-directed child absorption projects.
• Describes the kibbutz regime of four-hour schooling and four-hour labor (kitchen, fields), producing belonging through collective work and peer community.
• Remembers a multiethnic cohort (Iranian, Moroccan, Turkish, Egyptian and European arrivals) and early public-health anxieties such as polio quarantines.

• Left the kibbutz in adolescence to live with relatives and later married young (engaged at 17; married at 18), a strategy that also avoided compulsory military service for women.
• Recounts scarcity in the 1950s: rationing coupons, delayed appliances, and food as a valued ‘wedding gift,’ illustrating the material conditions of early state-building.
• Family life was built within Iraqi-Jewish networks, while her husband worked in maritime commerce (ZIM), linking domestic stability to Israel’s port economy.

• Immigrated to Canada in 1976, relocating to Montreal with her children first; her husband followed about four months later after employment constraints.
• Settlement was scaffolded by kin (a brother-in-law in Montreal) who arranged housing and early support, enabling family continuity amid relocation.
• Describes adjustment as emotionally positive despite language barriers, relying initially on her children as translators while establishing new synagogue and neighborhood routines.

This chapter interprets Gladys Perez Moallem’s life within the history of Iraqi Jewish rupture and post‑1951 dispersal, showing how violence, denationalization, and state-directed absorption reshaped family strategies, gendered labor, and diaspora belonging.
• Born 18 Sept 1932 in Baghdad and raised in the Bataween area, a center of Iraqi Jewish life with Alliance schooling and dense kin networks.
• Remembers a multi-level courtyard house and rooftop sleeping in summer—an everyday urban practice that also created neighborhood sociality.
• Her early childhood reflects a community that was culturally confident yet increasingly exposed to political volatility in the 1930s–40s.

• Recounts the Farhud beginning on Shavuot 1941, marked in her memory by gunfire and a bullet flying overhead while children spoke across rooftops.
• Her street avoided direct attack because a Christian neighbor with police authority placed a guard at each Jewish home, preventing entry by mobs.
• The episode illustrates how survival depended on fragile local protections amid a broader breakdown of state order and antisemitic violence.

• Describes the 1951 registration process in the synagogue: identity papers were crossed out, rendering Jews stateless while still in Iraq.
• Families were restricted to one suitcase and a small cash allowance; valuables and most property could not be taken and were effectively lost.
• After registration, daily life became immobilized—no legal work, no access to bank funds, and intensified fear of arbitrary arrest.

s.t: Airlift to Israel – Baghdad to Sha‘ar Aliyah
s.d:
• Left Iraq in June 1951 by air, describing a rudimentary flight experience followed by arrival processing that included DDT delousing.
• Stayed about a month at Sha‘ar Aliyah (immigration ‘gate’) in tents, lining up for meals and placement decisions.
• This moment marks the transition from Iraqi urban middle-class life to emergency absorption structures of the early Israeli state.

s.t: Ma‘abara Near Petah Tikva – Tent to Wooden Shack
s.d:
• Resettled to a ma‘abara near Petah Tikva: six months in a tent followed by roughly seven years in a wooden shack without electricity, indoor plumbing, or running water.
• She narrates herself as a young ‘family leader,’ advocating repeatedly for housing near Tel Aviv to enable education and employment access.
• These years capture both the austerity of early-state Israel and immigrant agency in navigating institutions to secure better conditions.

s.t: Work, Education & Marriage – Tel Aviv / Israel
s.d:
• Worked in Tel Aviv (including American Express) while also attending public lectures connected to Hebrew University, building skills and social networks.
• Met and married Jamil in Israel (married 1962), entering a partnership shaped by Iraqi social networks and shared ambition.
• Her story foregrounds women’s wage labor and educational aspiration as crucial to family recovery after forced asset loss.

• Immigrated to Montreal in 1969 after economic instability in Israel and her husband’s business losses, rebuilding again in a new diaspora context.
• Her husband entered trade (watchband import) and she later joined the business, leveraging administrative and accounting skills to stabilize it.
• Montreal becomes the long-term setting where Iraqi Jewish memory, work ethic, and family strategies of resilience are rearticulated.

This chapter situates Haim Mathalon’s trajectory within the shifting geographies of Iraqi Jewish life, wartime Iran, and postwar migration regimes, emphasizing how education, documents, and informal economic practices enabled movement across Middle Eastern and European corridors into Canada.
• Born 15 Feb 1928 in Baghdad; his father died when he was two months old, and he was raised primarily by his mother’s parents.
• Childhood unfolded in a Jewish quarter adjacent to synagogue life and Hebrew instruction, with limited mobility in narrow streets and dense urban traffic.
• His account preserves everyday textures of Baghdadi Jewish education (Moreh/Hebrew lessons; Alliance curriculum in…

• Departed Baghdad in 1939 (on Pesach, coinciding with news of King Ghazi’s death) and traveled by hired car and driver over two days to Tehran.
• The move was shaped by economic constraints and trans-imperial family resources—money held in Iran rather than Iraq—making Baghdad increasingly untenable.
• Arrival in Tehran reoriented his education and social world toward multilingual Christian and American institutional settings.

s.t: Education & Wartime Work – Tehran (Jesuit / Community School; NAAFI)
s.d:
• Attended a French Jesuit school and later an American ‘community school,’ reflecting wartime shifts in perceived global power from France to the Anglophone world.
• As a teenager, worked for the British NAAFI, selling rationed goods to soldiers by coupon and strengthening his English through everyday contact.
• Remembers Zionist-cultural activity in Tehran (songs, films, emissaries) that encouraged immigration to Israel even before statehood.

s.t: Israel as Transit & Risk – Foreign Exchange Networks
s.d:
• Spent time in Israel in the late 1940s/early 1950s, working with transnational money-transfer and foreign-exchange practices serving Iraqi immigrants.
• Was arrested and jailed briefly in Israel for illegal currency dealings, illustrating how new-state regulation intersected with immigrant survival strategies.
• These experiences map Israel not only as a destination but also as a node in wider Middle Eastern and European mobility circuits.

• Went to Manchester around 1950–1951 while planning onward migration, reflecting postwar British cities as temporary hubs for Iraqi Jewish mobility.
• Was called back to Tehran to complete outstanding financial transfers and documentation, highlighting the precarity of travel under an Iraqi passport stamped by Israel.
• The period underscores how paperwork, visas, and border scrutiny structured Sephardi/Mizrahi itineraries across Europe.

s.t: Return to Iran & Route via France – Paris/Sorbonne (1953)
s.d:
• Returned to Tehran (c. 1951–1953) and then traveled to Paris to secure Canadian immigration processing, since Canada lacked a Tehran consulate.
• Briefly enrolled at the Sorbonne, using earlier French training as cultural capital while awaiting visa decisions.
• France functioned as a bureaucratic and educational bridge between Middle Eastern displacement and North American resettlement.

• Arrived in Montreal in 1953 with minimal funds, relying on Jewish vocational networks for first employment and learning Canadian workplace norms.
• Moved into payroll/administration roles and then built an entrepreneurial path in the automobile and leasing business, leveraging credit systems and bank relationships.
• Later family life included commitment to Jewish schooling for his children, reflecting community-building strategies in postwar Montreal.

• By 2014, he was residing in the Miami area, reflecting later-life mobility common among North American Sephardi/Mizrahi families. 
• His oral history foregrounds multi-sited belonging—Baghdad memories, Tehran wartime adolescence, Israel/Europe transit, and Montreal entrepreneurship.
• The interview itself functions as a preservation of Baghdadi Jewish everyday life and the improvisational routes of mid‑century displacement.

This chapter positions Helene Daniel’s life within Iraqi–Iranian Jewish mobility across the mid‑20th century, showing how schooling, kin networks, and political upheavals shaped movement between Kermanshah, Baghdad, Tehran, and ultimately Montreal.
• Born in 1925 in Kermanshah (Karmasha), Iran, within a Jewish family connected to wider Iraqi-Iranian commercial and kinship networks.
• Early life was shaped by periodic family movement between Iranian cities and Baghdad, producing a multilingual repertoire (Arabic at home; later French and English in school; Farsi through everyday contact).
• She repeatedly identifies emotionally as Iranian, describing pre-revolutionary Iran under the Shah as…

• Spent much of the school year in Baghdad, living in Bab al‑Sharqi, a mixed but heavily Jewish area where her family maintained close kin relations (Mashaal, Shiri, Gabbai).
• Attended a French Catholic ‘nuns’ school through grade six, learning French and English in addition to Arabic and later Farsi.
• Recalls Baghdad as emotionally frightening in childhood, shaped by stories of danger and the memory of being present during the Farhud.

• Was in Baghdad during the Farhud (1941) and remembers Muslim neighbors protecting her household, preventing harm from the mob.
• The episode remains central to her affective memory: she describes recurring fear and nightmares about Baghdad decades later.
• Her testimony highlights how local intercommunal relations could offer protection even amid broader antisemitic violence and state collapse.

• Engaged by proxy in late 1944 while temporarily in Baghdad, and married in Tehran in 1945 at age 19 to Abraham Daniel (age 39).
• Marriage was embedded in extended family networks: maternal kinship ties and Mashaal connections structured matchmaking and support.
• Raised three sons born in Iran (Frankie 1946; Emile 1947; Freddy 1950), while her husband worked in bookkeeping/agency roles linked to Mashaal business life.

• Lived in Tehran on/near Kuche Bahrami, in a largely Iranian (non-Iraqi) neighborhood, with Iraqi relatives nearby but not in an enclave.
• Describes day-to-day domestic life organized through household labor and hired help; she did little cooking before migration, observing maids and family elders.
• Reports minimal antisemitism in pre‑1979 Iran and recounts warm relationships with Muslim neighbors, including participation in family celebrations (e.g., bris invitations).

• Recounts a traumatic armed home invasion while living in the Mashaal household (c. 1949), when she temporarily cared for Victor Mashaal’s children and Maurice.
• Describes violent assault on her husband, loss of money, severed telephone lines, and reliance on chance intervention and family networks for immediate survival.
• This episode illustrates the gendered burdens of protection and childcare within extended kin systems amid uncertainty and transnational family separation.

• Left Iran in early 1953, traveling by plane via Paris (after plans to travel by ship via England were blocked).
• The journey unfolded amid growing political anxiety in Iran and family encouragement from relatives already in Montreal.
• Paris served as a practical transit node linking Middle Eastern mobility routes to Canadian immigration channels.

• Arrived in Montreal in January 1953 and initially stayed with the Mashaal family until securing housing on Van Horne near Hillsdale.
• Joined a predominantly Iraqi Sephardi milieu (Spanish & Portuguese Synagogue; Iraqi social club at Île‑Bizard) and raised children through local schooling and bar mitzvah tutoring.
• Describes early immigrant hardship—especially winter, lack of domestic help, and the necessity of learning cooking, baking, sewing, and driving—while ultimately affirming Canadian belonging.

This chapter situates Henri Ouaknine within the late‑colonial and post‑independence history of Moroccan Jewry, tracing how family origin narratives (Iberian, Amazigh) and francophone education intersected with 1960s bureaucratic restriction to shape migration to Canada.
• Born 29 Oct 1947 in Casablanca into a family that situates itself within layered Moroccan Jewish histories: maternal memories of Iberian (Spanish) origins and paternal identification with Amazigh/Berber Jewish lineage.
• Describes a predominantly francophone upbringing shaped by French educational institutions and an urban milieu where Jews, Europeans, and Muslims lived in proximity.
• Early family narratives connect…

s.t: Family Origins & Identity – Northern Morocco / Amazigh (Berber) Lineage
s.d:
• Frames his mother’s family as tied to northern Morocco’s Spanish-influenced zone, where Spanish circulated in domestic settings and intergenerational memory.
• Reports that family research located the surname ‘Ouaknine’ as of Amazigh/Berber origin, highlighting the historical entanglement of Jewish and Amazigh communities in Morocco.
• These layered origin stories become a self-conscious identity repertoire that later informs his sense of belonging in diaspora.

s.t: Casablanca Social Worlds – Francophone Education, Synagogue, and Dafina
s.d:
• Recalls a structured Jewish rhythm of life: synagogue affiliation (Benaroch), Friday‑night prayer, and the preparation of dafina/cholent in communal ovens for Shabbat.
• Attended French-system schools (including lycée) and later the Alliance Israélite, noting curricular differences (Alliance combining Hebrew and Arabic alongside French).
• Describes neighborhood sociability that included Jewish, French, and Arab peers, with sports (athletics, swimming) central to childhood leisure.

s.t: Political Shift & Bureaucratic Constraint – Moroccanization and Passports
s.d:
• Locates emigration pressures in the 1960s amid ‘Moroccanization’ policies and structural discrimination: requirements for Muslim business partners and increasing obstacles to obtaining/renewing passports.
• Describes ‘bakchich’ (bribery) as an everyday bureaucratic technology of mobility, with him personally delivering envelopes and retrieving documents on behalf of an ill father.
• These experiences catalyzed his decision to leave, framing departure as a refusal to normalize systemic corruption and precarity.

s.t: Paris as Transit – Documentation and Waiting
s.d:
• Spent roughly three months in Paris while Canadian immigration processing moved more quickly through the embassy there.
• This liminal stay reflects a common North African Jewish strategy: using France as an administrative and linguistic bridge to North America.
• He traveled ahead of his parents to begin school in Canada after a minor medical issue delayed their paperwork.

• Arrived in Montreal on 12 Sept 1966, initially entering anglophone schooling (Grade 12) before switching pathways due to language demands.
• Continued into technical/occupational education (Institut de technologies Laval / later cégep landscape), reflecting immigrant recalibration of credentials and future planning.
• Montreal becomes the setting where Moroccan Sephardi identity is reworked through education, work, and evolving community networks in a francophone North American city.

This chapter situates Irène Saudai‑Buenavida within the history of Egyptian Jewry under mid‑century nationalism and regional war, tracing how multi-origin family networks, religious institutions, and coercive state policies reshaped a Cairo childhood into exile and community leadership in Montreal.
• Born 1 Aug 1947 in Cairo, only months before the establishment of the State of Israel, in a family she describes as a ‘salata baladi’—a layered mixture of origins and migrations.
• Family background includes maternal roots linked to Tiberias/Jerusalem and Egyptian life, while her father arrived from Baghdad at age 12; she also notes Spanish–Ottoman trajectories through her in‑laws.
• Her…

s.t: Childhood Under Threat – Cairo Bombardments and Fear (c. 1950s)
s.d:
• At around age eight, her first vivid political memory is war: sirens, bombardments, and hiding in underground spaces while neighbors shouted threats at Jews to extinguish lights or face violence.
• Describes escalating restrictions under Gamal Abdel Nasser: exclusion from schools, removal of Jewish markers from homes, and tightening control over communal religious life.
• Family decisions were structured by fear for children’s safety, including the protection of daughters from abduction rumors and boys from prison as presumed ‘Zionists’.

s.t: Synagogues, Ritual, and Soundscape – Sha‘ar Shamayim / Ben Ezra
s.d:
• Recalls Friday-night prayer at the major Cairo synagogue (‘Kinista Smaleyah,’ framed as Sha‘ar Shamayim), where liturgical music and choral voices created an ‘opera-like’ atmosphere.
• Highlights Ben Ezra synagogue as an anchor of historical memory, connecting local tradition to the Geniza legacy and the broader archival trace of Egyptian Jewish life.
• Shabbat meals centered on Iraqi-inflected tbit/defina cooked overnight; intergenerational gatherings at her paternal grandmother Rifka’s home were among her most cherished memories.

• Her father, who arrived from Baghdad as a child, built a small socks-manufacturing business through intensive labor, supporting a family of five.
• She describes how nationalization under Nasser undermined family economic security and constrained exit options, intensifying vulnerability alongside political intimidation.
• Household survival depended on women’s domestic labor, street-market bargaining, and scarce kosher meat access—an everyday economy shaped by scarcity and surveillance.

s.t: Sibling Separation – Brother’s Flight from Egypt (c. 1963)
s.d:
• A community leader warned the family that her 18-year-old brother faced imprisonment; the family escorted him to Alexandria to depart by ship, unsure they would ever see him again.
• This separation illustrates the staged nature of Egyptian Jewish exile, where families fragmented across routes and timelines amid limited communication and restricted transfers of funds.
• Her account emphasizes the emotional cost of ‘protective’ migration decisions made under coercive state power.

s.t: Escape from Egypt – Cairo to Paris (Oct. 1966)
s.d:
• Left Egypt in October 1966, six months before the 1967 war, after intensified threats toward Jewish families and warnings about the targeting of daughters.
• Describes harsh searches at the border and strict limits on property: one suitcase of used clothes per person and 20 Egyptian pounds per family—effectively leaving with nothing.
• Paris functioned as a brief staging stop (about one day), where documentation prepared by her brother enabled immediate onward travel to Canada.

• Arrived in Montreal in October 1966 and experienced ‘deliverance’ from oppression alongside the shock of early cold weather and unfamiliar winter clothing.
• With her brother’s help, the family relied on JIAS for initial housing (an apartment on Decarie in Ville Saint‑Laurent) and job placement attempts, confronting the ‘Canadian experience’ barrier.
• She later anchored communal life through synagogues (including Egyptian-style Habousha rite and then Spanish & Portuguese) and became a major organizer—founding an Egyptian Jewish association (2003) and leading women’s programming in Montreal.

s.t: Marriage & Transnational Family – Israel to Montreal (1975)
s.d:
• Married in Montreal in 1975 after meeting her husband Victor Buenavida in Israel; he was Egyptian-born, raised largely in Israel, and served in the Israeli military in multiple wars.
• Their marriage reflects the post-exile reconstruction of family networks across Israel and Canada, including close cousin marriage within dispersed Egyptian Jewish kinship circles.
• Her family story continues transnationally through ongoing ties to Israel (including their son living there) and her own civic and communal work in Montreal.

This chapter interprets Isaac Gaon’s family story as a Balkan Sephardi (Ladino) history of educational migration, Holocaust rupture, and postwar rabbinic leadership, tracing how intimate memory objects and languages anchor identity across London, the Balkans, and North America.
• Born in London in 1949 to Haham Dr. Solomon Gaon and Regina Gaon (née in Gibraltar), in a household shaped by Sephardi rabbinic leadership and trans-Mediterranean kin networks.
• His life story is inseparable from his father’s Bosnian Sephardi trajectory—an interwar migration that became, retrospectively, an escape from the Holocaust in Yugoslavia.
