• Through family memory, Isaac Gaon locates ‘home’ simultaneously in…

s.t: Sephardi Origins – Travnik and the Balkan (Ladino) Route
s.d:
• His paternal family is traced through a classic Ottoman–Balkan Sephardi itinerary: post‑1492 movement through Greece/Salonica and then into the Balkans, where Ladino culture persisted for centuries.
• Grandparents Isaac (Yitzhak) Gaon and Rachela Pinto represent this Sephardi naming world and its embeddedness in local trades and property relations.
• The narrative foregrounds Ladino not only as a language but as an affective archive of belonging, transmitted in songs, letters, and domestic speech.

s.t: Father’s Formation – Jesuit Schooling and Yeshiva (Travnik/Sarajevo Region)
s.d:
• Dr. Solomon Gaon (b. 1914, Travnik) received unusually wide education: Jesuit schooling (including Latin) alongside advanced rabbinic learning in a yeshiva near Sarajevo.
• This hybrid intellectual formation—European classical pedagogy and Sephardi rabbinics—prefigured his later communal leadership in the British Commonwealth.
• Family memory emphasizes multilingualism (15 languages) as both a personal gift and a hallmark of Balkan Sephardi cosmopolitanism.

s.t: Migration for Rabbinic Training – Travnik to London (1932)
s.d:
• In 1931–1932, amid anxiety about rising Nazism, his paternal grandparents arranged for Solomon Gaon to leave Yugoslavia and continue his education in London.
• London’s Sephardi community simultaneously sought recruits for rabbinic training, bringing Solomon and another future synagogue reverend (Eliezer Abu Noun) to Britain.
• This migration becomes a pivotal hinge: a ‘routine’ educational move that ultimately saved him from the destruction of Bosnian Jewry.

• In 1941, after Nazi entry into Yugoslavia, Solomon’s parents were deported; the family never learned the fate of his father, who was ‘taken away’ and disappeared.
• His mother was deported as well; she contracted typhoid and died en route to a camp, later buried in a Christian cemetery near Travnik, a grave the family continues to visit.
• These losses frame Isaac Gaon’s biography as a postwar continuation of a family line disrupted by genocide and displacement.

s.t: Ladino Letter & Memory Object – Travnik to London (1939)
s.d:
• A Ladino note (c. 1939) from his grandmother to Solomon’s London landlady survives as a rare family document: gratitude for care and maternal longing for reunion.
• After the war, Solomon returned to Travnik and recovered a silver siddur preserved by the former household/landlady—one of the only material links to his parents.
• These objects reveal how Sephardi memory travels through language (Ladino) and ritual materiality (siddur) when family archives are otherwise destroyed.

s.t: Sephardi Leadership – London and the Commonwealth
s.d:
• Solomon Gaon rose to become Sephardi Chief Rabbi of the Commonwealth, placing the family at the center of British Sephardi institutional life.
• Isaac Gaon recalls Ladino as a lived soundscape—his father singing Ladino songs—linking household intimacy to a broader tradition of Ottoman Sephardi culture.
• This chapter positions London as both refuge and platform for Sephardi religious leadership in the postwar period.

s.t: Transatlantic Continuities – London to New York to Toronto
s.d:
• From London, Solomon Gaon’s rabbinic work extended to North America, including a move to New York, reflecting the transatlantic circulation of Sephardi leadership.
• Isaac Gaon’s interview is recorded in Toronto (2017), situating later family life within the Canadian Sephardi landscape.
• The trajectory exemplifies how Balkan Sephardi lineages—shaped by Ladino culture and wartime rupture—reconstituted themselves across Anglophone Jewish centers.

This chapter situates Isaac Sedaka within the modern history of Baghdadi Jewry—its religious discipline, educational institutions, and professional adaptation under escalating restriction—tracing how expertise and networks shaped both survival in Iraq and resettlement in Montreal.
• Born 15 Aug 1938 in Baghdad into a family that narrated rabbinic prestige (a great‑grandfather remembered as Chief Rabbi of Baghdad under Ottoman/Turkish rule).
• Describes a home of strict observance: no cooking, shopping, or electricity on Shabbat; daily synagogue attendance with his father, a volunteer cantor who memorized prayers.
• Positions Baghdadi Jewish life as organized through neighborhood synagogues…

s.t: Neighborhood Geographies – Shorja and Slet Mi‘ir
s.d:
• Locates childhood in/near Shorja and the bazaar district, recalling the large synagogue Slet Mi‘ir near the Shorja market area.
• Explains how Baghdadi streets and place-names encoded older Jewish memory (e.g., ‘Samoel’/Shmuel as a protective-guest narrative in pre‑Islamic Arabia).
• These spatial recollections map Jewish Baghdad as both commercial and devotional, embedded in broader urban circulation.

s.t: Education – Alliance Israélite and Shamash School
s.d:
• Educated at Alliance (French, English, Arabic) and then Shamash for higher schooling, describing teachers recruited from France and England alongside strong local instruction.
• Frames schooling as a crucial form of cultural capital later useful in migration and professional life (especially French for Montreal).
• Remembers Baghdad’s Jewish student networks (clubs such as Laura Kadoorie/‘Lorethlori’) and a pre‑1948 social world of peers and extracurricular life.

• Recalls the Farhud as a moment of imminent danger in a city with collapsed order, noting higher casualty figures than official counts in communal memory.
• His uncle Abraham Mashaal arranged refuge at Laura Kadoorie school; a guard (described as Afghan) was bribed to conceal the presence of Jews.
• After three days, the family returned to find their home intact, illustrating how survival depended on advance warning, mobility, and protected institutional spaces.

• Worked in insurance brokerage/agency settings during 1948–1951, learning a specialized field as Jewish professional space narrowed.
• Describes how Jewish departures and state pressure closed offices and reshaped employment, forcing continual recalibration of work and partnerships.
• These years mark a transition from school-based social life to adult professional strategy under growing surveillance.

• From 1951 he operated as a major insurance agent by using Muslim partners’ names: he did the work while partners took larger shares as ‘name holders.’
• Built an office with significant staff and clientele, describing agent work as quasi-company representation (claims, surveys, tariffs), not merely brokerage.
• Highlights the paradox of personal respect from many Muslim clients alongside structural discrimination enforced through paperwork, naming, and state policy.

s.t: Family Dispersion – Relatives to Israel, Assets and Responsibility
s.d:
• Family members left for Israel in 1951, transferring responsibility to him to liquidate assets and send funds, delaying his own departure.
• This arrangement produced a prolonged ‘staying behind’ period in Iraq, where he combined family obligation with expanding professional success.
• The chapter illustrates how Iraqi Jewish migration could be staggered and strategic, shaped by property, denationalization fears, and remittance logistics.

s.t: Arabic Expertise & State Recognition – Marine Insurance Guide (1966)
s.d:
• Authored a ‘Guide to Marine Insurance’ in Arabic—presented as a pioneering technical text—recognized in Iraqi press and cited by officials.
• In 1966, prior to the Six-Day War, he was appointed head of a committee to translate insurance policies and tariff structures into Arabic.
• After 1967, he was removed from the committee, underscoring how expertise could be valorized and then abruptly revoked as politics hardened.

• After the 1969 public hangings, partners warned him not to appear at the office to avoid association with a Jew—reflecting heightened fear and social contagion of repression.
• He describes a period of enforced withdrawal (1969–1971) while awaiting a viable exit route and passport authorization.
• This stage captures the collapse of professional life under coercive nationalism, despite earlier respect and intercommunal ties.

• Secured a rare ‘special passport’ through a Muslim lawyer’s advocacy with the Ministry of Interior, citing his contributions and his wife’s need for treatment abroad.
• Reports receiving the passport within about 15 days and leaving as among the first families permitted to depart Iraq with official documentation.
• The episode shows how personal networks and state-level patronage could momentarily override systemic exclusion.

• Arrived in Canada in 1971 and rebuilt life in Montreal, carrying forward French-language education and Iraqi communal networks.
• His story links Baghdad’s religious discipline, education, and professional expertise to the Canadian context of immigrant re-start and community memory work.
• Recorded in Montreal in October 2017, his testimony foregrounds both intercommunal solidarity at the neighborhood level and state-driven persecution as decisive forces in Iraqi Jewish history.

This chapter situates Joe (Joseph) Faraj within the institutional landscape of Baghdadi Jewry and its mid‑century dispersal, tracing how communal administration, Farhud trauma, denationalization-era exit routes, and successive educational migrations shaped a new life in Montreal.
• Born 4 Aug 1934 in Baghdad, in a family whose livelihood and social standing were tied to the Jewish community’s institutional economy.
• His father served as administrator of communal assets—collecting rents from properties and farms and distributing funds to Jewish charities, schools, and hospitals.
• He frames this role as a form of communal stewardship linking household life to Baghdad’s wider Jewish…

s.t: House, Quarter, and Everyday Life – Tahes Takia
s.d:
• Raised in the Tahes Takia area, a Jewish neighborhood with a synagogue across the street (identified as ‘Hasqel’).
• Describes an older ancestral compound held by the family for over two centuries, housing dozens of relatives around a courtyard and a large communal living room for Shabbat and lifecycle events.
• In 1939 the family left the ancestral house due to rising water levels and deteriorating walls, marking an early rupture in place-based family continuity.

• Attended the Alliance school for boys; his sisters attended the Alliance school for girls, walking daily through several narrow streets to reach campus.
• Emphasizes the school’s social world as predominantly Jewish, shaping friendships that continued across decades and migrations.
• His recollections underscore how Alliance education anchored Baghdadi Jewish modernity while remaining embedded in neighborhood religious life.

s.t: Recreation & Environment – Tigris Swimming and Rooftop Sleeping
s.d:
• Recalls daily early-morning swimming: crossing the river and returning with neighborhood companions for more than six months a year in Baghdad’s long summers.
• Seasonal sleeping practices mapped climate onto domestic space: rooftops at night for breeze, basements at midday for cooler rest, bedrooms in winter.
• These embodied geographies situate childhood memory in the material ecology of Baghdad—heat, water, and built form shaping daily routine.

• At age seven, experienced the Farhud as street-level terror near Shorja, with looted goods passing by the house and the family barricading doors in fear.
• A policeman aimed at his father from the street; a shot struck the window bars and metal fragments injured his father’s face, leaving embedded pieces for weeks.
• The episode captures how state actors and mobs blurred during collapse of order, while the family survived by staying indoors with stored food and day-help unable to remain overnight.

s.t: Bar Mitzvah Deferred – Burning Hebrew Books (1947)
s.d:
• He did not have a bar mitzvah in Baghdad: in 1947, amid heightened suspicion linked to Zionism, the family burned Hebrew books to avoid accusations of espionage.
• He later experienced ‘bar mitzvah’ as a belated religious threshold in Israel when he first put on tefillin, around age seventeen.
• This chapter highlights how political fear reshaped religious education and public ritual during the final years of Iraqi Jewish life.

s.t: Exit from Iraq – Laissez-Passer to Cyprus (1950)
s.d:
• Left Iraq in 1950 through the denationalization-era exodus, traveling on a laissez‑passer rather than a passport; family departures were staged (sisters June/Sept 1950).
• Because he was sixteen, a new identity card was issued listing him as nineteen so he could depart alone; he flew to Cyprus and transferred to an Israeli plane for onward travel.
• At departure, authorities limited possessions (one suitcase, 50 dinars) and confiscated khaki clothes suspected as potential military uniforms.

s.t: Israel – Agricultural School, Army, and 1956 War Service
s.d:
• In Israel, attended an agricultural boarding school for a year, then moved to Tel Aviv for mechanic work and night studies (Max Fine), followed by 2.5 years of army service.
• Participated in reserve duty in 1956, using Arabic and Hebrew skills in intelligence-oriented tasks rather than frontline combat.
• Describes early Israel as materially scarce (rationing) and later as socially stratified, feeling discrimination against ‘Oriental’ Jews as second‑rate citizens.

• Moved to England in January 1959 for study (English, then math and physics), using London as a bridge between Israel and North America.
• This stage reflects the widening post‑exodus geography of Iraqi Jewish mobility, where education abroad offered alternative routes of social and professional advancement.
• His account frames migration decisions as pragmatic responses to opportunity, discrimination, and the search for stable civic belonging.

• Arrived in Montreal in October 1960, confronting cold climate and the ‘Canadian experience’ barrier in employment; he pursued accounting training and worked while studying at night.
• Built a long career in real estate, later retiring after decades of work, and raised three daughters and grandchildren in Montreal.
• He identifies first as Canadian ‘with the Jewish religion,’ foregrounding civic belonging while continuing Iraqi culinary traditions (tbit, brown eggs, okra, kebab) and an ethical ‘golden rule’ inherited from his father.

This chapter situates Joe Shuker’s trajectory within the late‑20th‑century unraveling of Iraqi Jewish security and the multi-stage routes that enabled departure, showing how education, illness-based exit permissions, and clandestine escape networks linked Baghdad to London and Montreal.
• Born 21 Dec 1949 in Baghdad to Selim Shuker (accountant) and Haninah Shuker (née Shami), in a household he recalls as materially comfortable and socially protected.
• Describes large homes with gardens, fruit trees, gardeners, live-in cooks and maids—an urban upper-middle-class Baghdadi Jewish domestic world.
• Had a sister who later died (1983), leaving him as the only surviving member of his immediate…

s.t: Education & Youth Networks – Frank Iny School
s.d:
• Studied at Frank Iny, a privately Jewish school with imported teachers (English and French instructors from abroad and Jewish Arabic-speaking teachers).
• Remembers the school as both strict and ‘enchanting,’ providing a strong educational foundation and a sense of safety for Jewish students.
• Also participated in a Jewish sports center (‘El‑mallab’) with tennis, ping-pong, basketball, volleyball, soccer and running fields—an institution of communal leisure.

s.t: Neighborhood Ecology – Jewish District and Nearby Arab Huts
s.d:
• Grew up in a mostly Jewish neighborhood, adjacent to an open area where poorer Arab families built huts without water or electricity.
• Recalls controlled permeability: gates were kept locked, but trusted neighbors were allowed to enter to use the tap, drink water, or wash feet.
• Everyday exchange included purchasing and receiving fresh tandoor bread and buffalo-cream (jamoosa) eaten with silan (date syrup).

• Had a bar mitzvah at age 13 in Baghdad, organized jointly with a close friend (Elas Delal) and conducted with Haham Sesson.
• Recounts the event as a family-hosted gathering with neighborhood children and parents, emblematic of tightly knit Baghdadi Jewish social worlds.
• Notes limited memory beyond later-viewed video, illustrating how forced migration can truncate autobiographical recall and peer reinforcement.

s.t: Political Uncertainty – Revolutions, Curfews, and Fear (1958–1963)
s.d:
• Remembers the 1958 revolution as an early shift, with deeper insecurity emerging by 1963 amid repeated coups and state instability.
• Describes curfews and military jeeps patrolling streets, with the terror of seeing a jeep stop outside one’s home—interpreted as potential disappearance of male family members.
• Although he was a child, these impressions mark the end of ‘safe’ childhood and the onset of a security logic that shaped the family’s exit planning.

s.t: Leaving Baghdad – Medical Pretext and Mother’s Illness (1965)
s.d:
• In 1965, at age 14, he left Baghdad mid-school year to accompany his mother, who had been ill for years (breast cancer) and required treatment in London.
• Travel occurred on a passport under the premise of accompanying a sick person—an exit strategy that would otherwise have been unavailable.
• He stayed in London as she received care; she died in 1965 at age 41, and he remained until her death.

• Completed schooling in England, including time in a boarding school (Pierrepont School, Surrey), learning to navigate English-language education while his mother moved through hospitals and convalescent homes.
• Recalls a formative Yom Kippur experience in boarding school with inadequate accommodations, highlighting the frictions of Jewish observance in non-Jewish institutional settings.
• During this period he became effectively stateless: Iraq denationalized him while abroad and he was warned not to approach the Iraqi consulate; England granted a student visa to complete studies.

s.t: Father’s Escape – Basra to Iran by Boat (Post‑1967)
s.d:
• After the 1967 war, his father Selim fled Iraq clandestinely—traveling from Basra to Iran with other families by small boat, paying for passage and being instructed to remain silent during checkpoints.
• On arrival in Iran, Jewish organizations assisted; the route included a brief Israel stop (about 48 hours) so he could reunite with family before continuing to Montreal to meet Canadian immigration timing requirements.
• He left behind home and car, reportedly giving the car to a trusted Muslim acquaintance; capture would likely have meant execution.

• Arrived in Canada in 1967 and entered McGill University, studying science and graduating in chemistry; also received a teaching diploma and taught high school math/chemistry.
• Intentionally failed an interview in French to avoid entering a chemistry plant job, choosing instead to invest in a jewelry retail business with a partner.
• Describes Canada as a relatively smooth adjustment compared to earlier dislocation, emphasizing stable work, education, and institution-building as pathways to belonging.

s.t: Marriage, Israel Sojourn, and Return to Canada
s.d:
• Married in 1985 after meeting his wife in Tel Aviv (arranged by family during a business trip in the diamond trade).
• Moved to Israel for seven years, managing a carton-board business; he later returned to Canada, citing difficulty with bureaucracy and everyday systems.
• Maintains a kosher home and transmitted Jewish education through schools (Talmud Torah, Herzliya, Akiva), framing Iraqi-Sephardi identity as rooted in family togetherness, shared meals, and communal sociability.

This chapter situates Joseph (Yusef) Dabby within the final decades of Baghdadi Jewish life after the 1951 exodus, highlighting how multilingual education, communal institutions, and post‑1967 state restrictions shaped an escape route through Iran and later diaspora resettlement in Montreal.
• Born in Baghdad in December 1950 (Arabic name: Yusef), into a family that remained in Iraq after the 1951 mass departure of Iraqi Jews.
• His father, Hedouri Dabby (‘Hourijinku’ nickname), ran an import business supplying construction metals, routing heavy shipments through Basra and the Tigris corridor.
• He never met his grandparents: they had already left or died by the time he reached adulthood,…

• Attended the Jewish Frank Iny School, where French was taught from kindergarten, Arabic alongside French through primary years, and English introduced later.
• Describes a rotating linguistic curriculum tied to external examinations (French brevet, Iraqi state exams, and British/Oxford-style exams), producing high multilingual competency.
• He emphasizes the ability to speak Iraqi Arabic in multiple dialects (Jewish, Muslim, Christian), using language as a tool of social navigation and relative safety.

s.t: Jewish Childhood Social Worlds – Mahlab Sports Club and Urban Mobility
s.d:
• Recalls a cohesive post‑1951 Jewish community world structured around Frank Iny and the communal sports club (Mahlab) with tennis, football, and other activities.
• Describes bicycling throughout Baghdad—including downtown Shari‘a Rashid—often without locks, emphasizing a remembered everyday security and social trust.
• Notes household rhythms of parties and visiting, with children circulating through Purim card games and social gatherings within a small Jewish milieu.

s.t: Shabbat Foodways – Tbeet Cooked on Embers
s.d:
• Shabbat cuisine centered on tbeet: a pot set over embers in a purpose-built hearth-like container, covered to hold heat for ~24 hours.
• Eggs cooked above the pot, turning brown from heat and steam; eggs were eaten for breakfast and tbeet for the main Saturday lunch meal.
• He highlights the sensory dimension—smoke-inflected taste and household engineering—as a core marker of Baghdadi Jewish domestic tradition.

s.t: Religious Practice & Bar Mitzvah – House and Synagogue
s.d:
• His mother maintained a kosher home and the family observed holidays with long walks (about 45 minutes) to a nearby synagogue housed within a Muslim neighborhood.
• He recalls praying in a courtyard-style house-synagogue where onlookers could observe from rooftops, reflecting the porous architecture of older Baghdad.
• He states that the boys had bar mitzvah celebrations held both at home and in synagogue, within a broader culture of frequent family gatherings.

s.t: Political Tightening – After the Six-Day War (1967)
s.d:
• After 1967, the Iraqi state imposed intensified restrictions on Jews: telephones disconnected, bank accounts frozen or tightly limited, and travel beyond the city requiring permits.
• He describes 1967–1970 as a period of heightened danger, with arrests and the sense of being trapped within Baghdad under surveillance.
• These measures transformed everyday life and made exit a matter of clandestine strategy rather than open emigration.

• Finished high school in 1969 but notes Jews were barred from university, shaping a forced pause in educational trajectory.
• Volunteered at Frank Iny (1969–70) and became an informal spokesperson when officials or visitors came—positioning him as a mediator between school and outside authorities.
• Through this role, he gained knowledge of community vulnerabilities and began crafting an exit strategy.

• Left Iraq in August 1970, describing the departure as an ‘escape’ rather than routine migration.
• Tehran functioned as the critical transit node enabling onward movement to Israel, reflecting a broader corridor used by Iraqi Jews outside official channels.
• This stage marks the collapse of Iraqi citizenship into precarious mobility and the reorientation of life toward the Israeli and diaspora landscapes.

• Arrived in Israel in September 1970 and immediately sought news of grandparents—learning they had all died, reaffirming generational discontinuity.
• Family memory includes the earlier decision not to register for 1950–51 mass departure after hearing of harsh ma‘abara conditions, delaying migration until forced flight.
• His early Israeli years are framed as a period of adjustment shaped by family dispersion and the afterlife of Iraqi Jewish community institutions.

• Resettled in Montreal around 1978 after an initial Israeli period, joining the growing Iraqi-Sephardi/Mizrahi presence in Quebec.
• His narrative links Montreal life to continued preservation of Baghdadi Jewish memory—especially language (dialect distinctions) and foodways (tbeet). 
• Interviewed in Montreal on 29 June 2017, he presents his biography as a lens on late Iraqi Jewish survival strategies and diaspora reconstruction.

This chapter traces Joseph Zagury’s trans-Mediterranean Sephardi trajectory from Moroccan childhood into Israeli youth migration and later circulation through France and Canada, emphasizing how education, language, and institutional work (kibbutz, army, operating rooms) produced durable forms of belonging across diaspora nodes.
• Born 23 Sept 1943 in Morocco and raised in a francophone Sephardi household; family origins are anchored in Safi (both parents born there).
• Childhood education began in French schools and later included Alliance Israélite instruction, reflecting the colonial-era educational landscape of Moroccan Jewry.
• He recalls a mixed environment where post‑1956 tensions…

s.t: Education & Youth Networks – French School, Alliance, and Jewish Scouts
s.d:
• Describes French schooling (‘école’) followed by Alliance, alongside participation in Jewish youth movements (Eclaireurs Israélites) that cultivated leadership and Zionist horizons.
• Narrates conflict with Arab peers on school routes, positioning himself as a protective figure for younger Jews—an embodied experience of minority life.
• Multilingual repertoire (French, Moroccan Arabic, later Hebrew/English/Italian/Spanish) becomes central to his later ethic that ‘language is culture.’

s.t: Aliyat HaNoar & Kibbutz Formation – Haifa to Hatzor/Ruhama (1957)
s.d:
• Migrated to Israel in 1957 as a youth through Aliyat HaNoar, arriving by sea (Casablanca → Marseille → Haifa) after a six-month camp period in France.
• Placed first in Kibbutz Hatzor and then Ruhama within a Hashomer Hatzair/Mapam milieu, working across agriculture and communal labor regimes.
• Frames kibbutz life as both discipline and belonging—shared work, collective socialization, and Hebrew acquisition through everyday immersion.

• Served in the Israeli military and describes participation in two wars, situating his generation within the state’s conflict chronology.
• Trained for and worked in operating rooms, including hospital work in Tel Aviv (Ichilov) and wartime medical tasks (Sinai transfers; prisoner care) aided by Arabic and French.
• This chapter highlights the transformation from Moroccan youth immigrant to Israeli medical professional within national institutions.

• Moved to France in 1966 to reunite with parents, rapidly entering clinical work after being tested by a physician in a small hospital/clinic setting.
• France becomes a site of professional consolidation and family formation: he met his first wife (a school friend), married, and had two sons (Yves and Robert).
• His mobility reflects the wider post‑colonial Sephardi diaspora in which France served both as refuge and professional platform.

s.t: Return to Israel – War Call-Up and One-Year Hebron Service (1974)
s.d:
• Returned to Israel in 1974, motivated by military call-up and an ethic of service; he describes a period of renewed enlistment and a year stationed in Hebron.
• Personal life shifted amid these moves, culminating in divorce after return to France and reorientation toward North American migration.
• This stage underscores how military obligations and family rupture shaped subsequent decisions about ‘home’ and stability.

• Arrived in Canada in 1979, undertaking professional re-credentialing and entering hospital operating-room work in Quebec, later residing in Ontario.
• Met his second wife (a nurse) in the operating room and built a new family life in Canada, while maintaining close ties to Israel and a multi-citizenship identity.
• His narrative frames diaspora success as rooted in adaptability: learning languages, understanding others’ cultures, and carrying Moroccan Jewish ritual memory into new civic contexts.

This chapter situates Kamal Gabbay’s trajectory within the Farhud-era dispersal of Iraqi Jews and the subsequent formation of Levantine and North American Sephardi/Mizrahi networks, tracing how Beirut’s francophone schooling, Mediterranean commerce, and Montreal community-building reshaped identity across multiple shores.
• Born in Baghdad in 1941 into a family combining professional and religious lineages: a father who was both dentist and Iraqi army major, and a paternal grandfather remembered as a rabbi.
• Family background includes extended kin engaged in imperial infrastructures, including maternal relatives connected to British railway representation in Baghdad and Syria.
• His birth…

s.t: Emergency Flight – Baghdad to Beirut by Lorry (Infancy)
s.d:
• At approximately three months old, the family left Iraq during the tense period surrounding the Farhud, traveling by large lorry arranged through his father’s army networks.
• This escape illustrates how military friendships and logistics enabled some Jewish families to exit quickly before violence and disorder fully unfolded.
• The move transformed his biography: although Baghdad is his birthplace, Beirut became the primary landscape of childhood formation.

s.t: Beirut Upbringing – Saniya Neighborhood and Francophone Schooling
s.d:
• Raised in Beirut (Saniya area), studying first with Jesuit ‘Frères’ schools and later at the Lycée Français, learning in French while speaking Arabic at home.
• Maintained a household with domestic help and a Jewish nanny who had accompanied the family from Iraq, supporting continuity of language and practice.
• Developed deep cross-communal friendships—Christian and Muslim classmates visited each other’s homes, played sports, and navigated the city’s mixed confessional geography.

s.t: Minority Precarity – Threats and Everyday Fear in Lebanon
s.d:
• Recalls intermittent threats (‘we will report you, you are Jewish’), producing a background sense of fear even amid Beirut’s cosmopolitan reputation.
• Describes moving through Sunni, Shi‘i, and Christian areas by train to reach school, generally without direct harm but with awareness of vulnerability.
• This chapter highlights the paradox of Lebanese Jewish life: social integration in daily routines alongside latent insecurity tied to regional politics.

s.t: Seasonal Lebanon – Aley Summer House and ‘Penguin’ Friend Group
s.d:
• Spent summers in Aley in the mountains, renting a house for several months; his father commuted back and forth to Beirut for work.
• As a young adult, joined a mostly Christian friend circle (‘the Penguin’ club) that organized trips, mountain outings, and nightly social plans.
• These practices situate Beirut within a mid‑century Mediterranean leisure geography—cars, seaside drives, and mountain escapes shaping youth identity.

s.t: Family Economy Shift – Dentistry to Import Trade (Beirut)
s.d:
• In Lebanon, his father was denied a license to practice dentistry—framed as discrimination tied to being Jewish—prompting a pivot into import trade.
• The family entered commerce in coffee, rice, wheat, and other staples, building a transregional business spanning Lebanon and the wider Middle East.
• Household life retained Iraqi rhythms (Friday and Shabbat meals, holiday observance, kosher foodways) under the guidance of his mother and nanny.

• Moved to Milan in 1964 with his brother to open a European office for the family’s coffee-focused business, using Italy as a logistical and commercial hub.
• Traveled widely across Europe for trade (England, Austria, Holland, Germany), improving English through work and expanding transnational commercial networks.
• Encountered documentation constraints in Italy (difficulty obtaining papers/passport), pushing him toward Canadian immigration.

• Arrived in Montreal in 1967 (during Expo), choosing the city through Iraqi-Sephardi ties and friendships forged in Beirut with visiting Canadian Iraqis.
• Opened a local office and continued in the coffee business across Canada, operating in French and English markets while maintaining Arabic for home and community life.
• Married in May 1969 in an Iraqi-style wedding; participated in the Spanish & Portuguese Synagogue environment and an Iraqi-centered social world in Montreal.

s.t: Family & Seasonal Life – Fort Lauderdale Snowbird Community
s.d:
• Developed seasonal life in Fort Lauderdale beginning in the late 1970s, later purchasing apartments that supported extended family visiting patterns.
• Describes a dense Montreal-origin snowbird micro-community in Florida, including relatives and friends living in the same building.
• Despite multi-sited residence, he identifies ‘home’ as Montreal and frames identity primarily as Iraqi and Jewish rather than Lebanese or Zionist.

This chapter situates Lilian (Liliane) Gozlan’s life within the global circuits of Sephardi mobility—linking Iberian-Ottoman ancestry, Egyptian Jewish urban life, East Asian mercantile routes, wartime survival under Japanese occupation, and post‑Suez displacement into Francophone and Anglophone North America.
• Born in Cairo in 1924 as Lillian Carmona, in a family that traced Sephardi origins from Spain through Ottoman Turkey before settling in Egypt.
• Remembers a paternal grandfather who ran a large warehouse selling household sundries and whose status was marked by a private horse-drawn carriage—an emblem of urban prosperity.
• Family language life was markedly polyglot (Spanish, French,…

s.t: Early Transnational Commerce – Cairo to Kobe (c. 1930)
s.d:
• Left Cairo around 1930 as her father moved the family to Kobe to source merchandise for Egyptian markets—dishes, toys, pens and other imported goods.
• Kobe’s small Jewish community (about fifty) improvised religious space by renting private homes for holiday gatherings, forming a portable synagogue model.
• Her formative memories begin primarily in Japan, where foreignness carried social curiosity rather than stigma and where she developed affection for Japanese neighbors and customs.

• Returned by boat (32 days) to Cairo in 1936–37 so her brother could celebrate bar mitzvah with grandparents, living near the Ismailiyah synagogue.
• Recalls fear of ‘the Arabs’ during this short Cairo period and limited integration into local childhood peer life, emphasizing family-centered experience.
• Her mother introduced her to Cairo’s Karaite Jewish quarter as a form of ethnographic witnessing, highlighting intra-Jewish difference and poverty.

s.t: Education & Daily Life – Kobe’s Canadian Academy
s.d:
• Attended first a small English school and then the Canadian Academy (a missionary-run institution), participating in daily sermons that explicitly referenced ‘the Jewish Bible’ so Jewish students were not excluded.
• Learned Japanese informally through neighborhood play; recalls Japanese New Year hospitality in which business partners hosted and dressed the Carmona children for several days.
• Describes bicycling widely and feeling socially ‘looked up to’ as foreigners—an inversion of later Middle Eastern minority experiences.

• As war intensified, the family relocated through Hong Kong, staying at the Peninsula Hotel as Japanese forces advanced; her father’s fluent Japanese positioned him as a translator.
• Survival depended on bureaucratic maneuver: advised by Spanish-speaking staff to present ‘Spanish origin’ rather than Egyptian passports, avoiding internment as ‘enemy nationals.’
• Lived through the war in hotel confinement with other foreigners, relying on reading, small networks, and extreme food scarcity funded by selling jewelry.

• After the war, the British repatriated the family to Egypt by warship due to Egyptian passports, settling in a large family apartment near the Ali Basha synagogue.
• Met her future husband Roger at a Jewish picnic, using English as cultural capital while building French through daily newspaper reading.
• Family networks fragmented across destinations—some relatives went to Israel, others to South America—foreshadowing the post‑1956 dispersion of Egyptian Jewry.

s.t: Marriage & Jewelry Trade – Cairo Domestic Life (1949–1956)
s.d:
• Married Roger (a Tunisian/French-connected background) in 1949; he entered/expanded a jewelry trade rooted in his father’s profession.
• Household life was Francophone, supported by Muslim domestic workers; she describes limited formal religious practice but continued holiday observance and synagogue attendance.
• Remembers a pre‑1956 period of relative normalcy, including a striking anecdote that Nasser visited synagogue on Yom Kippur in earlier years.

• In 1956, amid the Suez crisis, the family faced blackout conditions, street fighting, and expulsion orders: they were told to leave everything except clothing.
• Unable to access banks and limited in what could be carried, they departed quickly, attempting minor concealment of jewelry (a ring hidden in a hem) but leaving apartment and business behind.
• Describes a secondary rupture upon arrival in France, where belongings were searched and items stolen—compounding the experience of loss.

• Stayed about eight months in Bondy outside Paris with family connections while awaiting immigration papers, and placed children in French public schooling.
• France functioned as a bureaucratic bridge from expulsion to resettlement, made possible by her husband’s passport framework and kin networks.
• This chapter highlights how Francophone competence enabled relatively rapid educational integration for the children after displacement.

• Arrived in Toronto in 1957 to reunite with her older sister, initially living near Lord Seaton and later York Mills, rebuilding family life through schools and synagogue affiliation.
• Her husband re-entered the jewelry trade, first working for others and then establishing an independent business; she later joined Hadassah and the Oakdale club milieu.
• She continued to identify strongly as ‘Spanish’ Sephardi, reframing diaspora belonging through Iberian memory while living as a Canadian citizen.

This chapter interprets Lily Dabby’s life through the entwined histories of Iraqi Jewish denationalization, Cold War transit corridors, and postcolonial migration regimes, showing how language acquisition and education functioned as survival strategies across repeated displacements from Baghdad to Istanbul, Tehran, Israel, the United States, and Montreal.
• Born 3 July 1948 in Baghdad to Albertin and Sasan Dabby, in a household that she recalls as privileged within Iraq’s late-monarchy era.
• Her father held a prominent state-linked economic role: importer of fabric for Iraqi military uniforms and related state contracts, with visible markers of status such as multiple cars and gardened…

• Around 1950–51, the family traveled legally by plane to Israel to visit paternal relatives; Israeli entry stamps on Iraqi passports became decisive evidence.
• Upon attempted return, Iraqi authorities confiscated citizenship/residency rights, effectively exiling the family—she stresses they had not chosen the 1951 ‘exodus’ but were barred from re-entry.
• A remembered episode in Israel’s tent-city conditions (a childhood foot injury) illustrates the shock of early immigrant hardship that shaped later family decisions and resentments.

s.t: Transit as Permanent Uncertainty – Istanbul Hotels (1951–54)
s.d:
• The family relocated to Istanbul as a ‘stepping stone,’ living in hotels with constant readiness to depart and strict secrecy about past and future plans.
• She recalls Turkish nursery school, rapid language acquisition (Turkish rhymes and counting), and the child’s sensory memory of hotel life (kittens; a hotel fire and cold evacuation).
• This period frames displacement as a condition of suspended time: mobility without settlement, childhood shaped by fear and compartmentalization.

• Left Turkey at night under ‘hush-hush’ conditions and arrived by plane in Tehran (c. 1954–55), still without secure legal status.
• Initially received by a couple (Salomon Daniel and wife) and stayed with them before finding an apartment in central Tehran.
• The family’s ‘illegal alien’ status shaped intense parental surveillance: limited friendships, restricted movement, and fear of disclosure.

s.t: Growing Up Illegal – Tehran Isolation and Armenian Neighbor Support
s.d:
• Childhood in Tehran was marked by parental depression and isolation; schooling was erratic (tutors, homeschooling) because her father anticipated onward emigration to Britain.
• Armenian neighbors assisted with practical life (shopping, navigation) as parents initially lacked Persian and community ties.
• Family survival depended on offshore funds from prior Iraqi import arrangements—resources held in Europe used to sustain life at a near-poverty level.

s.t: American Mission Education – Community School (English Immersion)
s.d:
• At about age ten, she entered an American Presbyterian missionary ‘community school,’ with full English immersion, chapel services, and instruction in Christianity.
• She describes rapid multilingual mastery: Persian in streets, Turkish in sibling interaction, Arabic learned later through her grandmother, and English through schooling.
• Social life remained highly contained—friends existed mostly within school, with minimal home visiting due to parental fear and secrecy.

s.t: Legalization and Upward Shift – Tehran (American Express)
s.d:
• After a Shah-era amnesty for illegal residents (she estimates around age eleven), her father became the American Express representative for Iran, transforming household conditions.
• The family moved into better-furnished apartments, gained a car, and accessed leisure spaces such as the Gorgon Club (a German/European-oriented pool and tennis club).
• Yet Iraqi-Jewish clique dynamics persisted: as ‘latecomers’ and earlier non-Persian speakers, they experienced condescension within established Iraqi circles.

s.t: Israel Encounter as Teen – Family Reunion (1965)
s.d:
• Visited Israel as a teenager with her mother (c. 1965), meeting extended family largely based around Ramat Gan and experiencing family abundance for the first time.
• She recalls the trip as emotionally affirming yet not a desired destination for permanent settlement, given lack of Hebrew and the experience of being ‘plucked’ into a new linguistic world.
• This chapter also records ambivalence toward Zionism—resentment tied to their family’s hardship and exile—alongside continued familial ties to Israel.

s.t: Marriage and U.S. Migration – Madison, Wisconsin (1966)
s.d:
• Married Albert Abdallah Kutzadeh (Persian-Jewish background) in 1966 and moved to Madison, Wisconsin, where he held a university position in Middle East political science.
• She enrolled in university, rejecting a constrained domestic role, and built an English-language academic path in the United States.
• This migration represents a shift from refugee-like precarity to credentialed mobility, achieved through marriage and newly secure documentation.

s.t: Montreal–Israel–Iran Loop – Haifa Birth and 1973 Return
s.d:
• After a Montreal interlude (early 1970s), the couple moved to Israel (1972–73); her daughter Shantal was born in Haifa in spring 1973 while she pursued an English-literature master’s degree.
• They relocated to Tehran in late 1973 amid university unrest, then returned to Montreal after her husband regained a McGill position—illustrating repeated ‘home’ recalibrations.
• She describes 1970s Iran as politically turbulent (student riots) yet not personally antisemitic, distinguishing Persian politics from Arab nationalist rhetoric heard in Arabic broadcasts.

s.t: Anchoring in Montreal – Teaching and Post‑Revolution Family Flight
s.d:
• Settled long-term in Montreal after divorce, constrained by custody laws from leaving the province and rebuilding as a self-supporting educator.
• Earned education credentials and taught English (including ESL in French school boards), leveraging multilingual capacity across Quebec’s language politics.
• Her parents ultimately left Iran after the 1979 revolution, with her mother in Canada and her father departing before becoming persona non grata—an echo of earlier forced mobility.

This chapter situates Linda Ishayek’s life within the late history of Iraqi Jewry after mass emigration, foregrounding how educational institutions (Frank Iny, Shamash, Baghdad University) and shifting regimes (1958 revolution, 1967 war, Ba‘ath consolidation) shaped everyday caution, mobility, and the rare legal passport route that enabled resettlement in Canada.
• Born in Baghdad in 1951 and raised in a shrinking post‑exodus Jewish community (estimated 5,000–6,000), characterized by intense internal cohesion and limited intercommunal socializing.
• Early family geography is anchored in the Bataween area; her household later moved to al‑Masbah in 1963, tracking intra-urban Jewish mobility as…

s.t: Family Pedagogy & Prestige – Frank Iny Principalship
s.d:
• Her father, Abdullah Obadiah (b. 1908), was a mathematics professor at Baghdad University and later principal of Frank Iny, appointed as schools were consolidated after mass emigration.
• He had earlier studied mathematics at the American University of Beirut on scholarship, building English-language expertise and transnational academic networks.
• Within Frank Iny, Linda recalls a ‘privileged’ comfort: she was less intimidated by disciplinary figures because her father circulated through classrooms and oversaw school order.

s.t: Education – Frank Iny (Elementary) and Shamash (High School)
s.d:
• Attended Frank Iny for elementary schooling and Shamash for high school, within a predominantly Jewish student body and mixed faculty (Jewish, Muslim, Christian).
• Describes constrained Hebrew instruction due to government limits; foreign-language learning (English and French) was emphasized through imported teachers and external examinations.
• Extracurricular life included tennis/table tennis and weekly family visits to Club Mansour, yet social worlds remained primarily Jewish.

• Recalls a rare period in 1959 when travel was permitted; the family flew to Lebanon for about a month, staying in hotels and visiting mountain resorts rather than Beirut proper.
• This trip is remembered only faintly, yet it signals how temporary political ‘breathers’ enabled limited mobility for Jews who remained in Iraq.
• Lebanon appears as a nearby cultural horizon tied to her father’s earlier Beirut studies, even as everyday life remained Baghdad-centered.

s.t: Rupture and Anxiety – 1958 Revolution and After
s.d:
• Remembers fear after the 1958 revolution, followed by a relative ‘breather’ under Abd al‑Karim Qasim when Jews experienced several years of improved conditions and limited travel.
• After Qasim’s overthrow, insecurity returned; she recalls the climate of disappearances, with security forces taking men from homes and families living in constant apprehension.
• Her father used the Qasim-era opening for domestic travel (Basra, northern Iraq), touring as a family and sometimes with another Jewish family.

s.t: 1967 War Shock – Exam Raid and Street Fear
s.d:
• During the June 1967 war, she was sitting for baccalaureate examinations when a group of men entered the girls’ school, tore papers, and forced cancellation—an acute moment of vulnerability.
• The family relied on the single state broadcast; official claims of victory concealed reality, intensifying fear and uncertainty.
• After 1967, access to clubs and public leisure contracted further, while everyday safety depended on caution, silence, and strategic language-use in public markets.

s.t: University Barrier – Delayed Entry and Civil Engineering
s.d:
• After graduation, Jews were temporarily barred from university admission; she waited a year while her father provided mathematics instruction until he secured her entry through influence and respect.
• Studied civil engineering at the University of Baghdad, aware that political discourse was dangerous and that classmates sometimes attempted to provoke Jews into ‘Israel talk.’
• She recounts a self-protective strategy: redirecting suspicion back toward provocateurs (‘how do you know Israeli symbols?’), avoiding incriminating statements.

s.t: Legal Exit – Rare Passports and Departure (6 Aug 1972)
s.d:
• Graduated in 1972 and left Baghdad on 6 Aug 1972 with an Iraqi passport secured through her father’s former students—some of whom became ministers and intervened on the family’s behalf.
• Notes that many Jews escaped clandestinely via northern Iraq; her family was among the first ‘privileged’ cases to depart legally by passport.
• She left with a single suitcase of clothes and no photographs, emotionally apprehensive yet certain she would not return.

s.t: London Transit – Family Care and Sightseeing (10 days)
s.d:
• Spent roughly ten days in London with extended family, experiencing short-term care and sightseeing before onward travel.
• This stop illustrates the way kin networks provided immediate soft landing zones even when long-term resettlement was elsewhere.
• Her account highlights linguistic recalibration: exposure to British English in London before confronting Canadian English upon arrival.

• Arrived in Canada in August 1972, living downtown Toronto with her brother and registering at the University of Toronto for a master’s in civil engineering.
• Supported herself as a teaching assistant while adjusting to English variation and new academic expectations.
• Toronto served as an educational staging point before she sought stronger Iraqi-Jewish communal density elsewhere.

s.t: Professional & Family Life – Montreal Iraqi-Sephardi Networks
s.d:
• Moved to Montreal for work as a civil engineer, citing the stronger Iraqi Jewish community; later married Jamil Ishayek and built a family.
• Connected to Spanish & Portuguese Synagogue, including Iraqi prayer gatherings; transmitted Iraqi ritual styles especially around Pesach and Rosh Hashanah.
• Her later identity frames Canada as beloved home while retaining Iraqi origin as the primary descriptor when asked ‘where are you from.’

This chapter situates Mark Sibilia within the post‑1950s Egyptian Jewish diaspora as lived through Israel and Canada, highlighting how cantorial sound, Arabic cultural practices, and food-centered family networks carried ‘Egypt’ forward even after forced migration. His narrative shows identity as an everyday inheritance enacted through synagogue, language, and the social institution of shared meals.
• Born in Israel (exact town name recalled uncertainly), into a household shaped by Egyptian Jewish migration and Arabic cultural continuity.
• Early memories emphasize a spacious home with a garden of abundant fruit trees and the sensory geography of Israeli childhood play.
• He frames himself…

s.t: Childhood Move – Bat Yam and Shabbat Beach Walks
s.d:
• Moved to Bat Yam around first grade (age six or seven), situating childhood within the Tel Aviv coastal belt.
• Describes a weekly Shabbat rhythm: synagogue and Friday night meals, followed by long walks to the beach after Shabbat lunch with his father.
• Summer life centered on the beach and peer friendships, illustrating how Israeli public space shaped post‑migration belonging for children of Middle Eastern Jews.

s.t: Religious Formation – Yeshiva and Sephardi Liturgy
s.d:
• His parents ‘became religious’ in Israel; he attended yeshiva and was immersed in synagogue life and holiday cycles from a young age.
• He learned prayer and cantorial practice by ‘sticking’ close to his father, gradually being invited to lead small parts of services—learning on the go.
• His father is remembered as a widely recognized hazan in Israel, associated with radio broadcasts for the High Holidays, making liturgical sound a core family heritage.

s.t: Egyptian Cultural Continuity – Arabic Films, Sewing, and Foodways
s.d:
• His mother took him to Egyptian films and maintained Arabic language and sociability with friends, bringing Cairene cultural life into Israeli settings.
• He recalls women’s labor and artistry: his mother as an exceptional seamstress who could sew multiple dresses in a day, embedding skills within female social networks.
• Food anchors identity: meals featuring molokhia, ‘Moroccan’ fish, Friday-night couscous, and Shabbat slow-cooked dishes (‘dina’), with large holiday tables prepared without catering.

• Describes a dense kin universe: father with nine siblings and mother with eight, generating a constant calendar of anniversaries, weddings, bar mitzvahs, and large family cookouts.
• Extended-family rituals included intergenerational gift-giving, trucks of produce arriving for celebrations, and post-synagogue beach outings for large groups.
• He frames ‘family’ as the central Egyptian-Jewish inheritance—an ethos of gathering, debate, and food-centered intimacy that becomes his adult legacy.

s.t: Migration to Canada – Montreal to Toronto (with Brother)
s.d:
• Moved to Canada and initially lived with his much older brother, describing the shift as a new phase of sibling closeness after a childhood of distance.
• He then relocated with his brother from Montreal to Toronto, while his parents’ settlement pattern differed (mother remained in Montreal for a time).
• In Canada, he maintains Egyptian-Sephardi identity through synagogue affiliation, shared meals, and the affective ‘tone’ that emerges when Egyptian friends gather.

s.t: Later Life – Legacy Through Family Dinner (Toronto)
s.d:
• Married an Ashkenazi wife who learned and cooks Egyptian dishes, illustrating cross-ethnic Jewish family formation with culinary continuity.
• He emphasizes intergenerational transmission through weekly dinners and holiday gatherings—‘family is everything’—especially after becoming a grandfather.
• His closing message frames Egyptian Jewish culture as a model of intimacy and obligation: inherit it, practice it, and it returns ‘a thousand times.’

This chapter situates Maryse Ouaknine’s life within the mid‑20th‑century unraveling of Egyptian Jewish citizenship and security, linking a francophone Cairo upbringing to the shock of 1956 expulsion, Red Cross refugee transit, and long-term rebuilding in Montreal. Her testimony foregrounds how language learning, education work, and family foodways became strategies for sustaining Egyptian-Sephardi memory across generations.
• Born in Cairo in 1948 as Maryse Azuli, raised downtown in a mixed apartment building and street culture described as highly cosmopolitan.
• Family prosperity came through retail: her father Maurice Azuli owned men’s clothing stores, while her mother Margo Halak (born…

s.t: Family Memory & Jewish Cairo – Sha‘ar HaShamayim and Ben Ezra
s.d:
• Family memory locates major communal landmarks: her parents married at Sha‘ar HaShamayim on Adly Street, remembered through a wedding photograph and a Persian carpet still present when she visited decades later.
• Although she did not attend synagogue as a child, she narrates Jewish Cairo through ritual traces—kapparot before Yom Kippur (rabbi rotating chickens) and holiday meals anchored in home traditions.
• She reflects on Ben Ezra synagogue and the Cairo Geniza as a ‘treasure trove,’ underscoring Egypt’s deep Jewish archival presence.

s.t: Summer Geography – Alexandria and Mediterranean Leisure
s.d:
• Spent long summer periods in Alexandria—sometimes three months—staying with an aunt and uncle and living a beach-centered childhood.
• These seasonal moves exemplify Egyptian Jewish mobility within the country, mapping belonging across Cairo’s urban core and Alexandria’s coastal leisure economy.
• Her recollection emphasizes family togetherness and the ordinary pleasures that later contrast sharply with forced displacement.

s.t: Early Warning Signs – Arrests, Censorship, and Targeting (Early 1950s)
s.d:
• Recalls newspaper ‘blank spaces’ that she later interpreted as censorship, as well as demonstrations that pointed to Jewish-owned stores and led to arson.
• Narrates an episode where a beggar accused her father in the street, triggering police handcuffing and a bribery (baksheesh) negotiation to avoid imprisonment.
• Her uncle (father’s brother) was imprisoned for years after being accused of communist/Zionist sympathies, visited in harsh conditions where guards seized food.

• During the Suez crisis, police delivered papers ordering the family to leave Egypt within 48 hours; shops were chained and effectively nationalized.
• They departed with one suitcase each and minimal cash (described as the equivalent of only a few dollars), leaving bank accounts, furniture, and property behind.
• At the airport she remembers screams from families being taken for X-rays to check for swallowed diamonds—an auditory imprint of coercive departure.

• Left Egypt on a refugee flight (TWA) and arrived in Paris under Red Cross assistance, housed in a gymnasium converted into cubicles separated by sheets.
• Later moved through hotels and temporary housing, with parents barred from working and relying on scarce resources while awaiting visas.
• This transit stage marks the shift from comfortable urban life to bureaucratized displacement managed by humanitarian institutions.

• Spent additional weeks/months in Vichy in hotel accommodations, continuing a liminal existence while waiting for Canadian sponsorship and visas.
• Family survival depended on improvised domestic practices in confined spaces (small cooking setups, Turkish coffee in hotel rooms).
• The France interval (Paris–Vichy) lasted about six months before onward migration to Canada.

• Arrived in Montreal in June 1957 via sponsorship by an aunt and uncle; JIAS provided resettlement support and family members prepared an apartment ‘as if lived in’ (beds made, pantry stocked).
• As a francophone child, she was nonetheless directed into the English Protestant school system because Catholic francophone schools did not accept Jews—creating an early language dislocation.
• The family settled in/around Town of Mount Royal (TMR), first in a small duplex/quadruplex and later in an apartment on Plymouth, anchoring long-term Montreal life.

s.t: Teaching as Memory Work – Montreal (40-year Career)
s.d:
• Became a long-serving educator (noted as teaching for about 40 years), repeatedly using her own immigrant story to cultivate empathy for newcomer students.
• She describes ‘winding’ (misread as ‘winding’) as a lasting childhood shame that shaped her pedagogy and sensitivity to linguistic vulnerability.
• Later began writing her life story in French so grandchildren could inherit the narrative as an archive of Egyptian Jewish displacement and rebuilding.

• Returned to Egypt in 2008 with cousins as a ‘pilgrimage’ to say goodbye, visiting Sha‘ar HaShamayim and other Jewish sites under strict police permissions.
• Encountered confiscated Jewish belongings in antique shops (books bearing Jewish family names), refusing to purchase items taken through dispossession.
• Frames the visit as closure—‘the page is closed’—while emphasizing that the history should not be forgotten or ‘pushed under the carpet.’

• Interviewed in Montreal on September 22, 2022, she reflects on Egypt’s denial of citizenship to Jews despite centuries of residence and the forced, hurried nature of expulsion.
• Highlights intergenerational transmission through food (family recipe book, grandchildren cooking her mother’s dishes) and small embodied customs against the evil eye.
• Her testimony connects private domestic memory to public histories of nationalization, refugee transit, and Canadian resettlement institutions.

This chapter situates Maurice (Mossed) Benzacar within the long arc of Iberian Sephardi dispersion into Morocco and the mid‑20th‑century transformations of colonial rule, Zionist imagination, and migration to North America. His narrative links intimate family religiosity and Alliance education to Vichy-era vulnerability and to a later Canadian career of immigrant resettlement work that translated Moroccan communal ethics into institutional practice.
• Born in 1933 in Safi, Morocco (birth name Mossed Benzacar), within a family that narrates Iberian-Sephardi origins from Seville to Tetouan and then Safi.
• Paternal family memory emphasizes wealth, wheat commerce, and philanthropy; maternal…

• Moved to Marrakesh at age three when his father became representative in a wheat business, relocating the family from coastal Safi to the inland commercial center.
• Lived outside the mellah in a ‘riad’ with garden, domestic staff, and mixed (mostly Jewish) neighbors, speaking French with parents and Arabic with Muslim workers.
• Describes Marrakesh’s Jewish rhythms as intensely communal—family meals daily and especially Shabbat gatherings—framing the city as a ‘little Jerusalem.’

• Attended Alliance Israélite Universelle (Jewish-only) for secular studies with daily Hebrew hour, then cheder after school to learn prayer and reading.
• Highlights multilingual formation: French as household/school language, Arabic acquired through street and domestic interactions, and limited spoken Hebrew despite literacy.
• Youth culture included Jewish sports clubs (Maccabi-style teams; blue/white symbolism), reinforcing collective identity through recreation and schooling.

• Remembers Vichy-era antisemitism: Jews dismissed from French institutions, boy scouts disbanded as ‘French,’ and public culture saturated with Marshal Pétain imagery.
• Recalls episodes of French hostility (‘sales Juifs’) and segregated leisure spaces (e.g., swimming pool hours by religious group), alongside fear of imposed measures such as the yellow star.
• Also notes local protection: the pasha of Marrakesh intervened against instigated violence, illustrating the complex interplay of colonial power and local authority.

s.t: Zionist Horizon & JNF – Moroccan Jewish Public Culture
s.d:
• Describes a home and communal environment oriented toward Zion: listening to 1948 UN vote and Israel’s independence by radio, and associating Jewish pride with blue-and-white symbolism.
• Mentions fundraising infrastructures (Keren Kayemeth/JNF pledges, tzedakah boxes, emissaries/shlichim) as routine features of Moroccan Jewish life.
• As a teenager, attended Zionist youth meetings in Casablanca and considered aliyah, though family constraints delayed his personal move.

s.t: Work with American Air Force Projects – Morocco (1951–1957)
s.d:
• Worked from 1951 to 1957 on U.S. strategic base construction projects (e.g., Ben Guerir near Marrakesh), gaining English exposure and administrative skills.
• This employment linked local Moroccan labor economies to Cold War military infrastructures, providing technical experience later useful in Canada.
• The period coincides with growing uncertainty around Moroccan independence and accelerated Jewish migration planning.

• Married in 1955 to Élise Cohen (raised within a Moroccan family whose father was deported to Auschwitz after moving to Belgium), linking Moroccan Sephardi life to Holocaust-era European rupture.
• Traveled via Paris as part of emigration processing, visiting family in France before onward travel, and recalling the emotional impact of seeing El Al and Hebrew announcements for the first time.
• These transit moments illustrate how migration was scaffolded by kin networks and institutional intermediaries (HIAS/JIAS pathways).

• Arrived in Toronto in 1957, confronting cultural disorientation, winter climate, and early housing discrimination (‘no children’) despite being supported nominally by Jewish agencies.
• Recounts being mistaken for non-Jewish by Ashkenazi Jews and facing skepticism about Moroccan modernity, fashion, and middle-class life.
• Early survival involved precarious work (gas station, then milk delivery/management), while building social networks that later enabled community leadership.

s.t: Community Leadership – JIAS Volunteer and Staff (Toronto)
s.d:
• Became a key volunteer and later staff member for JIAS, insisting on dignity-centered resettlement: apartments prepared with furniture, food, and basic supplies before newcomers arrived.
• Helped successive waves of Jewish immigrants—not only Moroccan Jews but also Czech, Polish, Iranian, and Soviet arrivals—by finding housing, employment, and pathways to professional licensing.
• Positions this work as moral continuity with Moroccan communal life: a practical tzedakah ethic translated into Canadian institutional frameworks.

• Interviewed in Toronto on June 9, 2013, reflecting on Sephardi/Maghrebi memory, migration infrastructures, and the reshaping of Canadian Jewish communal awareness.
• His testimony foregrounds trans-Mediterranean Sephardi continuity (Seville–Tetouan–Safi) alongside modern disruptions (Vichy, decolonization, migration).
• He frames family and community cohesion—‘never separate’—as a core ethical inheritance transmitted to children and grandchildren.

This chapter situates Mayer Lawee’s life within the global geography of Iraqi Jewish wartime and postwar mobility, tracing how a Basra–Baghdad family navigated safety, commerce, and community through successive nodes from the Levant to South Asia, the Middle East, Britain, the United States, and Canada. His story highlights the role of Sephardi institutions—especially Spanish & Portuguese synagogues—and domestic ritual (Friday-night gatherings) in sustaining identity amid constant relocation.
• Born 29 July 1939 in Aley (Beirut district) at the onset of World War II, to Basra-born Iraqi Jewish parents embedded in regional commercial networks.
• His earliest biography is framed by wartime…

• As an infant, moved to Bombay and lived at the Taj Mahal Hotel during the war, with summers in Poona (Pune) in a mountain respite.
• Family life unfolded inside hotel infrastructures—transient yet stable enough for schooling of older siblings in Poona within a nuns-run setting.
• This chapter highlights Jewish wartime refuge-making through cosmopolitan port cities and commercial lodging rather than immigrant camps.

• Returned to Iraq for early childhood schooling (kindergarten) around ages three to four, living roughly a year or two in Baghdad.
• His father’s work linked to British wartime logistics: controlling car-part supply for British armed forces and avoiding black-market diversion.
• A family home in Baghdad later became leased to the French Embassy and was eventually confiscated by the Iraqi state, illustrating property loss through later political rupture.

• Spent a short period in Israel as the family explored business viability, including a car-dealership venture with another family.
• The interval is framed pragmatically rather than ideologically: the family assessed commercial feasibility and moved on when prospects seemed limited.
• This stage underscores Israel’s role as one node among several in an Iraqi Jewish family’s postwar search for stability.

• Moved to Egypt as another attempted site of establishment; Mayer recalls this as a period of stronger ‘community’ feeling compared to hotel life.
• A local synagogue affiliated with neighboring families (e.g., Mizrahis) anchored Jewish social life, even as the family remained mobile.
• Egypt is remembered as a key affective marker of childhood belonging despite later departures.

• In England, attended boarding school (Sandroyd) around age seven, beginning a long pattern of education-led mobility.
• He notes proximity to Iraqi royal history through school memory (King Faisal’s schooling in England and later violent overthrow in Iraq).
• English became the dominant family language across later moves, as Arabic and Egyptian dialects receded to comprehension rather than speech.

s.t: New York Chapter – Bar Mitzvah at Spanish & Portuguese (1949)
s.d:
• Moved to New York around 1949 (about age 10–11) as his parents sought business opportunity; he celebrated his bar mitzvah at the Spanish & Portuguese synagogue in New York.
• Describes an unusual overlap of Jewish and non-Jewish institutional life: he sang well and had choir experience in school pageants, carefully navigating religious boundaries.
• This stage underscores how Sephardi ritual institutions provided continuity amid rapid geographic change.

s.t: Ontario Boarding – St. Andrew’s (Kilt and Cadet Shooting)
s.d:
• Arrived in Ontario around 1955 and attended St. Andrew’s, a kilt-wearing school attached to cadet culture (48th Highlanders), where he became a competitive ‘sharp shooter.’
• As one of very few Jewish students, he describes persistent outsider status—social bonds among peers formed earlier, while he repeatedly entered midstream.
• Canada appears less as a single arrival point than as another institutional landscape navigated through boarding-school structures.

s.t: Montreal Home – Spanish & Portuguese and Iraqi-Jewish Continuity (c. 1960)
s.d:
• Settled in Montreal around 1960 and identifies it as ‘home,’ emphasizing stability after decades of movement.
• His father helped establish Montreal’s Spanish & Portuguese synagogue and guided community consolidation through partnerships and institutional leadership.
• Family continuity is framed through Friday-night Shabbat gatherings—large multi-family dinners, backgammon, and Iraqi foodways maintained across generations.

This chapter situates Mida Bassous within the interwar and post‑1948 history of Baghdadi Jewry, tracing a life that moved from francophone Catholic schooling and Jewish club culture in Baghdad to cosmopolitan employment worlds around Rose Debach, and then into the bureaucratic corridors of post‑1950 emigration through Italy and France before resettlement in Montreal. Her testimony foregrounds pride in Babylonian Jewish identity and the transmission of Iraqi traditions through food, ritual, and community networks in Canada.
• Born 10 March 1925 in Baghdad (Mida Toufik), one of seven children in a family she describes as unusually ‘avant‑garde’ for the period.
• Early childhood combined a…

s.t: Francophone Schooling – French Nuns’ School (Bab al‑Sharqi)
s.d:
• Attended a private French school run by Catholic nuns (rahbāt) near Bab al‑Sharqi, chosen because Alliance was geographically distant from the family home.
• Education was primarily in French with some English and Arabic; later she sought private English lessons to fill curricular gaps before girls’ access to Shamash expanded.
• This schooling produced deep familiarity with European cultural forms (music instruction, painting, etiquette), later easing adaptation to cosmopolitan work settings.

s.t: Urban Leisure & Jewish Clubs – Zawraa and Nadi Laura
s.d:
• Remembers a Baghdad of social clubs: men frequented Zawraa while women visited the Jewish ‘Nadi Laura,’ reached by horse-drawn carriage taxi (arabana).
• Her parents financed extensive extracurricular learning (piano, violin), reflecting a middle-class investment in cultural capital and feminine education.
• Describes the living room as a performance space—music, dancing, singing—highlighting Iraqi Jewish domesticity as both familial and socially outward-facing.

s.t: Family Origins & Trans-Asian Network – Father’s Hong Kong/Singapore Years
s.d:
• Her father’s biography embeds Baghdad within wider imperial/Asian circuits: as a teenager he was sent to Hong Kong for education and later lived in Singapore, returning to Baghdad only in 1923.
• Marriage history includes a first cousin-wife in Hong Kong and later remarriage to her mother (Victoria), illustrating kin marriage and transregional mobility in Iraqi Jewish elite networks.
• These family stories help explain the name ‘Mida’ as associated with Far Eastern naming usage and the layering of family memory across continents.

• Remembers the Farhud as a communal rupture though her immediate household was not directly looted, partly due to protective instructions in their area.
• Recalls relatives stabbed while buying fresh fish near the river and the fear of seeking medical care without trusted Muslim accompaniment.
• Her narrative underscores both the violence of the event and the uneven geography of harm, where some households survived through local protections.

s.t: Marriage & Rose Debach Cosmopolitan World – Baghdad
s.d:
• Married young (age 19–20) and entered a social world shaped by Rose Debach, Baghdad’s flagship department store, where her husband rose to senior managerial and buying roles.
• Through Rose Debach’s foreign clientele and hotel dining, she learned European etiquette (specialized cutlery) and acquired new culinary repertoires beyond Iraqi cooking.
• Wedding custom included a large henna celebration with belly dancers, followed by an unconventional post-ceremony honeymoon by train to Mosul—remembered as a ‘first’ in Baghdad.

s.t: Exit from Iraq – 1950–1951 and Lost Property
s.d:
• Left Iraq during the 1950–51 departure window as Jewish life became increasingly constrained after 1948; Rose Debach’s promised European posting was withdrawn amid anti-Jewish politics.
• Family assets were largely immobilized: her father died in April 1950, and properties remained in Baghdad; she recounts her mother’s strategic liquidation of cash just before freezing measures took effect.
• Her account highlights how emigration timing and financial tactics shaped later absorption—some relatives reached Israel with resources, avoiding ma‘abara conditions.

• Traveled to Milan in the early 1950s with the expectation that Canadian immigration processing could be completed in Europe after initial acceptance via British consular channels.
• Italy was experienced first as a ‘vacation’ with friends, then abruptly as bureaucratic dead end when documentation letters arrived too late and processing was reset.
• This stage demonstrates how migration was often contingent on paperwork and consular discretion rather than personal readiness.

s.t: Paris Waiting – Protracted Visa Struggle (≈1.5 years)
s.d:
• Moved to Paris because French language proficiency made it more livable; remained about a year and a half while pursuing Canadian immigration through lawyers and parliamentary advocacy.
• Describes consular antisemitism and demands for Iraqi ‘CID’ clearances, which Baghdad refused—forcing long delays and depletion of capital while living in hotels near the Luxembourg/Deux Magots area.
• Her daughter Yolande became bilingual (French/English) through this Paris interval, illustrating how children’s language acquisition was shaped by transit geographies.

• Arrived in Montreal in the mid‑1950s (she associates arrival with 1954/55), entering a small Iraqi Jewish milieu that included families such as Mashaal and Shahin.
• Recounts giving birth to her second daughter in Montreal in 1956 with minimal local support, highlighting gendered labor and improvisation in early settlement.
• Her husband rebuilt employment through department-store work and later Hitachi sales; she quietly built income through alteration work (non-Iraqi clientele) to maintain autonomy.

s.t: Community & Identity – Spanish & Portuguese and ‘Babylonian’ Pride
s.d:
• Joined Spanish & Portuguese synagogue life; her husband attended regularly, and Iraqi networks organized communal belonging through shared holidays and mutual aid.
• She articulates identity emphatically as ‘Babylonian Jew’—neither Ashkenazi nor Sephardi in her framing—expressing pride in the antiquity of Iraqi Jewish lineage.
• Interviewed in Montreal on 29 June 2017, she reflects on continuity through foodways, language, and repeated travel to Israel (over 25 visits) while affirming Canada as ‘home.’

This chapter situates Moise Amselem within the Sephardi geographies of northern Morocco, linking local origins to later professional and communal leadership.
• Born on July 4, 1932, in Larache (northern Morocco), in a city he recalls through deep historical layers (Lixus and its Roman legacy).
• Describes a childhood embedded in extended-family care and early confidence, framing ‘leadership’ as a disposition shaped from a young age.
• His Larache background reflects the multilingual (Spanish-zone/francophone) horizons of Moroccan Jewry, where educational mobility became a key resource.

This chapter highlights education as a transnational resource that structured later migration and professional recognition.
• Chose Geneva to study pharmacy, finding a well-organized Jewish environment (kosher boarding) alongside close academic supervision.
• Recalls administrative obstacles and the need to defend his diploma—an apprenticeship in bureaucracy that later reappeared in Quebec’s credentialing process.
• Geneva consolidated a portable professional identity: technical competence, francophone cultural capital, and mobility-oriented networks.

s.t: Early Career and Institutional Responsibility – Casablanca Hospitals
s.d:
This chapter connects early professional responsibility to wider political change and Jewish communal horizons.
• Established himself as a hospital pharmacist in Casablanca in his early twenties amid the departure of many French professionals. 
• Describes managing pharmacy work at a very large scale (up to 1,700 beds), emphasizing the rapid assumption of responsibility.
• Remained closely attuned to Jewish collective fate and clandestine emigration, showing how career, politics, and solidarity intersected.

s.t: Community Building and Family Life – Kenitra Pharmacy
s.d:
This chapter frames Kenitra as a site of both family formation and local institution-building.
• Purchased a pharmacy in Kenitra, married, raised children, and sustained an active communal life.
• In the absence of an Alliance school in Kenitra, he organized and mentored youth through the synagogue, teaching Judaism through informal education. 
• This stage crystallizes his role as an organizer bridging public service (health), communal leadership, and cultural/religious transmission.

s.t: Border Bureaucracy and Mobility – Tetouan to Ceuta
s.d:
This chapter foregrounds border regimes and the everyday technologies of movement.
• Recounts a nighttime attempt to cross a border: initially refused, then authorized via a telex from Tetouan—illustrating the fragility of mobility under surveillance.
• Used Ceuta (Spanish enclave) as a test-case for circulation, combining practical errands with confirmation that exit and return were feasible.
• Shows how migration is often preceded by ‘trial mobilities’ negotiated through documents, relationships, and small gestures of reciprocity.

s.t: Administrative and Political Pressures – Rabat/Kenitra Region
s.d:
This chapter explains how political constraints and schooling futures shaped the decision to emigrate.
• Describes how his ‘past’ continued to ‘persecute’ him through rumors and indirect messages—such as a child relaying that his father ‘cannot leave Morocco.’
• Situates the pressure within Moroccanization (especially in education and administration), where children’s secondary schooling options became a decisive trigger.
• Emphasizes a strategy of direct clarification with authorities, revealing how professional reputation could sometimes be used to negotiate uncertainty.

This chapter presents migration as a planned project rather than a sudden rupture.
