The episode turned an apparently luxurious journey into a reminder that migration required constant improvisation, even for a family accustomed to considerable material comfort.
Paris also confirmed the family's deep connection to French culture. Behar had been educated partly through French institutions and had grown up reading French literature, so the city formed part of a cultural world he already knew. Yet the family's destination remained Quebec, where relatives,…

s.loc: Port of Le Havre, Le Havre, France
s.d:
After the European overland journey, the family reached Le Havre to board the Homeric for Canada. A change in travel arrangements transformed their original air itinerary into a transatlantic voyage. The family's first-class tickets were converted into ship accommodations, giving Behar his first sustained experience of ocean travel and extending the migration from a series of European stops into a decisive Atlantic passage.
The delay of the ship also produced a final period of European shopping and preparation. Behar recalled his parents acquiring French cheese, pâté, preserved foods, and other provisions for the journey. The scene captures the material dimension of displacement: families…

The family reached Quebec City in October 1959, entering Canada through the Old Port. Behar remembered seeing snow for the first time and being struck by the monumental Château Frontenac, which he immediately associated with the elegance he had known in Egypt. The shipboard transition ended with immigration formalities and a reunion with relatives waiting at the port.
The family's arrival was also a social transition. Behar and his brother stayed temporarily with their grandmother, while their parents lived with relatives before securing housing in Saint-Laurent. The openness of Canadian relatives contrasted with the uncertainty they had experienced in Egypt. Quebec therefore became the…

After several months with relatives, Behar's parents secured an apartment in Saint-Laurent, establishing the family's first stable Canadian household. The move brought him into a more diverse school environment than his brief experience at Strathcona Academy, where he had struggled with climate, language, school culture, and the predominantly Ashkenazi Jewish social world.
Saint-Laurent restored some of the cultural familiarity he associated with childhood. He encountered teachers from England and a mixed student body that included Jews and Christians from several backgrounds. His academic performance improved sharply, particularly in French, mathematics, and other subjects in which his…

In Montreal, Behar's father encouraged him to pursue a conventional profession at McGill University. He entered the Bachelor of Commerce program with the expectation that he might become an accountant, but quickly discovered that accounting did not suit his interests. A vocational assessment instead pointed toward marketing, advertising, and sales, areas that connected his creative instincts with his family's commercial background.
Behar supplemented formal study with practical research experience at Green Shields, where he discovered an enthusiasm for corporate research and business analysis. He also supported his father's mergers and acquisitions work by gathering information on Canadian…

s.t: New York: MBA and North American Reach (c. 1970)
s.loc: New York University, New York, United States
s.d:
After completing his commerce degree, Behar followed advice from friends to pursue an MBA rather than accept a corporate career path that would have taken him to Edmonton. He enrolled at New York University, entering on probation because of differences between Canadian and American grading systems. He quickly made the Dean's List and embraced the practical, urban environment of New York.
The NYU experience broadened his North American perspective through exposure to the American Stock Exchange, working professionals, and New York's business culture. He later brought this knowledge back to Montreal, where his work with French-Quebecois family firms drew on American management practices,…

Back in Montreal, Behar became a marketing consultant, a role his father encouraged him to pursue after corporate employment proved unappealing. The work lasted roughly 25 years and allowed him to combine creativity, research, management, and bilingual communication. He helped small and medium-sized French-Quebecois family businesses apply North American business knowledge and develop stronger public identities.
His campaigns appeared in newspapers, magazines, radio, television, billboards, and on Montreal buses, including advertising along the Décarie Expressway. Around age 50, he stopped working full time to care for his father, who lived another twelve years. In later life, Behar…

Robert Sidi was born in May 1951 in Beirut, Lebanon, into a Jewish family whose histories connected Lebanon, Palestine, Bulgaria, and Turkey. His paternal grandfather left the Bulgarian army around 1900, passed through Palestine, and then settled in Lebanon. His paternal grandmother was also from Bulgaria, while his maternal family had longstanding roots in the Levant, with his grandmother coming from Safed and his grandfather's ancestors associated with Lebanon.
Sidi's childhood therefore began within a layered Sephardi Jewish environment shaped by migration, multilingualism, and family memory. His parents, Albert Sidi, an architect and engineer, and Sally Sidi, raised two sons in a largely…

Sidi grew up in Clemenceau, a central Beirut district near the French embassy, the American University of Beirut, and Hamra. His memories describe a cosmopolitan urban childhood in which French was spoken at home, Arabic with household staff, and English entered his education later. He moved easily among Christian, Muslim, Armenian, and Jewish friends, especially through school, beaches, clubs, and neighborhood life.
His family was secular but consciously Jewish. They celebrated Rosh Hashanah and Passover gatherings, including long family Seders featuring Lebanese and Middle Eastern food, while not observing every religious practice. Sidi recalled his maternal grandmother as a close…

Sidi attended College de la Salle, a Catholic school in Ras Beirut operated by the De La Salle Brothers. He remembered only a small number of Jewish pupils among a larger Muslim and Christian student body. Instruction moved among French, Arabic, and later English, reflecting the multilingual educational culture of Beirut. He joined clubs, participated in activities, and eventually headed some of them, making school a major site of social interaction beyond the boundaries of his family.
Although the school included regular Christian prayer, Sidi was not pressured to participate in confession, communion, or other rites. As a child he sometimes attended because he enjoyed the ritual and music,…

Like many families in Beirut, the Sidi family spent parts of the summer in the Mount Lebanon resorts, especially Aley. Sidi associated these periods with his maternal grandmother, who remained one of the most important figures in his childhood. Away from the city, their relationship unfolded through ordinary pleasures: visits to a café, sweets, conversation, and time together while his grandmother smoked a nargile. The mountain setting provided a seasonal extension of Beirut family life rather than a separate social world.
These memories also illuminate the family's linguistic and cultural fluidity. Sidi generally spoke Arabic with his grandmother but mixed in French when Arabic words did…

Sidi had a Bar Mitzvah, although he remembered religious study as difficult and described himself as only modestly interested in religion. A teacher came to the house, and he also studied with a rabbi. Because he struggled to memorize the prayers, another person stood beside him so that he could repeat the liturgy. The celebration itself was memorable for its large gathering, communal atmosphere, gifts, and return to the family home afterward.
The event illustrates the distinction Sidi drew between Jewish identity and religious observance. He understood himself as Jewish in an ethnic, historical, and familial sense, while his household remained largely secular and was not closely integrated…

For Sidi, 1967 marked a decisive before-and-after in his experience as a Lebanese Jew. The Six-Day War brought hostility from some neighbors and classmates who had previously treated his family as ordinary members of the neighborhood. Radio propaganda and public celebrations were directed toward Jewish residents, and Sidi recalled fear at school when the war began. His Armenian friend walked him home, and classes were suspended for several days.
The experience complicated an identity that had previously felt both Jewish and distinctly Lebanese. Sidi recalled that people later apologized and that relations with neighbors were partly repaired, but the earlier sense of security never fully…

In 1970, Sidi left Lebanon with his family and arrived in Canada. He had originally planned to go to England for further study and had sought greater independence by attending a school in Brummana, where he had his own room. Instead, his father's rapid application process through the Canadian, American, and Australian embassies led to Canadian approval within weeks. Sidi learned of the decision unexpectedly when his grandmother revealed that the family was leaving.
The move was not experienced simply as an escape from Lebanon. Sidi emphasized that many Lebanese Jews left with sorrow because life had remained meaningful and familiar despite mounting uncertainty. His mother had long imagined…

Rose Simon Schwartz was born in Cairo, Egypt, in 1950 and grew up in the mixed Attaba district in a modest apartment shared with her parents and paternal grandparents. Her father, Isaac, was an Egyptian-born banker of Greek Sephardi family background, while her mother, Odette Shamma, came from a Syrian Jewish family that had also settled in Egypt. The household was shaped by family solidarity, Greek customs, and a multilingual environment.
Her grandparents preserved Ladino across generations, while the family also used Greek, French, and Arabic. Rose remembers Greek music, dancing, communal meals, and an unusually close intergenerational household. The family maintained friendly relations…

Rose's childhood Jewish life centered on Sha'ar HaShamayim Synagogue, known locally as the Temple Ismailia and located on Adly Street. Her parents married there, and the synagogue was also associated with earlier family marriages. Rose recalls a magnificent interior with marble, separate spaces for men and women, and highly formal Jewish ceremonies. Her family attended together on the major holidays, while her father alone attended the synagogue on Shabbat morning.
At home, Shabbat meals were prepared from Thursday night by Rose's mother and grandmother, followed by Kiddush around the family table. Major festivals brought together aunts, uncles, cousins, and extended relatives, often…

s.loc: Lycée Français du Caire, Cairo, Egypt
s.d:
Rose and her brother attended the Lycée Français du Caire, where Rose remembers a socially mixed school environment. In her earlier years, instruction moved between French and Arabic, and students came from different religious and communal backgrounds. Her education reflected the cosmopolitan character of mid-century Cairo, while later changes in schooling exposed students more directly to the political transformation surrounding the Jewish community.
Rose's home language environment was equally complex. Her father spoke Greek, Ladino, French, Arabic, and English, while her mother spoke French and Arabic. The family's continued use of Ladino linked Rose to a Sephardi heritage rooted in Spain…

Rose recalls a gradual deterioration in Jewish life after 1948, followed by a sharper escalation in 1956. Families became increasingly cautious about speaking publicly as Jews or discussing Israel, while arrests, harassment, riots, and the nationalization of foreign and Jewish businesses intensified insecurity. Her father, Isaac, saw the changes through his work at Barclays Bank, where he was gradually pushed aside from his position directing letters of credit because he was Jewish.
The family then spent years preparing to leave. They possessed Greek passports, which made departure easier than for some Jews without recognized nationality, but the paperwork still took about a year. Rose…

In 1963, after years of preparation, Rose and her family finally left Cairo. They departed by airplane, carrying selected belongings while leaving furniture and other possessions behind. Rose remembers the emotional contradiction of the moment: she looked down at Cairo from the plane and felt that the familiar good life had disappeared, while her parents experienced profound relief at being allowed to leave.
The airport marked the transition from a childhood shaped by Egyptian Jewish life to an uncertain migration abroad. Rose's parents had spent years managing passports, finances, property, and the practical constraints imposed on departing Jews. Their departure was therefore not a…
s.cr: Willem van de Poll, Nationaal Archief, via Wikimedia Commons

s.d:
After leaving Egypt, the family traveled to France, where they stayed for approximately one month. The interview does not identify the French city, but Rose describes the stop as a decisive psychological transition. Her family stayed in a hotel, received assistance from a Jewish organization, and met three of her father's cousins who had left Egypt much earlier. For her parents, France was the first place where they could walk and speak without the constant fear they had experienced in Cairo.
The French interlude was also a transit point rather than the family's intended destination. Rose's Canadian papers had already been completed in Egypt, so the month was not spent waiting for…

s.loc: Old Quebec Port, Quebec City, Canada
s.d:
Rose's family did not continue from France to Canada by air, despite an initial recollection in the interview that they had. She corrected herself and explained that they traveled from France by ship, together with a father's cousin who had also left Egypt. The voyage brought the family into Quebec City, the first Canadian point of arrival recorded in Rose's narrative.
From Quebec City, the family continued by train to Montreal. This sequence captures an important physical transition from Mediterranean and European migration routes to Canadian settlement. Rose's account emphasizes the emotional significance of the journey: her parents had left Egypt with relief, but Rose, still a child, did…
s.cr: Philippe Du Berger via Wikimedia Commons

s.t: Montreal: Sephardi Community and New Life
s.d:
After arriving in Montreal by train, Rose's family was met by a relative who had already settled in Canada and served as their sponsor. JIAS provided immigrant assistance and helped the family find an apartment. Rose entered an English-language Protestant school system because French schools available to her were Catholic and did not admit Jewish students. The transition reshaped her education and social world while adding another language to an already multilingual life.
Montreal became the family's long-term home and the setting for Rose's later communal leadership. By the 2018 interview, she described herself as active in the Sephardi community, president of the Association of Jews from…

Born on 12 November 1938 in Baghdad, Ruth Meir entered a large Baghdadi Jewish family whose life combined religious observance, commerce, education, and urban prosperity. Her birth name was Albertine, also called Berta, and she later became known as Ruth. Her father was a businessman who imported spices and tea, with commercial links to India and England, and later traded silk fabrics.
The interview evokes a cosmopolitan Baghdad in which Jewish and Muslim residents interacted through business and neighborhood life. The family belonged to a substantial Jewish community, maintained a large household, and practiced a deeply rooted religious tradition. Ruth's childhood memories therefore begin…

At about age seven, Ruth's family moved to Alawiyah, which she remembered as one of the most prestigious areas of Baghdad. The family home was a three-story residence with two rooftops, two basements, balconies overlooking water, a large garden, and extensive domestic help. Ruth attended a Jewish kindergarten and then an English school, where her closest friend was the daughter of a member of the Iraqi parliament.
Her memories of this period emphasize the texture of Baghdadi Jewish life: polished clothing, silk and cotton linens, Persian carpets, gardens of roses, and a household organized around Shabbat and the Jewish calendar. Her father's commercial activity linked the family to British…

Ruth was still a young child during the Farhud of 1941, the anti-Jewish violence that transformed her family's sense of safety. She recalled her father's preparations before the attacks, including blocking the windows and reinforcing the doors. During the violence, the family remained inside, while her father hid in the basement because he feared that attackers would target the head of the household.
The event remained an enduring memory of terror. Ruth remembered hearing reports of people being killed, homes being entered, and possessions being stolen, and she described nighttime fear that continued long after the immediate danger had passed. Her testimony connects the Farhud to a broader…

After the establishment of Israel in 1948, Ruth recalled a sharp deterioration in the position of Baghdad's Jews. She described arrests, accusations of Zionism and espionage, public executions, restrictions on movement, and the withdrawal of citizenship. Jewish families increasingly avoided school, work, and public spaces because they could not know whether relatives would return home safely.
The community responded through collective strategies of mutual protection. Ruth remembered Jewish families gathering in synagogues where security made them feel safer, sometimes with hundreds of people sheltering together. Her account presents 1948-1951 as a period in which citizenship itself became…

The family's departure from Baghdad was prepared under severe constraints. Ruth recalled that their citizenship was revoked, their bank account was frozen, and they were unable to recover debts or freely dispose of property. Her father secretly concealed cash and valuables inside the wooden frames of their suitcases because the family could take only a small amount of luggage.
The departure also separated Ruth from the material archive of her childhood. She remembered leaving without books or photographs and losing the suitcase that contained the family's remaining valuables. For years, she accompanied her father to Sha'ar Aliyah in Israel to search for it. The story of the missing suitcase…

When Ruth and her family reached Israel in 1951, the welcome was sharply different from the prosperous home they had left in Baghdad. She remembered being sprayed with DDT, becoming ill, and then being placed in a temporary facility with narrow metal beds and straw mattresses. Food was distributed in communal lines, and the family waited for transfer into longer-term immigrant housing.
Ruth's account emphasizes the disorientation of early aliyah. The family arrived with limited possessions and no functioning financial base, while the young state struggled to absorb immigrants arriving from Iraq, Europe, and across the Middle East. The contrast between their former household and the…
s.cr: Benno Rothenberg / Meitar Collection / National Library of Israel / The Pritzker Family National Photography Collection, CC BY 4.0

s.loc: Beit Dagan Camp, Beit Dagan, Israel
s.d:
The family was transferred to a ma'abara near Rishon LeZion, in the area between Rishon LeZion and Beit Dagan. Ruth remembered living first in a tent and later in a wooden t'srif, without running water, electricity, or adequate sanitation. Food was rationed, bread was distributed from trucks, and communal bathrooms were primitive.
The family's long stay in the ma'abara lasted roughly six years. Ruth's father, once a successful Baghdad businessman, could not easily reestablish his profession and devoted himself increasingly to the synagogue. Ruth and her siblings worked to help save enough money for better housing. The eventual purchase of an apartment in Ramat Gan represented not simply…
s.cr: Avraham Malavsky; Israel Preker / PikiWiki, Public domain

s.d:
By the mid-1950s, Ruth's family had accumulated enough resources to purchase a new apartment in Ramat Gan. She described the move from the ma'abara into a finished apartment as a profound experience of luxury after years of temporary housing. The new home represented the family's gradual reconstruction of stability in Israel.
Ruth also married Ned Meir, another Iraqi Jewish immigrant who had arrived in Israel as an infant and grew up as a sabra. He studied at Alliance and later at the Technion, combining French, English, and Hebrew. Their marriage joined two Iraqi Jewish migration histories and became the foundation for the next stage of Ruth's life, including family formation, professional…
s.cr: Théodore Brauner / National Photo Collection of Israel, Public domain

s.t: Israel Defense Forces: Service and Responsibility
s.loc: Israel Defense Forces, Tel Aviv, Israel
s.d:
Ruth served in the Israel Defense Forces after moving out of the ma'abara. Her high dapar score led the army to consider her for an officer's course. A kidney stone temporarily lowered her medical profile and interrupted that path, but after her health improved she returned to active service and received military promotions.
Her principal responsibility was in a taksiriah, where she supervised confidential military material, including examinations and maps. She managed a team of eight women and remembered military service as a formative experience of discipline, confidence, and national belonging. The uniform, ceremonies, and singing of Hatikvah carried particular emotional significance for…
s.cr: Benno Rothenberg / Meitar Collection / National Library of Israel, CC BY 4.0

s.d:
After marriage, Ruth and Ned moved to Beersheba, where their young daughter Michelle joined the household. Ned worked in engineering connected to the developing industrial and scientific infrastructure of southern Israel. Ruth remembered the daily bus connection to Dimona, where he worked with instruments and suppliers from Canada and the United States.
This period placed the family within a rapidly changing Israeli economy. Ned's engineering career advanced through technical work, while Ruth focused on family life and the household. The experience also created an unexpected bridge to Canada: contact with Honeywell led to a Canadian opportunity and eventually prompted the family to consider…
s.cr: Yaakov Goren / Dimona City Archive via PikiWiki, Public domain

s.d:
Ned's work in Dimona connected the family to the technical world surrounding Israel's developing nuclear and industrial infrastructure. Ruth recalled his work with engineering instruments and suppliers, including Honeywell. He was recruited for technical expertise and later considered a move to Canada where he could pursue a master's degree while working.
The Canadian decision became a family migration rather than a short professional visit. In 1966, Ruth and Ned left Israel with Michelle and expected eventually to return. They did not sell their Israeli home or furniture, and Ruth remembered Canada as a country of snow, unfamiliar food, and uncertain housing. The family's move therefore…
s.cr: Alfred J. Pearson / Toronto History / City of Toronto Archives, Representative historical image

s.t: Toronto: Jewish Community and New Beginnings
s.d:
The family arrived in Toronto in 1966 and initially stayed in a hotel while searching for housing. Ruth and Ned quickly discovered the importance of the city's Jewish neighborhood network. A visit to Bathurst Street, where Ned found familiar rye bread, helped them recognize that Toronto contained a community whose food, institutions, and social life could make migration more manageable.
They rented a new two-bedroom apartment near Steeles Avenue and Bathurst Street, and Ruth gave birth to Tammy after the move. Ned worked for Honeywell, later moved to Stone & Webster, and eventually established Autocon Engineering. The family's Toronto life developed through work, children, housing, and…

Ruth's own professional career began after the family purchased a house in 1968. With a young child at home, she first earned income through childcare and household work. A friend involved in real estate then recognized her organizational ability and brought her into property management. She assumed responsibility for six buildings in Etobicoke that required extensive renovation.
Ruth negotiated with contractors, supervised conversions from oil to gas heating, renovated hallways and doors, and helped increase rents and property values. Her work earned a local reputation, including praise from a member of parliament who associated her name with neighborhood improvement. The episode marked a…

s.t: Bay and Bloor, Toronto: Corporate Leadership
s.d:
Ruth's expanding responsibilities brought her to major residential properties on Bay Street and Bloor Street. She managed new buildings, hired marketing and rental staff, handled tenant screening, collected rents, and prepared financial statements. She established La Habitat Management Inc., building a professional organization around the practical knowledge she had developed through earlier renovations.
The company was acquired by Pagebrook, and Ruth became president of Pagebrook Properties Management, overseeing approximately 115 employees. The organization expanded across Toronto and other Canadian markets, including Vancouver, Alberta, and Niagara. Her work placed an Iraqi Jewish…

s.t: Toronto: Public Company and Independent Leadership
s.loc: Mink Mile, Bloor Street, Toronto, Canada
s.d:
The public-company experience of 1987 was followed by a new phase of independent professional leadership. Ruth retained shares, established her own management company again, and secured AGF as an early major client. Her work extended beyond routine administration into strategic property management, financial reporting, staff development, and long-term client relationships.
Ruth's professional philosophy centered on respect for employees. She described treating staff as members of the family, listening to personal problems, and rewarding honesty rather than enforcing rigid hierarchy. Her career reached a high point while her children married and built families of their own. The same period…

s.t: Princess Margaret: Family, Loss, and Memory
s.loc: Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, Toronto, Canada
s.d:
Ruth's account of the final stage of Ned Meir's life is inseparable from the family they had built in Toronto. After a rapid illness, he received treatment at Sunnybrook and Princess Margaret Hospital. Ruth described caring for him through a devastating period and remaining attentive to his dignity, humor, and hopes for the family even as his condition deteriorated.
Ned died on 12 October 2000, and Ruth's closing reflections return to family continuity. She remembers a husband who wanted, in another life, the same wife, children, and grandchildren. Her own final wish in the interview is that her grandchildren will see the recording and know who their savta was. The testimony thus closes with…

Salim Mashaal was born in Kermanshah, Iran, in 1931, into a family whose social and economic life remained strongly connected to Iraq. His parents, Menashe Mashaal and Semha Daniel, were born in or associated with Baghdad, and Salim consistently described himself as Iraqi rather than Persian. The family maintained a large home in Kermanshah and moved seasonally between Iran and Baghdad.
Kermanshah was also a significant commercial center during Salim's childhood, a position he associated with the development of the oil economy and its location between Baghdad and Tehran. The household employed Jewish cooks and housekeepers from Mosul, reinforcing the family's Iraqi cultural environment. At…

Because Kermanshah lacked the schooling the family wanted, the household spent the winter months in Baghdad and returned to Iran during the summer. Salim recalled living with his family in a small residential enclave called Samqa, with a park nearby and a household staffed by a cook and chauffeur. The seasonal movement was routine rather than exceptional, and several relatives followed the same pattern.
Salim first attended Madame Aadil's school and then the Alliance Israélite Universelle boys' school in Baghdad. His education exposed him to Hebrew, French, Arabic, and English, although he did not complete the program, leaving around the ninth or tenth grade. He remembered Baghdad through…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, D. Gazala, Jewish Encyclopedia

s.d:
Salim's childhood in Baghdad culminated in the upheaval of 1941. He remembered the Farhud but said he retained few specific memories of the violence itself. He was active in the government Boy Scouts, and recalled being sent into the city to purchase household supplies during a period when insecurity had become visible. He also remembered watching aircraft attack an army camp from the roof of the family house.
The family left Baghdad after the Farhud and did not return to live there. Salim described their departure through Khanaqin, where a business associate of his father helped them cross the border without showing passports. The episode became a decisive break in the family's Iraqi…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, Library of Congress, Matson Collection

s.d:
The family's 1941 departure from Baghdad passed through Khanaqin, a border city on the route toward Iran. Salim recalled that his father's business partner, described as influential among local Muslims, had a house in the area and enabled the family to cross without the usual passport inspection. The journey was made in two cars, carrying a large family household at a moment of political uncertainty.
Khanaqin therefore functioned as a practical transit point rather than a new home. From there the family entered Iran and continued to Kermanshah. Salim's account emphasizes the importance of personal relationships and commercial networks in making the border crossing possible. The route also…

After leaving Baghdad in 1941, Salim returned to Kermanshah, where the family resumed its established Iranian residence. He remembered only fragments of the house itself, but described a substantial household supported by Jewish domestic workers from Mosul. The family's language remained predominantly Arabic, even in Iran, while Salim learned some Persian informally rather than through formal study.
Kermanshah was a relatively small environment for the family's Iraqi Jewish circle. Salim recalled roughly five or six Iraqi Jewish families, including the Shahrabani and Dallal families. He associated the city with an important commercial economy linked to the oil industry and the road between…

As a teenager, Salim traveled to Lebanon for a summer, recalling that he was about sixteen years old. The family rented a house and brought its accustomed domestic arrangements with them, including a cook. The visit was connected not only to leisure but also to the family's broader commercial network, since Salim's father maintained an office in Lebanon.
The Lebanese stay illustrates the family's regional mobility before Salim's emigration to North America. Salim remembered the business being managed by Yacoub Shaoul and described Lebanon as another place where the family combined residence, commerce, and social connections. He recalled eating mostly at home, with occasional visits to…

When Salim left Iran for the United States, his route passed through Lebanon and Damascus. He traveled by air to Damascus and then waited about a week for the next stage of the journey. During this pause, people connected to the family's Lebanese network helped him move between Damascus and Beirut.
The transit illustrates the practical role of family and commercial networks in postwar migration. Salim stayed with or was assisted by the Shaoul Yahuda family in Lebanon, who collected him in Damascus and later returned him there for the onward journey. His route was therefore not a single direct departure but a sequence of regional connections linking Iran, Lebanon, Syria, and the North…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, Library of Congress, Matson Collection

s.d:
Salim's journey from the Middle East to the United States included an Atlantic air route through Gander, Newfoundland. In the interview he recalled the sequence as Damascus, Gander, and then New York. Gander was therefore not a destination of settlement but an aviation waypoint in the postwar transatlantic system.
The stop marks a striking geographical transition from the Middle East to North America. Salim was about sixteen or seventeen when he reached the United States, traveling primarily for education. The airport's wartime and postwar role provides useful context for the infrastructure that made such long-distance migration possible. This chapter is representative of the transit…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, Royal Air Force official photographer, Imperial War Museums collection

s.d:
Salim arrived in Connecticut in 1947 to continue his education, following his older brother Edward. He attended Milford Academy, a preparatory school, and described himself as living at the school. The move represented a major change from the seasonal household of Iran and Iraq to an American educational environment.
At Milford, Salim studied in preparation for university and became part of a small network of other Iraqi students. He later continued into business studies at university. The Connecticut years are important because education was the immediate purpose of his first North American migration, while the family's business interests were already extending into New York. Milford thus…
s.cr: Library of Congress, Historic American Buildings Survey

s.d:
In 1949, the family purchased a house in New Rochelle, New York, while Salim and Edward were studying in the United States. Salim recalled the house as a substantial four-story property with a large lot, Persian carpets, and art. His mother lived there for a period while the children attended school, making New Rochelle a family base during the years of transition.
The house was eventually sold in 1953 or 1954, after the family's move to Canada, although Salim's own arrival in Montreal occurred in 1951. The New Rochelle residence therefore overlaps two stages of the family's migration. It demonstrates how the family maintained a North American domestic base while still managing commercial…
s.cr: Library of Congress, Historic American Buildings Survey

s.t: New York: University and Carpet Trade
s.loc: Washington Square, New York, United States
s.d:
During his years in the New York area, Salim combined university study with participation in the family's commercial enterprise. He attended New York University and studied business. The family's carpet operation already had a New York office, opened in the early 1940s, with David Dallal as a partner, linking Salim's education to an established commercial network.
Salim remembered the business as a wholesale carpet trade in which dealers purchased imported Persian carpets in quantity. He recalled the office near Fifth Avenue and Twenty-Seventh Street and explained that favorable currency arrangements helped make Iranian carpets competitive in the American market. New York was therefore both…

Salim arrived in Montreal in 1951 as part of a family migration shaped by immigration constraints in the United States. His account emphasizes that the family came through ordinary immigration rather than a refugee program. The first Montreal residence was in Outremont, where the family bought a house near the borough's city hall.
Salim described early Montreal as inexpensive and almost village-like compared with New York. The family adjusted to the climate by accepting the conditions of their new environment. This period established the practical foundation for his Canadian life: family settlement, commercial activity, and a gradual shift in social identity from an immigrant household to a…

s.t: Town of Mount Royal: Enterprise and Family
s.loc: Town of Mount Royal, Montreal, Canada
s.d:
After the family's first year in Outremont, Salim recalled that they built a house in Town of Mount Royal, at a time when parts of the area were still developing. The move accompanied a broader expansion of the family's economic activity in Canada, first through carpet wholesale and retail and later through real estate.
Salim described an early development project involving the Iraqi architect Naim Behor, who encouraged the family to purchase land and construct houses. Although the first group of houses produced losses, the family sold the remaining land and eventually moved into real estate. Town of Mount Royal consequently became associated with both family life and entrepreneurial…
s.cr: Library of Congress, Detroit Publishing Company

s.t: Montreal: Canadian Home and Iraqi Heritage
s.d:
By the 2018 interview, Salim described Canada as home. His reflections emphasized a practical philosophy of adaptation: accept the circumstances of a new country, build a life, and look toward the future rather than remaining fixed on earlier losses. He identified himself primarily as Iraqi in cultural terms while insisting that his children should be Canadian first.
His strongest surviving expression of Iraqi Jewish heritage was culinary and social. He continued preparing Iraqi food, speaking some Arabic within the family, and maintaining a strong sense of connection with other Iraqis. He also recalled the importance of Jewish tradition, family networks, and the endurance of Iraqi Jewish…

Sami Sourani was born on April 14, 1934 in Baghdad, Iraq, and spent his earliest years within an extended Iraqi Jewish family. He remembered living in his grandfather's unusually large house, one of the substantial residences of the Baghdad Jewish community, where several generations could gather. The household included a synagogue-oriented rhythm of life, a rooftop used for summer sleeping, a clay oven, food stores, and several Kurdish Jewish servants. His grandfather's routines, including early visits to the synagogue, fresh household production, and large Friday meals, became part of Sami's memory of communal life.
The family environment also connected religion, kinship, and material…

In 1941, Sami's childhood was marked by the Farhud, the violent anti-Jewish attacks that followed the pro-German coup associated with Rashid Ali. His maternal grandfather moved Sami, his mother, and his brothers to a safer family residence before the violence intensified. Sami remembered Jews remaining inside their homes for weeks, while armed mobs attacked Jewish houses, looted property, and killed residents. The family listened to cries from nearby streets and depended on cautious exchanges through a window to obtain bread and other necessities. The experience transformed the family's sense of security in Baghdad.
Sami's account emphasizes the destruction of trust as much as physical…
s.cr: Public domain, source image from Haim Saadoun / Ben-Zvi Institute publication

s.t: Baghdad: Jewish Schooling and Bar Mitzvah
s.d:
After the Farhud, Sami's parents kept his education close to home. He attended a mixed private elementary school and later studied at the Shamash School, a major Jewish educational institution in Baghdad. Although he had earned marks high enough to qualify for King Faisal College, his father rejected the boarding-school option because of distance and insecurity. Shamash was therefore both an educational choice and a strategy of family protection. Sami remembered its demanding classrooms, large enrollment, medical services, and links to a wider network of Jewish doctors and charitable institutions.
His religious life remained intertwined with schooling and neighborhood institutions. Sami…
s.cr: Beth Hatefutsoth Photo Archive, courtesy of Naim Dangoor

s.d:
During the late 1940s, Sami became involved in the clandestine networks that prepared young Iraqi Jews for departure. He joined a small Tnoah cell in which several teenagers studied Hebrew with a guide. Other groups trained participants in physical self-defense. Sami's cousin Jamil Sourani, who had received training in Israel, returned to Baghdad to help organize the movement associated with the emerging airlift. Sami was still a teenager, yet he was entrusted with practical tasks that linked ordinary families to a clandestine migration infrastructure.
One of his most striking responsibilities involved moving small amounts of money for Jews who could not transfer their savings through formal…

In 1950, Sami left Baghdad with his mother and brothers under the Iraqi legislation that allowed Jews to depart while freezing or confiscating their property. His father remained behind temporarily, hoping to recover assets. Sami remembered the restrictions imposed at the airport: gold had to remain in Iraq, money was sharply limited, and passengers could carry only basic clothing and personal possessions. He nevertheless carried books, recalling that he had about forty books with him. The departure was emotionally charged because his father remained behind as the aircraft prepared to leave.
The airlift was part of a much larger movement of Iraqi Jews, organized through rapidly expanding…

The flight from Iraq did not take Sami directly to his new home. In Cyprus, the family stopped for several hours and stayed in a British army bunker. The short transit was physically modest but symbolically important: the family had crossed out of Iraq and entered an international corridor created for the mass movement of Iraqi Jews. Sami remembered receiving a simple sandwich and a cup of carob tea, an improvised substitute for ordinary tea that reflected the scarcity of supplies awaiting the newcomers.
The Cyprus stop also illustrates how migration operated through a chain of temporary spaces rather than a single journey. Sami's account describes small aircraft, British facilities, and the…

s.loc: Lod Airport and Sha'ar Aliyah, Israel
s.d:
From Cyprus, Sami's family flew to Lod Airport and was taken to Sha'ar Aliyah, where new arrivals lived in tents. The transition was abrupt. Sami contrasted the family's previous home in Baghdad, where they had enjoyed relative material comfort, with the mud, wind, rain, and uncertainty of a temporary camp. The family remained there for about one week. The presence of a nine-month-old brother shaped their treatment in the camp, including the provision of a small lantern so the family could have light at night.
This first Israeli setting was therefore a space of both hardship and incorporation. The tent camp represented the immediate consequences of mass immigration into a state absorbing…

After the camp, Sami and his family joined an uncle in Petah Tikva. What they expected to be a short stay lasted almost eight months. The family's temporary arrangement reflected the pressures of early Israeli settlement, when housing, work, and education had to be assembled gradually. One brother spent time in a kibbutz, while the family continued to depend on relatives. Later, Sami's grandmother moved to an apartment in Ramat Gan, providing another stage in the family's settlement.
Petah Tikva thus became an intermediate community rather than a final destination. It connected the family to relatives, immigrant networks, and the expanding urban corridor of central Israel. Sami's memories…
s.cr: Benno Rothenberg / Meitar Collection / National Library of Israel / The Pritzker Family National Photography Collection

s.d:
Sami eventually moved to Jerusalem to study economics. His university years were marked by severe postwar scarcity. He described living in a converted military barrack with thin walls, insects, limited heating, and very few books. Students depended on tightly scheduled library access, and one teacher even encouraged them to use discarded wrapping paper for assignments. Food was rationed, employment was scarce, and the family had little money. Sami therefore combined study with paid work, seeking ways to support his parents while continuing his education.
His studies were strongly quantitative, emphasizing mathematics and statistics rather than economics as abstract theory. He first worked in…
s.cr: Benno Rothenberg / Meitar Collection / National Library of Israel / Israel State Archives

s.d:
Before settling into government work in Jerusalem, Sami worked in Tel Aviv for the philatelic service. The position introduced him to administrative work and to a professional environment in which his analytical ability became visible. His supervisor, a German immigrant, noticed that Sami did not simply execute instructions mechanically. Instead, he examined problems and searched for better methods. The supervisor encouraged him to pursue university study and promised to preserve work for him whenever he had a few free days.
The Tel Aviv chapter is therefore less a story of permanent residence than of professional transition. It shows how Sami moved from the economic insecurity of immigrant…
s.cr: Israel Preker via PikiWiki Israel; original photograph by Hans Pinn

s.d:
Sami arrived in Canada by plane in 1963, after his years of study and work in Israel. His Canadian career centered on Ottawa, where he entered federal government work and became deeply involved in the analysis of public procurement, accounting, and economic policy. He described arriving in a quiet capital whose streets emptied early in the evening. Rather than treating the unfamiliar environment as a barrier, he studied the structure of government, its accounting systems, and the relationships between procurement decisions and employment.
Sami developed economic models that translated purchasing decisions into their effects on jobs rather than simply comparing monetary values. He later said…

Although much of Sami's professional life unfolded in Ottawa, Montreal became the family's principal Canadian home. The interview was recorded there in 2017, and Sami repeatedly described Canada as home and himself as Canadian. His parents eventually joined him in Montreal, while his brothers developed professional lives in Canada and the United States. Sami's family thus became part of a wider Iraqi Jewish diaspora whose members rebuilt careers and households across North America.
Montreal also became a site of continued Sephardi and Mizrahi heritage. Sami identified himself as Mizrahi, at least in part, and remained connected to the Spanish and Portuguese Synagogue. He recalled the…
s.cr: Office national du film du Canada / National Film Board of Canada

s.d:
Sandra Koukou describes her paternal family as tracing its roots to Babylon, a foundational point of Mesopotamian Jewish memory. In her account, the family’s long history in the region precedes the twentieth-century movements that eventually carried the Koukou family from Iraq into Iran. This remembered antiquity matters because Sandra repeatedly frames later migration not as a break with the past, but as the continuation of an Iraqi Jewish identity shaped by language, food, kinship, and communal institutions.
The interview presents Babylon as a cultural point of origin rather than a documented residence for Sandra herself. She dates the family’s connection to the city to roughly 2,600 years…

Haspel Koukou, Sandra’s paternal grandfather, moved the family from Basra, Iraq, to Iran in the 1930s. Sandra recalls that this relocation occurred before the family directly experienced the persecution associated with the Farhud. The move established the geographic pattern that would define the family’s twentieth-century history: an Iraqi Jewish household carrying its language, customs, and communal loyalties into a new Persian setting while remaining conscious of its origins.
Basra remained an important reference point in Sandra’s understanding of family identity. Her grandfather Haspel and grandmother Naima were both from Iraq, and the paternal family continued to speak Arabic at home…

Haspel Koukou moved his family onward to Isfahan after being invited to participate in a car dealership. There he pursued a distinctly communal project: building a Jewish school for children who lacked a modern educational setting. Sandra’s account emphasizes his desire for a Western education and his determination to provide Jewish children with desks and chairs rather than leaving them to study on the floor.
The school story is preserved in the memoir Sandra co-wrote with her father, Yusef Koukou. To raise funds, Haspel sought access to deteriorated Torah scrolls and eventually carried them from the synagogue with his son, accompanied, as Sandra recalls it, by song and dance during a…

Haspel Koukou later moved the entire paternal household, including his five children, from Isfahan to Tehran. Sandra dates the move to approximately 1943, when her father Yusef Koukou was nineteen. The relocation occurred during World War II, when Iran had become strategically important to the Allied war effort and a major corridor for supplies.
In Tehran, Haspel continued his efforts to sustain an Iraqi Jewish community. Sandra recalls that a wealthy Jewish businessman, Meir Abdullah, helped establish a synagogue after Haspel appealed to him to create a permanent place of worship. The family’s move therefore brought together Iraqi Jewish identity, Tehran community life, and wartime economic…

Sandra’s maternal family followed a different wartime route. Her mother, Evelyn Dudi, was born across the river from Basra, while her uncle lived in Pune, India. During World War II, Evelyn’s mother, Masouda, sent her seven children by boat toward India because she feared for their safety amid political instability in Iran.
The children could not initially reach their intended port and were assisted by a Muslim woman who transported them onward by train to their uncle in Pune. Sandra remembers this as a moment when the children might otherwise have been trafficked, and she emphasizes the uncle’s role in sheltering them within an Iraqi Jewish community. Pune became part of the maternal…

s.loc: National Museum of Iran, Tehran, Iran
s.d:
Sandra Koukou was born in Tehran on 30 July 1956, into an Iraqi Jewish family that had established itself in Iran. She recalls a prosperous childhood in a large family home with a garden, fruit trees, and vegetable patches, while her grandparents lived on the floor below. Her grandfather’s Arabic radio broadcasts and family gatherings preserved a strong emotional connection to Iraq.
Sandra attended the Community School of Tehran, where instruction was primarily in English, with French and Persian also part of her education. She describes the school as an international environment containing students from many countries, religions, and languages. At home, her parents and grandparents spoke…

s.loc: Rhode Island School of Design, Providence, United States
s.d:
As a young artist, Sandra Koukou pursued formal training at the Rhode Island School of Design in Providence, Rhode Island. She recalls receiving strong recommendations from her teachers and following the same broader educational current as many of her internationally educated peers, who continued their studies in the United States and Europe.
Her years in Providence coincided with the final years of the Shah’s Iran and the political upheaval leading to the 1979 Iranian Revolution. Sandra describes becoming increasingly anxious about her family and especially her father’s factory interests in Iran. Although she was building an independent artistic life in the United States, family…

Sandra returned to Tehran in early 1980, after the Iranian Revolution, because she feared for her family and her father’s business. Her father, Yusef Koukou, was subsequently imprisoned at Evin Prison after being caught up in the revolutionary authorities’ prosecution of his Muslim business partner and as a Jewish capitalist whose factory was strategically important.
For roughly two years Sandra and her mother pursued every possible avenue to secure his release. She describes visits, court procedures, and a dramatic confrontation at the prison gates, eventually persuading a judge to reopen the dormant case file. Her father was sentenced to several years but was not executed. During…

While her father remained imprisoned, Sandra worked for a Belgian company involved in the construction of copper industries in Kerman, southeastern Iran. The project was part of a major industrial effort, and Sandra’s work placed her inside the administrative infrastructure connecting Tehran offices with a large construction site.
She reorganized hundreds of shipment files so that each ship, plane, and truck had a complete record containing bills of lading, insurance papers, correspondence, and packing lists. The work required navigating Iranian bureaucracy during the Iran-Iraq War, when industrial materials and steel structures were moving through the country under difficult conditions.…

Sandra’s industrial work also connected her to Bandar Abbas, the Persian Gulf port where shipments for the copper project accumulated. She recalls that roughly 300 files documented materials arriving by different modes of transport, but Iranian administrative delays left the cargo sitting in storage and accumulating fees.
By reorganizing the paperwork, Sandra could trace each shipment through its bill of lading, insurance documents, correspondence, and packing lists, allowing workers to retrieve the records needed for particular components. The port, formerly known in the period’s changing political vocabulary as Bandar Khomeini in Sandra’s recollection, became a logistical node linking the…

Sandra left Iran for Belgium after marrying a Christian engineer connected to the industrial project. She describes the departure as a chance to escape the restrictions of revolutionary Iran and to regain the freedom to study, work, and live as a woman outside the surveillance and fear that had marked her family’s years after 1979.
She lived in the Brussels area for approximately eight years. Her daughter was born in Anderlecht in 1984, while her son was born in the United States in 1987. Sandra spoke French with her husband, drawing on the language she had learned at the Community School in Tehran. Belgium was therefore both a refuge from revolutionary Iran and a complex new domestic…

During Sandra’s eight years in Belgium, approximately one and a half years were spent in Abu Dhabi, where her husband was involved in building three power stations. Sandra and her young daughter lived there during this professional posting, extending the family’s already international pattern of movement.
The Abu Dhabi period belongs to a broader expatriate world in which engineering contracts, industrial construction, and professional mobility linked the Persian Gulf to European and Middle Eastern households. For Sandra, however, this mobility was inseparable from the emotional aftermath of Iran. She had left behind her father’s imprisonment and a family still struggling to exit the…

s.loc: Spanish and Portuguese Synagogue, Montreal, Canada
s.d:
In 1990, Sandra moved with her husband and children to Montreal. Canada offered a practical destination for a bilingual family seeking greater stability, and Montreal already contained an established Iraqi Jewish community. Sandra describes the move as the point at which she could finally place her children in Jewish schools and begin learning more deeply about her own heritage.
Her children attended École Maimonide and later Herzliah High School. Sandra became active in the Spanish and Portuguese Synagogue of Montreal, and she worked with her father on his memoir, helping transform his prison experience and Jewish reflections into a family record. In Montreal, she increasingly understood…

Sassoon Shahmoon was born in Jerusalem in 1934, the first child of Ezra Eliyah Shahmoon and Lydia Aziza Haim. His family embodied a distinctly mobile Iraqi Jewish world extending from Baghdad through Shanghai and Bombay to Palestine. His father had left Baghdad as a young man for commercial opportunities in China, while his mother had been born and educated in Bombay in a strongly British cultural environment.
The interview presents Jerusalem less as a remembered childhood landscape than as the point at which several Sephardi and Iraqi Jewish family histories converged. Shahmoon retained little direct memory of the city because he left while very young, yet his later account repeatedly…
s.cr: Government Press Office, National Photo Collection of Israel

s.t: Kent: Wartime Refuge and Family Shelter
s.d:
Around 1938, the Shahmoon family left Jerusalem for England, settling not in London but on an uncle's large estate in Kent. Shahmoon recalled that the estate contained several houses and provided a temporary family setting as political uncertainty intensified in Europe. The family remained there until approximately the beginning of the Second World War, when the next stage of their journey became necessary.
This Kent interval was brief but formative. It placed a young Iraqi Jewish child within an English environment before the family crossed the Atlantic. Shahmoon later returned to Kent as an adult, remembering its landscape and the view toward the White Cliffs of Dover. The episode…

s.loc: Roslyn Elementary School, Westmount, Montreal, Canada
s.d:
With the outbreak of war, the family traveled by convoy across the Atlantic and arrived in Montreal around 1940. Shahmoon remembered entering Canadian life through the Roslyn School, where he joined the class of the future poet Leonard Cohen. The family remained in Montreal for about one year, establishing a temporary North American foothold before moving onward to the United States.
Montreal was thus both a wartime refuge and an early site of cultural transition. Shahmoon arrived as a child carrying an inherited Iraqi Jewish religious world into a new urban setting. His recollections of school, family correspondence, and the later return of relatives show how Montreal remained connected to…
s.cr: Bibliothèque et Archives nationales du Québec

s.t: New York: Family Reunion and Grandparents
s.loc: 737 Park Avenue, New York, United States
s.d:
After roughly a year in Montreal, the family moved to New York because Shahmoon's paternal grandparents had also reached the city. His grandparents, originally from Iraq, became important figures in his childhood and lived with an aunt and uncle in Manhattan. Shahmoon remembered his grandfather as a particularly observant Iraqi Jew and his grandmother as quiet and reserved.
The New York reunion brought the family into a dense urban setting where Sephardi practices were maintained alongside an American social world. Shahmoon learned some Judaic Arabic from his grandparents because they did not speak English. Their household also became a place where relatives gathered for Rosh Hashanah,…

s.t: Upper East Side: Sephardi Family Life
s.loc: Park Avenue and East 85th Street, New York, United States
s.d:
By the end of the Second World War, Shahmoon's grandparents were firmly established in New York, living in a large apartment near Park Avenue. The location became a family center where relatives gathered for holidays and where Shahmoon experienced the domestic texture of an Iraqi Jewish household. He recalled food, conversation, prayer, and the distinctive customs that shaped his early understanding of Jewish life.
Among his strongest memories was the family's Passover practice of pouring wine for the plagues and dropping it from a high apartment window. Such recollections reveal how inherited Sephardi customs were preserved through playful and highly local forms in Manhattan. The apartment…

s.t: Kehilath Jeshurun: Bar Mitzvah and Ritual
s.loc: Congregation Kehilath Jeshurun, New York, United States
s.d:
As a teenager, Shahmoon developed a more formal Jewish education in New York. He had his bar mitzvah at Kehilath Jeshurun under Rabbi Joseph Lookstein. The service combined an Ashkenazi melody with Sephardi pronunciation, a combination Shahmoon remembered as unusual for the synagogue at the time and emblematic of his family's religious background.
The episode illuminates the negotiation of Sephardi identity within an American Orthodox environment. At home, Shahmoon had learned to read with the pronunciation used by his family, while his formal training introduced him to a different liturgical setting. His later recollection of Judeo-Arabic, Shabbat, zemirot, and holiday observance shows that…

s.t: Ramaz: Jewish Education and Urban Commuting
s.loc: Ramaz Upper School, New York, United States
s.d:
After elementary school, Shahmoon's father insisted that he continue his Jewish education at Ramaz. As a boy living in New Rochelle, Shahmoon traveled by train into Manhattan on weekdays, making the journey to attend the school. He later described the education as good, although he felt that his late start had limited the depth of his preparation.
Ramaz became a significant institutional bridge between the family's Iraqi Jewish traditions and the Modern Orthodox educational culture of New York. The daily commute also linked suburban family life to the religious and intellectual center of the Upper East Side. Shahmoon's memories of liturgy, Hebrew reading, and family practice suggest that…

s.t: Jerusalem: Return Visit and Family Ties
s.d:
Around 1960, after completing his schooling, Shahmoon made a return journey to Israel, traveling by way of England. He recalled that his father routinely stopped in England to visit his sister, and the journey reflected the family's continuing connections across the Jewish world. Shahmoon arrived in Israel in a distinctive red English sports car, an object that attracted attention in the streets.
The visit also illustrates the continuing importance of Israel within the family's emotional geography. Shahmoon's father maintained a strong attachment to the country and later kept a house in Herzliya, visiting regularly. For Shahmoon, travel to Israel became one strand in a larger pattern of…

s.t: East Hampton: Summer Community and Courtship
s.loc: East Hampton Village, New York, United States
s.d:
During the years before his marriage, Shahmoon spent summers in East Hampton, where people rented shared houses and the seasonal setting brought together a social circle of unmarried adults. He had been returning there for several years when he met Barbara, who would become his wife. The interview places their relationship within a distinctly New York social geography that extended beyond the city into Long Island's summer communities.
This period marked a transition from inherited family structures toward a household of his own. Shahmoon recalled setting himself a personal deadline for marriage, influenced partly by the example of his father. The East Hampton years therefore represent more…
s.cr: Samuel H. Gottscho, Library of Congress

s.t: New York: Marriage and Family Formation
s.d:
Shahmoon married Barbara at age 44, after the couple had been together for several years. The marriage marked a decisive shift in his personal relationship to Jewish observance. He explained that he had not been especially observant when he first met Barbara, but that having children made the transmission of Jewish identity increasingly important to him.
Family life also reactivated inherited ritual practices. When their son David was born, the family celebrated his brit milah at the Spanish and Portuguese Synagogue in New York. Shahmoon's later reflections connect marriage, parenthood, and religious continuity, showing how migration history became a lived family tradition rather than simply…
s.cr: Thomas J. O'Halloran, Library of Congress

s.d:
Around 1987, Shahmoon returned to Montreal, a city that had already been part of his childhood migration. The return was reinforced by long-standing connections to Iraqi Jewish friends and business networks. His father, who had developed a reputation as a successful investor, had been encouraged by Montreal associates to purchase farmland around St-Laurent and Pointe-Claire before the construction of major highways transformed the landscape.
Montreal therefore represented both return and continuity. Shahmoon's adult life remained linked to the city's commercial and communal networks, while his family's experience reflected the broader mobility of Iraqi Jewish families across North America.…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons contributor, representative modern image

s.t: Yemin Moshe: Family Care in Jerusalem
s.d:
In 1992, Shahmoon spent a year in Jerusalem, renting a house in Yemin Moshe while caring for his father. His sisters joined them for shorter periods, and the arrangement reflected the family's continuing attachment to Israel and to the places that had shaped earlier generations. Shahmoon's father, by then an elderly man, preferred to live in Israel and had spent many years maintaining a house in Herzliya.
The Yemin Moshe period brought the migration story into a final stage of intergenerational care. Shahmoon returned to the region not as a child migrant but as an adult son accompanying an aging parent. The setting also linked his contemporary family life to the earlier Jerusalem of his…

Sassoon Shahmoon was living in Montreal at the time of his 2018 Sephardi Voices interview. He described the move to Montreal as a good decision for his family, emphasizing the city's suitability for raising children and the importance of institutions such as Akiva School. The family continued to live there and maintained connections with both Sephardi and broader Jewish communal life.
By this stage, Shahmoon identified himself as an immigrant, a Canadian and American citizen, a businessman, and an observant Jew. He emphasized the importance of transmitting Jewish identity to his children and remembered the rituals of his upbringing as a lasting inheritance. Montreal thus became not merely a…

Steve Acre, born Sabih Azra Ereb in Baghdad in 1932, grew up as the seventh of nine children in an Iraqi Jewish family whose recent history connected Basra commerce with Baghdad urban life. His father had moved the family north after the losses of the First World War, and Baghdad became the setting for Steve's childhood, schooling, family responsibilities, and encounters with a diverse urban society.
At school he studied in the Alliance system, where French and English complemented the Arabic spoken at home. He remembered neighborhoods containing Jewish, Muslim, and Christian families, as well as summer work at the Alwatany cinema, where he translated English dialogue into Arabic. These…

Although Steve Acre was born in Baghdad, his family story remained closely tied to Basra, where his parents had married and where his maternal relatives continued to live. The city represented an older family world shaped by Jewish commerce, shipping, warehouses, and connections across the Persian Gulf and India.
In 1949, Basra became the first stage of Steve's clandestine departure from Iraq. Traveling with his brother Joseph and other young Jews, he reached the city after leaving Baghdad and stayed for about three weeks with his aunt while preparing to cross toward Iran. The move transformed Basra from a family memory into a point of departure within a wider Jewish refugee migration shaped…

From Basra, Steve Acre and a group of sixteen young men attempted to cross the Shatt al-Arab toward Iran. Their first two attempts nearly ended in capture. On the third attempt, an intermediary drove them toward the frontier, then abandoned the truck after seeing border police. The group hid among bushes and continued on foot.
For two days they traveled by night and concealed themselves by day, navigating partly through the stars. With help from local farmers, who accepted gold coins, they eventually crossed the river in a narrow balam boat shortly after midnight. The crossing was illegal and depended on timing, secrecy, and assistance from people who understood the patrols. The river thus…

After crossing the Shatt al-Arab, Steve Acre entered Iran and reached Abadan, where members of the local Jewish underground were waiting during the night to receive refugees. The city, an important oil center on the river, became a temporary refuge rather than a destination. Steve and the other travelers were placed in separate Jewish homes, giving them shelter after the dangerous border journey.
The Abadan episode illustrates the informal infrastructure that supported Iraqi Jewish migration before Steve reached Israel. Refugees moved through a chain of clandestine contacts, safe houses, and transportation arrangements rather than through an ordinary immigration system. After roughly one…

From Abadan, Steve Acre traveled by train to Ahvaz, an inland center on the Karun River. He stayed there for approximately three days before continuing north. The stop was brief, but it formed part of the carefully organized sequence through which Iraqi Jewish refugees were moved across Iran toward a point of departure for Israel.
Steve's recollection emphasizes the physical transformation of the journey: from the river crossing and hidden farm shelters to organized rail transport and increasingly distant cities. Ahvaz was a logistical link rather than a settled community, yet it belonged to the wider geography of postwar migration that connected southern Iran to Tehran. The route depended…

After Ahvaz, Steve Acre traveled by train to Tehran, where he was held with other Jewish refugees at a cemetery for approximately four to five weeks. He arrived with almost nothing, lacking winter clothing despite the cold weather. Tehran was his first experience of snow, a striking contrast with the climate of Baghdad.
The refugee system then prepared Steve for departure by creating a temporary family unit for travel documents and arranging a laisser passer. Refugees were instructed to say that they were traveling to Cyprus, while the actual route diverted toward Israel. This concealment reflected the political restrictions surrounding Jewish migration. Tehran therefore marked both a period…

In December 1949, Steve Acre left Tehran by airplane as part of a group traveling under false family arrangements. The aircraft was supposed to continue to Cyprus, but after passing over Syria it turned toward Lydda Airport in Israel. Steve was deposited there before the aircraft continued on its stated route.
The arrival marked the decisive end of his clandestine escape from Iraq. Within months, Steve was drafted into the Israel Defense Forces and eventually assigned to the Air Force. Because his eyesight prevented pilot training, he studied flight control and became part of an early group of controllers working at Lydda. The airport also became a point of personal reconnection: while…

After his arrival in Israel, Steve Acre learned that his mother and siblings had reached the country and were living in the Sha'ar Aliyah ma'abara near Haifa. During his Air Force service, he took a short leave and traveled to the refugee camp to find them. The camp consisted of tents and offices where new arrivals were located by family name.
Steve recalled hearing his mother's voice before he saw her, describing the reunion as emotionally overwhelming after the separation and danger of the previous years. The family reunion also revealed the difficult material conditions facing Iraqi Jewish refugees. His relatives moved through several ma'abarot before eventually receiving housing in…

Steve Acre spent about four years in the Israeli Air Force after arriving in Israel, including work as a flight controller at Lydda. After leaving military service, he became involved in the development of eight villages near Beersheba, communities associated with the settlement of Moroccan Jews. The work connected his own refugee experience to the wider project of building new Israeli communities.
Steve soon became disillusioned by what he perceived as corruption in the distribution of supplies and attempted to raise the issue publicly. His criticism brought him into conflict with political intermediaries, including figures associated with Mapai, and he eventually resigned. The episode is…

After leaving his work near Beersheba, Steve Acre was offered an overseas assignment in either Paris or Rangoon. He chose Rangoon because he hoped to study Far Eastern history and believed the university still taught in English. On arrival, he discovered that instruction had shifted largely into Burmese, limiting his ability to pursue the degree he had imagined.
Instead, Steve worked with the Israeli military attaché as a secretary and cipher clerk, while his knowledge of Arabic proved useful in his reporting. He also obtained and translated material from Gamal Abdel Nasser soon after its publication. Rangoon became an unexpected professional education, combining diplomatic work, language…

After roughly two years in Rangoon, Steve Acre took six months of unpaid leave and began a planned journey around the world. He purchased a flexible one-year ticket that allowed him to stop and continue across multiple destinations. One of the first major stops was Hong Kong, part of a route that also included Singapore and Australia.
The journey represented a new phase in Steve's mobility. Earlier movement had been forced by persecution and refugee conditions; this journey was undertaken by choice and curiosity. He was now able to travel as an experienced Israeli, a multilingual professional, and an aspiring historian. Hong Kong formed part of a global itinerary that expanded the geographic…

Singapore was another major stop in Steve Acre's round-the-world journey after his service in Rangoon. He later remembered being stranded at the airport on a Friday evening when an airline strike disrupted his onward travel. Because Jewish institutions were unavailable at that moment, he turned to the Masonic Temple, drawing on a family tradition that had begun with his grandfather and father.
The episode illustrates how Steve's identity was supported by overlapping networks rather than by a single community. His Jewish Agency connections, multilingual skills, and Masonic membership could all provide practical assistance while traveling. Singapore thus became more than a transit point: it…

After continuing through Australia, Steve Acre arrived in Vancouver, a city he had not previously known. He visited the local Jewish Agency office and was introduced to Layla Azulay, a Montreal woman working there who also spoke Hebrew. A casual invitation to see an Indian film, The World of Apu, became the beginning of their relationship.
Steve later recalled that Layla became his wife, marking a turning point in a journey that had originally been planned as a temporary leave from his overseas assignment. Their relationship redirected his geographic trajectory toward Montreal. Vancouver therefore represents an unexpected intersection of global travel, Jewish communal networks,…
s.cr: Rob; original collection noted as John F. Bromley / photographer Ernie L. Plant

s.d:
In 1957, Steve Acre settled in Montreal after marrying Layla Azulay. Their first months were improvised: they stayed briefly with her parents and then rented a room in a shared apartment while Steve searched for work. He had expected to return to Israel, but his wife's serious injury during their honeymoon and the responsibilities of establishing a household changed that plan permanently.
Montreal became the setting for Steve's long-term professional and family life. He entered the insurance field, drawing unexpectedly on his father's earlier commercial losses in Basra, and he and Layla raised one son and two daughters, eventually becoming grandparents. By the time of his 2017 Sephardi…

Suad Mashaal Gabbay, known in Canada as Sue Gabbay, was born in Baghdad on October 7, 1943, into a large Iraqi Jewish family of eight children. Her parents, Menashe Mashaal and Semha Daniel Mashaal, belonged to a deeply rooted Babylonian Jewish milieu. Her father worked in import-export, with business interests and commercial agencies connected to Firestone, General Motors auto parts, Iraq, and Iran. Her maternal grandmother, Farha Daniel, was also part of the extended Mashaal family network, illustrating the close kinship structures remembered by Gabbay.
Although Gabbay's own memories of Baghdad are limited because she left as an infant, the city remained the starting point of a family…

At approximately three months old, Gabbay left Baghdad with her parents for Tehran, where her father's commercial activities already gave the family an established connection. She recalled that the move reflected a deteriorating political situation in Iraq and the family's desire to leave a place of unrest. Tehran also contained a substantial Iraqi Jewish community, making the move part of a regional pattern of Jewish mobility rather than an isolated departure.
Gabbay spent her early childhood in Tehran and remembered a household organized with substantial domestic help. At home the family spoke Arabic, while she encountered Persian through household workers and learned English at school.…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, Stanley Scott Collection, Office of History, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers

s.d:
In 1948, the Gabbay family underwent a decisive separation. Gabbay's parents left Iran with the older children while Sue, her younger brother Emil, and another brother remained behind because the family could not secure the necessary visas. The younger children stayed with an uncle and cousins, including Helen and Abraham Daniel. Gabbay later remembered this period as one in which she and her siblings were effectively left behind while the family pursued migration elsewhere.
Her strongest childhood memory of Iran was a frightening robbery at the family home, when a group of men entered at night asking for her father. The episode became a lasting marker of vulnerability during a period of…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, Sepah Square, Tehran in 1946

s.d:
In the fall of 1950, Gabbay's father returned to Iran to collect the younger children and brought them to London, where the family stayed for several months. The stop was a transitional stage between Iran and Canada. Gabbay remembered living in a hotel, where her father hired a nanny to help care for her and her young brother Emil. She also recalled the visible effects of postwar Britain, including rationing and limited access to food, while the family supplemented its meals with provisions brought from Iran.
London also became an educational and linguistic bridge. Gabbay attended school for part of her stay and recalled that she already spoke English when she arrived, alongside her earlier…
s.cr: Ben Brooksbank via Wikimedia Commons, Leadenhall Street from Bishopsgate, 1955

s.d:
In 1951, the family settled in Montreal after Canada provided an immigration route when the family could not remain in the United States. Gabbay's father bought a house in Outremont, eventually living there with the children as the family reunited.
