The Conservative government lost the 1880 election, ending Disraeli's second period as prime minister. He nevertheless remained a major political figure and continued as Leader of the Opposition. His career by then had extended across almost four decades of parliamentary life.
The defeat marked a transition from executive office to the final stage of Disraeli's public career. His legacy already combined literature, parliamentary oratory, Conservative politics, and an expansive conception of the British Empire. His Sephardi ancestry, Anglican public identity, and literary portrayal of society remained distinctive elements of the historical figure remembered as Lord Beaconsfield.

s.t: Curzon Street: Death and Historical Legacy
s.d:
Benjamin Disraeli died on 19 April 1881 at 19 Curzon Street, London, after illness that developed into bronchitis. The final residence represented a late chapter in a life that had moved from a London childhood in a family of Sephardi Jewish ancestry to the highest offices of the British state.
His historical legacy spans literature, political oratory, the development of the Conservative Party, and British imperial policy. His novels remained part of Victorian literary history, while his two premierships and relationship with Queen Victoria secured a lasting place in British political memory. His ancestry also makes him an important figure in the study of Sephardi identity within modern…

people.aka: Daniel Israel López Laguna; Daniel Israel Lopes Laguna; Daniel López Laguna

s.d:
Around 1640, Daniel Israel López Laguna was born in Portugal within a crypto-Jewish or New Christian milieu. The surviving biographical record is sparse, and the exact birthplace is not established, but the sources consistently place his origins in Portugal and connect his family to the wider Sephardi world.
His early life unfolded within the religious and cultural pressures experienced by Iberian families of converso background. This setting helps explain the later importance of Judaism, Spanish literary culture, and mobility across the Atlantic and European worlds. The subsequent trajectory from Iberia to France, Spain, and Jamaica became central to his identity as a poet and translator.
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, Lisbon in 1572, Georg Braun and Franz Hogenberg

s.d:
As a child, Daniel Israel López Laguna was taken to Peyrehorade in southern France, where he received an important part of his early formation. His own retrospective verse remembers France as a formative school during his adolescence, linking the place with the intellectual development that preceded his Spanish studies.
The move placed him within a transregional Sephardi environment extending between Iberia and southwestern France. Later scholarship identifies Peyrehorade as a family setting from which he proceeded toward Spain for higher study. This stage is therefore significant for understanding the combination of French education, Spanish literary culture, and Jewish family memory that…

In Spain, the young Daniel Israel López Laguna pursued classical letters in a university setting. Modern scholarship associates this phase with Salamanca, a major center of early modern learning. His movement into the Iberian academic world deepened the literary and linguistic skills that later supported his poetic rendering of the Psalms.
The Spanish period also exposed him to the institutional pressures surrounding New Christians and suspected Judaizers. According to the biographical tradition, he was eventually arrested by the Inquisition and held for many years. The experience became inseparable from the literary project he later completed in Jamaica, where memories of captivity and…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, Salamanca University, Salamanca, photo by Tony Hisgett

s.d:
After escaping the Inquisition and securing his release, Daniel Israel López Laguna reached Kingston, Jamaica, around 1680. The English colony offered a setting in which he could openly resume Judaism, transforming the meaning of an earlier life marked by secrecy, persecution, and imprisonment.
Jamaica became the principal setting for his mature religious and literary life. In the island's Sephardi community, Spanish and Portuguese Jewish networks connected local commerce and family life with wider Atlantic circuits. His settlement in Kingston thus marked both a geographical escape and a renewed public affiliation with Jewish communal culture.
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, Port Royal, Jamaica, 17th century, Edward Barlow

s.d:
By 1693, Daniel Israel López Laguna had become a naturalized resident of Jamaica. Established in Kingston, he belonged to a growing Jewish population whose commercial and family networks linked the island to London, the Caribbean, and the wider Western Sephardi world.
During these Jamaican decades he devoted sustained effort to his Spanish poetic version of the Salmos. The work drew on his knowledge of Hebrew and his command of Spanish verse, while his experience of persecution gave the biblical poems an autobiographical resonance. The island was therefore both a place of communal reintegration and the principal workshop of his literary legacy.
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, Kingston, Jamaica, 1905, Caribbean Photo Archive

s.d:
After long residence in Jamaica, Daniel Israel López Laguna traveled to London, where members of the Laguna family were living. There he encountered Mordecai Nunes Almeyda, whose patronage provided the financial support needed to bring Laguna's major literary project into print.
The London setting placed the poet within the institutional world of the Spanish and Portuguese Jewish community. The work received an approval from David Nieto and another from Joseph ibn Danon, demonstrating the recognition it received among learned Sephardi circles. Bevis Marks serves here as a representative communal landmark for the London network surrounding the publication.
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, Bevis Marks Synagogue, photo by Deror avi

s.loc: City of London, London, United Kingdom
s.d:
In 1720, Daniel Israel López Laguna published Espejo fiel de vidas que contiene los Psalmos de David en verso in London. The book presented a poetic and paraphrastic rendering of the Hebrew Psalms in Spanish and was dedicated to his patron, Mordecai Nunes Almeyda.
The volume reflects an unusually multilingual Sephardi literary culture, with commendatory material in Spanish, Portuguese, Hebrew, Latin, and English. Laguna employed numerous poetic forms, including octavas, tercetos, décimas, and seguidillas. His allusions to the Inquisition also transformed the biblical text into a vehicle for remembering persecution and seeking redemption.
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, Espejo Fiel de Vidas, Beit Hatefutsot exhibit photograph

s.d:
After the London publication, Daniel Israel López Laguna returned to Jamaica and rejoined his wife, Riki, and their sons David, Jacob, and Isaac. His return reconnected the published work with the community in which much of its long gestation had taken place.
The surviving record gives no secure exact death date. The supplied biography places his death in Jamaica around 1720, while documentary evidence connected with his will places Daniel Lopez Laguna in Kingston in the early 1720s. His legacy rests on Espejo fiel, a major Spanish poetic engagement with the Psalms and a testimony to Sephardi mobility, memory, and religious renewal.
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, Old King Street, Kingston, Jamaica, Duperly Brothers

s.d:
Abraham Gómez Silveira was born in Arévalo in 1656, a Castilian town whose historical setting frames the paradox at the center of his later career. His life began in Spain, yet his intellectual formation would unfold principally within the mobile networks of the Western Sephardi diaspora.
The biographical record presents his birthplace as important precisely because it contrasts with the world in which he became a writer. From a young age, Silveira was educated in the Sephardi community of Amsterdam, where Spanish-language Jewish culture, rabbinic learning, and communal institutions shaped his literary identity. His trajectory therefore links Castile to the major Amsterdam center of Sephardi…

As a young man, Abraham Gómez Silveira was educated in the Sephardi community of Amsterdam, one of the principal centers of Jewish life in early modern Europe. His formation combined rabbinic education with the literary culture of Spanish used by Western Sephardi communities.
The Amsterdam setting helps explain the unusual breadth of Silveira's later writing. He became conversant with Jewish theology, sermon literature, polemical argument, and poetic forms, while remaining deeply invested in the intellectual and rhetorical resources of the Iberian tradition. The Portuguese Synagogue and associated institutions provide an appropriate historical setting for this phase, when communal learning…
s.cr: Jacob van Ruisdael, via Wikimedia Commons

s.d:
In 1677, at only twenty years old, Abraham Gómez Silveira completed a volume of sermons in Spanish that received a warm welcome from the rabbis and intellectuals of his Amsterdam community. The episode marks the public emergence of a writer already shaped by the city's Sephardi educational culture.
His early success also demonstrates the importance of preaching as a literary and communal practice. Silveira's Spanish connected learned Jewish discourse with the linguistic world inherited from Iberia, while the Amsterdam setting provided an audience and institutional framework for its circulation. This chapter situates him within the Western Sephardi cultural milieu before his later movement to…

Soon after his early success in Amsterdam, Abraham Gómez Silveira disappeared from the Amsterdam record and reappeared in Antwerp. According to his accusers, he had begun producing writings considered scandalous and doctrinally suspect, transforming his literary activity into a source of communal controversy.
The Antwerp episode reveals the tension between Jewish communal authority and Silveira's unusually independent literary voice. He sought the protection of the Amsterdam rabbis, protesting attacks that affected both his honor and that of his family. His response also foreshadowed the recurring mixture of polemics, humor, and literary provocation that would characterize his mature work.

Following the controversy in Antwerp, Abraham Gómez Silveira invoked the protection of the Amsterdam rabbis against attacks that he regarded as destructive of his reputation and his family's honor. The episode reconnects his biography to the communal institutions in which his education had begun.
The Amsterdam return is significant for understanding Silveira's position within the Western Sephardi diaspora. He remained committed to Jewish learning while developing a literary practice that could challenge communal expectations. His predilection for polemical writing and ludic discourse became increasingly visible, including works that adopted invented Christian names and satirical forms. The…

Silveira's most ambitious project grew from the challenge posed by the Protestant theologian Isaac Jaquelot, whose 1699 book addressed Jews, particularly Sephardim. Abraham Gómez Silveira responded with the vast manuscript Disertaciones sobre el Mesías, ultimately extending to twelve volumes and developing over more than thirty years.
The work defended the immutability of Mosaic Law and a literal reading of Scripture, while repeatedly interrupting theological argument with proverbs, jokes, anecdotes, and poetic Silveiradas. His lively Spanish and ironic engagement with Christian polemic turned the imagined debate into a meditation on minority identity, intellectual asymmetry, and the…
s.cr: Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, Sergé Technau, via Wikimedia Commons

s.d:
A surviving manuscript from 1723 preserves additional evidence of Abraham Gómez Silveira's literary range. The Relación de la Inquisición recounts the suffering of Antonio de Fonseca, while two further histories treat Jesus Christ and the Magdalene and the controversial messianic figure Sabbatai Sebi.
The manuscript is preserved as MS. 581 in the Bibliotheca Rosenthaliana of the University of Amsterdam, linking Silveira's literary production to one of the major repositories of Sephardi and Jewish intellectual heritage. Its survival underscores the breadth of his interests, from Inquisition narratives and messianism to satirical religious history and the contested boundaries of…
s.cr: Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, via Wikimedia Commons

s.d:
Abraham Gómez Silveira died in Amsterdam in 1740, completing a life that connected Castile, the Western Sephardi diaspora, and the intellectual world of the Dutch Republic. His career encompassed sermons, Jewish apologetics, academic vejámenes, poetry, and an extensive corpus of anti-Christian polemic.
His enduring significance lies in the way he transformed polemical writing into a flexible literary form. Through Spanish-language satire, theological argument, invented personae, and popular sayings, Silveira created a distinctive voice for Sephardi readers. His work also dramatized the distance between a Jewish minority and Christian interlocutors, while demonstrating how Amsterdam's…
s.cr: Jacob van Ruisdael, via Wikimedia Commons

s.loc: Synagogue de la Paix, Strasbourg, France
s.d:
Éliette Abécassis was born in Strasbourg on 27 January 1969, into a practicing Moroccan Jewish family whose religious life shaped her early cultural vocabulary. Her father, Armand Abécassis, was a philosopher and historian of Jewish thought, and her childhood unfolded within the life of the Strasbourg Jewish community. The family environment connected French intellectual culture with Sephardic religious traditions and memories rooted in Morocco.
This formative setting became a recurring point of reflection in Abécassis's later autobiographical writing and in her treatment of identity, tradition, and transmission. Her literary work repeatedly revisits the tension between inherited religious…

At about 17, Abécassis left Strasbourg for Paris after completing the baccalauréat, beginning a decisive phase of literary preparation. She studied in the demanding hypokhâgne and khâgne classes at the Lycée Henri-IV, an institution associated with the classical French tradition of advanced humanities education. The move placed her within the intellectual institutions of the capital and marked a transition from a closely knit Sephardic family environment toward a broader French academic culture.
The Parisian preparatory system gave her a foundation in literature, philosophy, and the humanities before her entry into the École normale supérieure. This stage is important for understanding the…

s.loc: École normale supérieure, rue d'Ulm, Paris, France
s.d:
Abécassis subsequently entered the École normale supérieure on rue d'Ulm, one of France's principal institutions for advanced study in the humanities. Her formation there consolidated a rigorous engagement with philosophy and prepared the academic credentials that would lead to the agrégation de philosophie. The institution also placed her in a national intellectual milieu where the study of ideas could be connected to questions of religion, ethics, and history.
Her later writing demonstrates how this philosophical training remained active even after she turned toward professional literature. In works such as Qumran and Petite Métaphysique du meurtre, philosophical questions are embedded in…
s.cr: E. Le Deley, via Wikimedia Commons

s.d:
At 23, Abécassis spent a year in the United States on a study scholarship, associated with Cambridge and the intellectual resources of Harvard. This transatlantic stage widened the geographical range of her philosophical and literary formation and gave her access to libraries, archives, and institutions relevant to the study of Judaism and ancient texts. It was during this period that the project that became Qumran took shape.
The American experience was therefore not a detached episode but part of the research process behind her first novel. Her later account of the book describes a sustained search for information concerning the Dead Sea Scrolls, Jewish history, and the intellectual worlds…

In 1993, Abécassis obtained the agrégation de philosophie, completing a major stage of professional academic qualification. Her passage through the École normale supérieure had established a disciplined engagement with philosophical argument, while the agrégation opened the way to university teaching. The achievement also helps explain the distinctive intellectual character of her later novels and essays, where narrative is frequently used to investigate ethics, metaphysics, religion, and the nature of evil.
Although Abécassis soon became known primarily as a writer, the academic formation remained visible throughout her work. Her later essays, including Petite Métaphysique du meurtre,…

The research for Qumran extended beyond libraries in France and the United States to Israel, especially Jerusalem and the archaeological landscape associated with the Dead Sea Scrolls. Accounts of Abécassis's preparation describe research lasting roughly three years, during which she pursued information about Jewish history, ancient manuscripts, and the religious worlds that would become the intellectual framework of her first novel. Jerusalem provided a living cultural setting in which textual scholarship and contemporary Jewish life could be encountered together.
This research phase is significant because it shows the movement from academic philosophy toward historical fiction through…

The archaeological site of Qumran supplied the geographical and symbolic center of Abécassis's first novel. Her research for Qumran included investigation in Jerusalem and at Qumran itself, as well as work in libraries and archives in the United States. The site is associated with the caves where the Dead Sea Scrolls were found, making it an especially charged landscape for a writer interested in Jewish texts, contested knowledge, and the relationship between archaeology and interpretation.
The novel transforms this landscape into a metaphysical mystery involving missing manuscripts, religious identity, and the possibility that ancient texts can alter modern understandings of history. For…
s.cr: Dennis G. Jarvis, via Wikimedia Commons

s.d:
In 1996, Abécassis published Qumran, her first novel, in Paris with Ramsay. The book emerged from the preceding years of research into the Dead Sea Scrolls, Jewish history, and the intellectual worlds surrounding ancient manuscripts. It presented a form of metaphysical detective fiction in which a young religious Jew investigates mysterious deaths and the disappearance of a valuable manuscript, bringing questions of faith and historical knowledge into a contemporary narrative.
The publication marked the decisive transition from academic formation to professional literary career. The novel achieved immediate international attention and was subsequently translated into eighteen languages,…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons contributor, via Wikimedia Commons

s.d:
In 1997, Abécassis began teaching philosophy at the University of Caen. The move to Caen followed her advanced study in Paris and her research period connected with Qumran, creating a bridge between university teaching and the literary career that was already underway. Her position reflects a professional identity that remained divided between academic philosophy and increasingly successful fiction.
The Caen period also coincided with the publication of L'Or et la cendre in 1997, followed by the philosophical essay Petite Métaphysique du meurtre in 1998. These works demonstrate the continuity between her classroom discipline and her literary practice, especially in their attention to moral…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons contributor, via Wikimedia Commons

s.d:
By 2000, Abécassis was established as a professional novelist, and La Répudiée appeared with Albin Michel. The novel focuses on a woman within a highly traditional Jewish environment and develops themes of marriage, religious authority, desire, and the pressures of communal belonging. Its reception also connected her literary work to cinema, because the novel's story grew from the same creative world as the screenplay that became Kadosh, directed by Amos Gitaï.
This Paris chapter captures the expansion of Abécassis's practice beyond the first success of Qumran. She was now moving among novel writing, philosophical reflection, and screenwriting, while continuing to examine the place of…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons contributor, via Wikimedia Commons

s.loc: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris, France
s.d:
In 2009, Abécassis published Sépharade, a novel centered on Moroccan Jewish memory and the search for inherited identity. The story follows Esther Vital, a Jewish woman born in Strasbourg, whose personal life becomes a route into the history of Sephardic communities and the traditions associated with Morocco. The book moves across generations and places, bringing family memory, marriage, religious practice, and historical displacement into a single narrative.
Published in Paris and later translated into Spanish as La novia sefardí, the novel makes Sephardic identity itself a central literary subject. Its historical imagination reaches from Fès, Meknès, and Mogador to the modern French Jewish…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons contributor, via Wikimedia Commons

people.aka: Elisa Cohen; Elisa B. Cohen de Chervonagura

s.t: San Miguel de Tucumán: Birth and Formation
s.loc: Plaza Independencia, San Miguel de Tucumán, Argentina
s.d:
Elisa Cohen de Chervonagura was born on 14 August 1954 in San Miguel de Tucumán, a city that would remain central to her intellectual biography. Her later work repeatedly returned to the Jewish community of Tucumán, Judeo-Spanish, and the linguistic consequences of Jewish immigration.
The available biographical record identifies her as an Argentine writer, professor of Letters, doctor in Letters, and CONICET researcher. Her scholarly profile developed around sociolinguistics, critical discourse analysis, Spanish morphology, disappearing languages, and the cultural history carried through language.

s.t: San Miguel de Tucumán: Teaching and Letters
s.loc: Facultad de Filosofía y Letras, San Miguel de Tucumán, Argentina
s.d:
In 1979, Elisa Cohen de Chervonagura began her teaching career in the Facultad de Filosofía y Letras of the Universidad Nacional de Tucumán. The institution became the principal setting of her academic formation, teaching, research, and postgraduate activity.
Her subsequent career connected Spanish language, literary studies, sociolinguistics, and language pedagogy. The faculty's humanities environment provided the institutional framework in which she later investigated Jewish immigration, Judeo-Spanish, discourse, and the relationship between language and society.

s.t: San Miguel de Tucumán: Judeo-Spanish Research
s.loc: Cementerio Israelita de Tucumán, San Miguel de Tucumán, Argentina
s.d:
In 1988, En Busca de la Palabra Perdida established an important strand of Elisa Cohen de Chervonagura's research: the study of the last speakers of Judeo-Spanish who lived in Tucumán. The work drew on interviews to examine language, society, and history through living testimony.
This approach linked sociolinguistics with the history of Sephardi communities and the problem of language disappearance. By treating speech as historical evidence, the project documented aspects of a local Jewish linguistic heritage that might otherwise have remained outside conventional written archives.

In 1992, Elisa Cohen de Chervonagura received a Beca Sefarad from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Spain for research in the Humanities and Social Sciences. The fellowship was carried out at the Consejo Superior de Investigaciones Científicas in Madrid.
The Madrid period placed her study of Sephardi history, Judeo-Spanish, and language in a wider Spanish scholarly context. It connected her Tucumán-based research to institutions concerned with Spain, Jewish cultural history, and the documentary and linguistic legacies of the Sephardi diaspora.

s.t: San Miguel de Tucumán: Doctoral Recognition
s.loc: Rectorado, Universidad Nacional de Tucumán, San Miguel de Tucumán, Argentina
s.d:
In 1993, Elisa Cohen de Chervonagura completed her degree as Profesora y Doctora en Letras at the Universidad Nacional de Tucumán. The doctorate formalized a scholarly trajectory already grounded in teaching and linguistic research at the university.
Her academic work increasingly combined language analysis with social history, particularly questions involving immigration, Jewish communities, and the relationship between discourse and institutions. This interdisciplinary orientation became characteristic of her later publications and research projects.

s.loc: University of New Orleans, New Orleans, United States
s.d:
In 1998, Elisa Cohen de Chervonagura was invited as a professor to the University of New Orleans for its Master's program in Spanish. The appointment extended her teaching and research beyond Argentina and placed her work in an international academic setting.
The New Orleans experience complemented her continuing interests in Spanish, sociolinguistics, and the movement of linguistic and cultural traditions across diasporic communities. It also formed part of a broader pattern of international teaching, conferences, and scholarly exchange documented in her professional biography.

s.t: San Miguel de Tucumán: Language and Morphology
s.loc: Biblioteca Dr. Emilio Carilla, San Miguel de Tucumán, Argentina
s.d:
By 2001, Elisa Cohen de Chervonagura had developed a sustained program of research on Spanish morphology, discourse, and language in use. Seis estudios sobre la palabra brought together studies based on authentic oral and written texts and proposed new perspectives for morphological analysis.
Her work on Diálogo de la Lengua likewise approached Juan de Valdés through a pragmatic perspective, emphasizing communication, social situation, and the relationship between linguistic signs and their users. These publications demonstrate the breadth of her interdisciplinary linguistics.

s.t: San Miguel de Tucumán: Linguistic Communities
s.loc: Quinta Agronómica, San Miguel de Tucumán, Argentina
s.d:
In 2006, Comunidades Lingüísticas extended Elisa Cohen de Chervonagura's concern with how institutions organize social and linguistic space. The volume examined unequal groups, institutional texts, social representations, and the discursive conflicts that can exist beneath apparently harmonious institutional narratives.
This work reflects her broader commitment to critical discourse analysis and to understanding language as a record of social relationships. Her research continued to connect linguistic practice, institutions, and the experiences of communities shaped by migration and cultural difference.

s.loc: Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Jerusalem, Israel
s.d:
In 2009, Elisa Cohen de Chervonagura received the Cátedra San Martín and became a Visiting Professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. During this period she also gave lectures at the Harman Institute of Contemporary Jewry and participated in the Forum of Latin American Jewish Studies.
The Jerusalem appointment brought her work on Jewish immigration, Sephardi history, Judeo-Spanish, and Latin American Jewry into direct conversation with a major center of Jewish scholarship. It marked an important international dimension of her research career.

s.t: San Miguel de Tucumán: Jewish Community History
s.loc: Cementerio Israelita de Tucumán, San Miguel de Tucumán, Argentina
s.d:
Around 2010, Elisa Cohen de Chervonagura directed research concerning La comunidad lingüística y sus instituciones and the historical development of the Jewish community of Tucumán. The project situated language within the institutions and social networks through which a community represented itself.
Her scholarship continued to connect Jewish communal history with language, discourse, and institutional memory. This perspective is consistent with her longer investigation of Sephardi migration, disappearing linguistic practices, and the cultural history preserved in local testimony and community records.

s.t: San Miguel de Tucumán: CONICET Research
s.loc: CONICET Tucumán, San Miguel de Tucumán, Argentina
s.d:
By 2016, Elisa Cohen de Chervonagura was identified as an independent CONICET researcher working at the Facultad de Filosofía y Letras of the Universidad Nacional de Tucumán. Her research continued to investigate the history of Tucumán's Jewish community through documentary and oral sources.
Her work on two women buried in the Jewish Cemetery of Tucumán illustrates her method: combining Jewish history, social memory, and discourse to examine how social and ideological contexts shaped individual lives. The project exemplifies her sustained study of Jewish immigration and community history.
s.cr: Archivo General de la Nación Argentina, Wikimedia Commons

s.loc: The Paragon, Hackney, London, United Kingdom
s.d:
Grace Aguilar was born on 2 June 1816 at The Paragon, Hackney, in northeast London, into a family of Portuguese Sephardi Jews. Her parents, Emanuel Aguilar and Sarah Aguilar, were active in the London Sephardi community, and Emanuel served as a Parnás, or lay leader, of the Portuguese synagogue. The household combined communal responsibility with an intensive home education, giving Aguilar an early grounding in Jewish history, scripture, and religious practice.
This setting established the central tension that shaped Aguilar's later writing: a strong attachment to Judaism alongside sustained engagement with the wider Victorian English culture. Her family's Sephardi ancestry, the memory of…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, unknown author

s.d:
At about four years old, Aguilar was taken from London to Hastings because of her fragile constitution. The seaside environment became an important part of her childhood formation. According to the contemporary memorial account, she began collecting and arranging shells there and developed a sustained habit of reading, preserving books, and observing the natural world. Her health was delicate, but the move did not confine her intellectually. Instead, the coastal setting encouraged curiosity, collecting, and a close attention to landscape.
Hastings is therefore significant less as a permanent residence than as an early health retreat and formative landscape. The experience contributed to the…
s.cr: Library of Congress, Photochrom Print Collection, via Wikimedia Commons

s.d:
When Emanuel Aguilar contracted tuberculosis, the family left London for the Devon coast in search of healthier air. During these years, Aguilar's education became increasingly deliberate. Her mother provided religious instruction, while her father used his enforced rest to teach her Jewish history. He also recounted oral traditions concerning crypto-Jews, Sephardim who had converted publicly under pressure from the Inquisition while preserving Jewish practice privately.
The Devon period was decisive for the formation of Aguilar as a writer because family illness, mobility, and study operated together. She produced an early complete manuscript, Gustavus Vasa, and began to convert inherited…
s.cr: Francis Bedford, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

s.d:
In 1835, after a severe attack of measles, Aguilar's family moved to Brighton. The town became an important literary base during a period of rapid production. Her first published volume, The Magic Wreath of Hidden Flowers, appeared in this context, while she continued writing poetry, fiction, and religious materials. The move also brought her into a more visible relationship with the commercial literary world beyond the immediate Jewish community.
Brighton was a place where health, family responsibility, and literary ambition converged. Aguilar continued to write despite chronic illness and began developing the domestic and historical genres that later defined her reputation. Her work…
s.cr: Anne Rushout, Yale Center for British Art, via Wikimedia Commons

s.d:
By 1840, the Aguilar family had returned to London and settled at 5 Triangle, Hackney, where Sarah Aguilar operated a preparatory establishment for boys. The household was simultaneously a family residence, educational setting, and literary workshop. Aguilar helped manage the school while continuing to write, and the address became a practical base from which she entered the wider British literary market.
From Hackney, Aguilar cultivated connections with Benjamin Disraeli and his father Isaac D'Israeli, and eventually secured publication through R. Groombridge and Sons. She also established a transatlantic relationship with Isaac Leeser, editor of The Occident in Philadelphia. This phase…
s.cr: It's No Game, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0

s.d:
After the death of Emanuel Aguilar in 1845, Grace and her mother moved from Triangle to Clapton Square. This was her last London home and the setting for the final, highly productive phase of her English career. Her publications included The Women of Israel, a major three-volume study of Jewish women across biblical, rabbinic, and modern contexts, and continued work for both Jewish and general periodicals.
The Clapton years reveal the full scope of Aguilar's project: she linked Jewish history, midrash, women's education, and literary fiction while addressing the position of Jews within Victorian society. Her writing could speak simultaneously to Jewish readers and Christian readers, and it…
s.cr: New York Public Library Digital Collections, via Wikimedia Commons, public domain

s.d:
In 1847, Aguilar's worsening health led to a planned journey to the Continent. On 17 June 1847, she left England with her mother Sarah, her brother Emanuel, and a companion, travelling to Blackwall to board the steamer Sir Edward Banks for Ostend. The journey was undertaken for medical reasons, after prolonged spinal illness and increasing physical weakness.
The departure was also a symbolic transition. Before leaving, Jewish women in London presented Aguilar with a gift and an address recognizing her work on behalf of Judaism and Jewish women. Her final journey therefore joined personal illness with a public acknowledgment of her place in the Anglo-Jewish world. The route from London…
s.cr: Historic and Public Figures Collection, New York Public Library, via Wikimedia Commons, public domain

s.d:
The steamer carrying Aguilar and her family reached Ostend, the Belgian port that formed the maritime gateway to their overland journey into Germany. The surviving account of the trip records a route through Belgium toward Frankfurt. Aguilar kept a substantial Frankfort Journal, eventually extending to roughly thirty-four thousand words, documenting the journey and her changing condition.
Ostend is important in the map because it marks the point where Aguilar's final English world opened into a broader European journey. Her travel was not undertaken for tourism alone: the stated purpose was medical consultation and recovery. The port thus represents a transition between the British Sephardi…
s.cr: Project Gutenberg, via Wikimedia Commons, public domain

s.d:
Aguilar reached Frankfurt in 1847 to visit her brother Emanuel, who was living there as a musician, and to consult a German physician. At first the change of climate seemed beneficial, but her condition deteriorated. Her Frankfort Journal records the final phase of her life in a city that was also a major center of German Jewish history and commerce.
Frankfurt gave Aguilar a final geographical setting in which her English, Sephardi, and Jewish identities intersected. The city was associated with a long-established Jewish community and the wider European networks through which Jewish intellectual and commercial life circulated. Aguilar's stay was brief, however. After several weeks, medical…
s.cr: William Henry Fox Talbot, Institut für Stadtgeschichte Frankfurt am Main, via Wikimedia Commons, public domain

s.d:
After several weeks in Frankfurt, Aguilar's worsening condition prompted a move to the baths at Schwalbach, a spa destination in the German states. She remained there for about three weeks, following the medical practice of seeking relief through a change of air and spa treatment. The intervention did not restore her health, and she eventually returned to Frankfurt.
This short movement is significant because it shows how nineteenth-century ideas about climate therapy, mineral baths, and restorative travel shaped the final months of an otherwise intensely literary life. Aguilar's journey remained closely tied to illness, but her writing continued to frame experience through religious trust…
s.cr: Isaac Lobatto Rz, Rijksmuseum, via Wikimedia Commons

s.loc: Jewish Cemetery, Rat-Beil-Straße, Frankfurt am Main, Germany
s.d:
Aguilar returned to Frankfurt after the unsuccessful stay at Schwalbach and died on 16 September 1847, aged 31. She was buried in the city's Jewish cemetery, at the cemetery on Rat-Beil-Straße, which had been established in 1828. A later memorial account described her grave as close to the wall of the Protestant cemetery and recorded a headstone bearing a butterfly, five stars, and a verse from Proverbs 31:31.
Her burial in Frankfurt closed a life that had moved between London, English seaside and rural settings, and continental Europe while remaining anchored in Sephardi Jewish identity. Aguilar's published legacy included The Spirit of Judaism, The Women of Israel, Home Influence, and…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, public-domain/archival photograph of Rat-Beil-Straße Jewish Cemetery

s.d:
Isaac Chocrón Serfaty was born on 25 September 1930 in Maracay, Venezuela, into a Sephardi Jewish family whose background linked Venezuelan life to wider North African Sephardi networks. His parents, Elías Chocrón and Estrella Serfaty, formed the immediate familial setting of a childhood marked by movement between educational and cultural environments.
The Maracay beginning is significant because it places Chocrón within the social and intellectual formation of modern Venezuela while retaining a distinct Jewish inheritance. His later work repeatedly explored identity, family, marginality, and the pressures of social convention. The combination of Sephardi heritage, multilingual educational…

After the family moved to Caracas following the death of Juan Vicente Gómez, Chocrón continued his schooling in the capital. He attended the Escuela Experimental Venezuela, where he encountered future cultural figures including Román Chalbaud and Vicente Nebreda. This urban educational environment widened the social and artistic horizons of a young writer growing up between Jewish family life and predominantly Catholic Venezuelan institutions.
The Caracas years established an early pattern of movement between institutions, languages, and cultural worlds. His education also included the Colegio América and earlier study at Nuestra Señora de la Consolación in Maracay. These experiences…

s.loc: Bordentown Military Institute site, Bordentown, United States
s.d:
For his secondary education, Chocrón traveled to Bordentown, New Jersey, where he attended the Bordentown Military Institute. The move placed a Venezuelan Jewish adolescent within a distinctly American educational setting shaped by discipline, residential schooling, and preparation for higher education. The experience formed part of a larger transnational trajectory that would carry him through several universities in the United States and England.
Bordentown was therefore less a permanent destination than an important stage in Chocrón's educational mobility. His later writing repeatedly examined the tensions between individual identity and social convention, concerns that can be read…

s.loc: Hall of Languages, Syracuse University, Syracuse, United States
s.d:
At Syracuse University, Chocrón pursued higher education and received a Bachelor of Arts, with accounts placing the degree in 1952. His university years broadened a formation that would never be confined to literature. The study of economics and the social sciences supplied an analytical framework that later coexisted with his dramatic interest in institutions, social relations, and the structures shaping individual lives.
Syracuse also represents the beginning of a distinctly American university trajectory that continued at Columbia University. Chocrón's education was unusually interdisciplinary for a future playwright: economics, international affairs, and literature became complementary…

s.t: New York: Columbia and Comparative Study
s.loc: Low Library, Columbia University, New York, United States
s.d:
Chocrón next continued his studies at Columbia University in New York, where he studied Comparative Literature and earned a Master's degree in International Relations, with one biographical account dating the latter to 1954. Columbia gave him an academic setting in which literary interpretation and international affairs could coexist within a single intellectual formation.
This period is important for understanding the later synthesis in Chocrón's work. His theatre often places individuals within networks of social expectations, national identity, and cultural difference, while his prose and essays show sustained interest in language and the arts. The Columbia stage therefore belongs to a…

s.loc: Whitworth Building, University of Manchester, Manchester, United Kingdom
s.d:
Chocrón extended his international education to Manchester, England, where he pursued advanced study in Economic Development at the University of Manchester. The available biographical accounts place this degree within the 1950s, although they do not establish a more precise year. This English phase completed a remarkably wide academic itinerary before his professional return to Venezuela.
The Manchester period also underscores the distance between Chocrón's formal academic training and his eventual vocation. He had accumulated credentials in economics, international relations, and comparative literature, yet the central trajectory of his life increasingly became creative writing. His later…

s.t: Caracas: Public Service and Literary Return
s.loc: Aula Magna, Universidad Central de Venezuela, Caracas, Venezuela
s.d:
In the mid-1950s, Chocrón returned to Venezuela and entered public service, working in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Corporación Venezolana de Fomento, and the Ministry of Hacienda. His professional experience connected his international education to the institutional life of a rapidly changing Venezuelan state, but administrative work did not become his lasting vocation.
The decisive transition came through literature. In the 1950s he published Pasaje, a collection of stories that announced his emergence as a writer, and in 1959 he premiered Mónica y el florentino. His return to Caracas thus marked a movement from public administration toward fiction and dramaturgy. The city became…

s.loc: Universidad Central de Venezuela, Caracas, Venezuela
s.d:
In 1959, Chocrón premiered Mónica y el florentino, beginning the sustained theatrical career for which he became nationally prominent. The play places characters of different origins and languages together in a Florentine pension, using difficulties of communication to explore deeper forms of existential solitude. Its concerns with prejudice, unconventional relationships, and the limits of communication established themes that would recur throughout his theatre.
The following work, El quinto infierno, continued the exploration of solitude while adding a concern with Venezuelan national identity. From this point onward, Chocrón's Caracas career developed through a sequence of plays that…

During the 1960s through the 1980s, Chocrón became a central figure in the institutional and artistic renewal of Venezuelan theatre. Works such as Asia y el lejano Oriente, Tric-trac, La revolución, and Alfabeto para analfabetos expanded his experiments with social criticism, identity, homosexuality, and the Theatre of the Absurd. His writing combined spare language with increasingly complex social and autobiographical dimensions.
Chocrón also became a cultural organizer and educator. He helped found El Nuevo Grupo, directed the Escuela de Artes at the Universidad Central de Venezuela, and in 1984 founded the Compañía Nacional de Teatro. These activities connected literary creation with…

s.t: Caracas: Teresa Carreño and Final Years
s.d:
In 1994, Chocrón became director of the Teatro Teresa Carreño, one of the major performing-arts institutions of Caracas. His administrative leadership extended a lifetime commitment to the stage beyond authorship into cultural management, arts education, and the public infrastructure of theatre. He later received an honorary doctorate from the Universidad Central de Venezuela in 2000.
Chocrón remained associated with the central concerns of his writing: solitude, family, identity, aging, and the pressures of social convention. His work circulated beyond Venezuela in Latin America and Spain, reinforcing his place in the history of modern Hispanic theatre. He died in Caracas on 6 November…

Born in 1912 in Cairo, Edmond Jabès grew up in a prominent Jewish family of Sephardi origin within the cosmopolitan society of Egypt. Later biographical research places the family in the affluent Garden City area, where French was an important household and cultural language. His father worked in banking, and the family belonged to the established Jewish bourgeoisie of Cairo. The young Jabès therefore encountered several cultural worlds at once: Egyptian urban life, French literary culture, and the inherited memory of a long-established Jewish community.
His early formation combined a secular family environment with French education. During the 1920s, he studied in French institutions in…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, 1912 map of Cairo and Old Cairo

s.t: Cairo: French Education and Early Poetry
s.d:
Edmond Jabès began publishing small poetic works in 1929, while still shaped by the multilingual and cosmopolitan environment of Cairo. His education in French schools gave him access to the literary traditions of France, and he wrote principally in French from an early age. This linguistic choice would later become one of the defining tensions of his work, because French was simultaneously his literary instrument and the language of a country in which he would eventually live as an exile.
During the 1930s, Jabès became part of the Cairo literary avant-garde, developing friendships with writers such as Georges Henein and correspondence with Max Jacob. He helped establish La Part du sable, a…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, Cairo view in the 1920s

s.t: Paris: Sorbonne Study and Literary Encounters
s.d:
In 1930-1931, Edmond Jabès spent a formative period in Paris, studying at the Sorbonne. The journey extended the French education he had begun in Egypt and brought him into closer contact with the literary world that had already attracted him through reading and correspondence. Paris became a recurring point of reference rather than a simple destination, linking academic study with literary friendship and the wider networks of French modernism.
The Parisian period also anticipated later relationships with major figures in French letters. In 1935, Jabès met Max Jacob in Paris, while Paul Éluard helped bring attention to his early work. He maintained connections with writers associated with…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, Newberry Library, Sorbonne postcard, 1917

s.t: Cairo: War Years and Literary Formation
s.d:
Returning to Cairo, Edmond Jabès continued writing and publishing in French through the 1940s and early 1950s. His poetry during this period developed from the experimental interests of his youth while remaining rooted in the social and cultural environment of Egyptian Jewish life. Later collected under the title Je bâtis ma demeure, these writings established the poetic foundation from which his mature work would emerge after exile.
The period also brought significant recognition. In 1952, Jabès was made a Knight of the Legion of Honor for literary accomplishments, an important distinction for a writer whose career was still closely tied to Cairo. Yet his position remained culturally…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, Tom Beazley, Streets of Cairo, 1941

s.t: Paris: Exile after the Suez Crisis
s.d:
The decisive migration occurred in 1957, when Edmond Jabès left Egypt during the aftermath of the Suez Crisis and settled permanently in Paris. His departure was bound to the deteriorating position of Jews in Egypt and transformed what had previously been a cultural identity into an existential condition of exile. He left behind the country in which he had been born, educated, married, and established as a writer.
In Paris, the experience of displacement became the central organizing problem of his writing. The move also placed him within a French literary environment that could now receive his work more directly. Je bâtis ma demeure, published in 1959, gathered poems written across the…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, historical photograph of Rue Norvins, Paris

s.d:
In 1963, Edmond Jabès published the first volume of Le Livre des questions in Paris with Gallimard. The book marked a major transformation in his literary career, bringing together fragmentary prose, poetry, dialogue, aphorism, invented voices, and questions. The work emerged from the experience of exile and from an increasingly explicit meditation on Jewish history, memory, and the catastrophe of the Shoah.
The seven-volume cycle, completed between 1963 and 1973, became central to Jabès's place in French literature. Its fragmented form drew on the plural textual traditions of Jewish tradition, including the Midrash and Kabbalah, while resisting conventional genre boundaries. The work later…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, Rémi Mathis, Gallimard building

s.t: Montreal: World Exposition and French Recognition
s.loc: Expo 67, Cité du Havre, Montreal, Canada
s.d:
The year 1967 marked an important expansion of Jabès's public identity beyond Paris. He became a French citizen and, in the same year, was among four writers who presented their work at the World Exposition in Montreal. His appearance alongside Jean-Paul Sartre, Albert Camus, and Claude Lévi-Strauss situated his writing within a prominent international presentation of French intellectual and literary culture.
The Montreal episode is significant because it brought together several dimensions of Jabès's trajectory: an Egyptian-born Jewish writer, a permanent resident of Paris, and a newly naturalized French citizen whose work was increasingly recognized beyond France. His literary identity…

s.t: Paris: Final Years and Literary Legacy
s.d:
Jabès spent the remainder of his life in Paris, where the themes developed after exile continued to shape his mature work. His later books extended the cycle of reflections on the book, language, hospitality, Jewish memory, and the condition of the stranger. The trajectory that had begun in Cairo and passed through exile therefore ended without resolving exile into a simple return: Paris became the enduring place from which he wrote about displacement, memory, and belonging.
Edmond Jabès died in Paris in 1991. His final literary period included Book of Hospitality, a work that continued his concern with the ethical relation between the stranger and the host. After his death, his work…
s.cr: Wikimedia Commons, Alexandre Vialle, Père-Lachaise Cemetery

s.d:
Esther Bendahan Cohen nació en Tetuán, Marruecos, en 1964, dentro de una familia judeoespañola y sefardí. Era hija de Mari Cohen y Pinhas Bendahan. La ciudad había sido durante siglos un espacio de encuentro entre poblaciones judías y musulmanas, con una memoria hispánica especialmente intensa en el norte de Marruecos.
Su posterior escritura convirtió esa infancia tetuaní en un archivo literario de memoria, exilio e identidad. En Déjalo, ya volveremos, Bendahan reconstruye la experiencia infantil y la desintegración de la comunidad judía de Marruecos. El Mellah ofrece así un punto de partida geográfico para comprender la relación entre la autora, la tradición sefardí y la ciudad que…

s.t: Madrid: Exilio familiar y nueva ciudad
s.d:
Cuando Esther Bendahan era muy pequeña, sus padres decidieron dejar Tetuán y emprender una nueva vida en Madrid. En el relato autobiográfico asociado a Tetuán, la autora presenta esa salida como parte de un exilio silencioso que afectó a numerosas familias judías de los países musulmanes. Para la familia Bendahan, Madrid pasó a ser el lugar de pertenencia cotidiana.
El traslado produjo una continuidad cultural más que una ruptura absoluta: Bendahan recuerda que en su casa se hablaba español, se comía comida española y se pensaba en español, mientras la conciencia sefardí se desarrollaba de forma gradual. La experiencia de pasar de una ciudad marroquí de tradición hispánica a la capital…

s.t: Madrid: Estudios de psicología y filología
s.loc: Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Madrid, España
s.d:
En Madrid, Bendahan desarrolló una formación académica que combinó Psicología y Filología francesa. La primera disciplina aportó una atención sostenida a la interioridad y a las relaciones humanas, mientras la segunda abrió su trayectoria hacia la literatura francesa y el estudio comparado de identidades, alteridades y tradiciones culturales.
Su formación universitaria sería decisiva para la convergencia posterior entre escritura, crítica literaria y divulgación cultural. La referencia a la Universidad Complutense sitúa este periodo en uno de los principales espacios intelectuales de Madrid. Más adelante, Bendahan ampliaría esta preparación mediante seminarios, talleres de creación y…

Desde 1986 hasta 2007, Esther Bendahan fue subdirectora del programa cultural semanal Shalom de TVE 2, donde participó en la realización, las entrevistas y los guiones. Posteriormente fue directora y presentadora del programa hasta 2010. El medio televisivo amplió su labor de divulgación de la cultura judía y sefardí ante una audiencia española.
Esta etapa consolidó una práctica pública basada en la entrevista, el guion, la conversación intelectual y la mediación cultural. Su trabajo audiovisual se integró con una producción escrita cada vez más amplia, que incluyó artículos y reportajes en El País y en diversas revistas. La experiencia de Shalom es, por tanto, un capítulo clave en la…

s.t: París: Albert Cohen y la Sorbona
s.d:
En 2004, Bendahan impartió un curso sobre Albert Cohen en la Sorbona, dentro de una trayectoria de docencia y reflexión sobre literatura francesa. El escritor suizo de origen judío se convertiría después en el centro de su investigación doctoral, especialmente por su tratamiento de la relación con el otro y del imaginario judío.
El paso por París representa la dimensión transnacional de su formación filológica. Su trabajo sobre Cohen enlaza la tradición literaria francesa con preguntas sobre identidad, alteridad y experiencia judía. Esta línea de investigación culminaría en una tesis doctoral presentada en 2015, mostrando cómo una actividad docente anterior podía transformarse en una…

El recorrido formativo de Esther Bendahan incluyó también seminarios en la Universidad de Toulouse. La fuente biográfica no fija un año concreto para estos encuentros, por lo que el episodio debe entenderse como parte de una etapa prolongada de formación y especialización en el ámbito de la filología francesa y la creación literaria.
Estos seminarios se integran en una trayectoria que también menciona talleres de literatura contemporánea, cursos de cuento corto y estudios de escritura creativa y periodística. La dimensión francesa de su formación complementó su experiencia madrileña y contribuyó a una práctica intelectual que combina ficción, ensayo, crítica y reflexión sobre la identidad…

Bendahan realizó seminarios vinculados con la educación sobre la Shoah en Yad Vashem, así como un seminario en Jerusalén para educadores dedicado al recorrido de Sefarad a Jerusalén. Estas experiencias conectaron su interés por la memoria histórica con la pedagogía y con la transmisión de la historia judía.
El trabajo con Yad Vashem también se prolongó en España mediante su participación en actividades educativas y mediante la coordinación de un proyecto de colección de libros de Yad Vashem en la editorial Losada. El eje de memoria, educación y transmisión cultural complementa su escritura sobre el exilio sefardí y amplía su actividad más allá de la creación literaria.

s.t: Madrid: Deshojando alcachofas y consolidación literaria
s.loc: Círculo de Bellas Artes, Madrid, España
s.d:
En 2005, Deshojando alcachofas, publicada por Seix Barral, obtuvo el reconocimiento del público y el Premio FNAC nuevo talento. El reconocimiento marcó una etapa de consolidación de Bendahan como escritora, después de años dedicados a la televisión, el periodismo cultural y la formación filológica.
La recepción de su narrativa reforzó una obra interesada por la memoria, la experiencia personal y las relaciones entre cultura y subjetividad. En los años siguientes publicó La cara de Marte, que recibió el Premio Tigre Juan, y continuó desarrollando una escritura situada entre la literatura española contemporánea y una conciencia histórica sefardí. La trayectoria literaria se convirtió…

s.t: Madrid: Premio Torrente Ballester y nueva novela
s.d:
En 2011, Bendahan ganó el Premio Torrente Ballester en lengua castellana por Amor y ley. El tratado del alma gemela, publicado por Ediciones del Viento en 2012. La distinción se incorporó a una trayectoria narrativa que ya incluía varias novelas y una atención constante a los vínculos entre experiencia individual, cultura y memoria.
El reconocimiento también forma parte de la consolidación de Bendahan dentro de la literatura española contemporánea. La fuente destaca que fue una de las pocas mujeres en obtener el premio. Su producción literaria de este periodo mantiene un diálogo con cuestiones de identidad, relaciones humanas, alteridad y sumisión, temas que aparecen de distintas maneras en…

s.t: Madrid: Doctorado e investigación sobre Albert Cohen
s.loc: Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Madrid, España, Rectorado
s.d:
En 2015, Bendahan obtuvo el doctorado en Filología francesa con una investigación dedicada a Albert Cohen. La tesis, titulada El imaginario judío y “el otro” en la obra de Albert Cohen, estudia la idea de alteridad y su influencia en la obra del escritor, prolongando una línea intelectual que ya había aparecido en su docencia y seminarios.
El doctorado articuló de manera explícita literatura francesa, imaginario judío y reflexión sobre el otro. La investigación se integró en su actividad posterior como profesora, conferenciante y autora invitada en universidades españolas y americanas. De este modo, la formación filológica de Madrid y sus experiencias internacionales confluyeron en una…

s.t: Tetuán: Regreso literario a la ciudad natal
s.d:
En 2017, Bendahan publicó Tetuán, un libro dedicado a la ciudad de su nacimiento y presentado como una recuperación de recuerdos, sabores, historias y de la memoria de sus habitantes judíos. La obra convierte el regreso a Tetuán en una forma de exploración literaria de la infancia y del exilio familiar.
La autora describe una ciudad simultáneamente marroquí y española, marcada por el antiguo Protectorado Español y por una comunidad judía cuya permanencia había terminado para muchas familias. El libro reúne memoria familiar, gastronomía, humor, jaquetía y referencias a la historia sefardí. Tetuán reaparece así como espacio de origen y como territorio literario que puede ser recorrido desde la…

s.t: Madrid: Centro Sefarad-Israel y programación cultural
s.d:
La trayectoria pública de Bendahan incluye su trabajo como responsable de la programación cultural de Centro Sefarad-Israel en Madrid. El centro tiene su sede en el Palacio de Cañete, y su actividad se orienta a la divulgación del legado sefardí, la cultura judía y las relaciones con Israel.
Esta etapa prolonga la combinación de literatura, memoria y divulgación cultural que caracteriza su perfil. Además de su labor institucional, Bendahan continúa escribiendo artículos, participando en conferencias y colaborando con universidades e instituciones culturales. Su trayectoria reúne así la experiencia de la televisión, la investigación filológica, la narrativa y la gestión cultural dentro de un…

Ezio Levi d’Ancona was born in Mantua in 1884 into a Ferrara family of Sephardi Jewish origin. The Mantuan setting situated his early life within the intellectual and urban culture of northern Italy, while his family background connected him to the longer history of Italian Sephardim. His later career as a philologist and Hispanist retained this dual orientation, combining Italian literary scholarship with sustained attention to the Spanish world.
The family’s Ferrarese roots are central to understanding Levi’s cultural formation. His later work ranged across Romance philology, medieval poetry, comparative narrative, and modern Spanish literature, reflecting a scholarly identity shaped by…

In 1906, Ezio Levi completed his degree in letters at the University of Pavia, studying at the Collegio Ghislieri. This stage established the formal academic foundation for a career devoted to philology, literary history, and the comparative study of Romance traditions. His university training prepared him for the specialized research that would later link medieval Italian literature with Spanish and broader European literary cultures.
The Collegio Ghislieri was an important scholarly environment within Pavia, a university city with a long intellectual tradition. Levi’s graduation marked a transition from general literary education toward advanced study and teaching. The next phase took him…

s.loc: Istituto di Studi Superiori, Florence, Italy
s.d:
After Pavia, Levi continued his studies at the Istituto di Studi Superiori di Firenze. There he studied with Pio Rajna and Alessandro d’Ancona, two influential figures in Italian literary scholarship. Their intellectual environment deepened his engagement with Romance philology, literary history, and the study of medieval and early modern texts. Florence became an important center in the formation of his scholarly method.
The Florence period also connected Levi to the academic world in which his later research took shape. His early interests included the juglaresque tradition, Duecento poetry, and comparative fiction, while his later work increasingly turned toward Spain. The city therefore…

Levi later broadened his studies in Berlin, extending an already international academic formation beyond Italy. The move placed his work within the wider European culture of philology, where comparative linguistic and literary research connected scholars across national traditions. Although the source does not specify a precise date or institution for his Berlin studies, it identifies the city as part of his advanced education before his early teaching appointments.
Berlin formed part of a sequence that also included Paris, demonstrating the breadth of Levi’s scholarly mobility. His later research combined Italian medieval literature, comparative novel studies, and increasingly Spanish…
s.cr: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division

s.d:
Levi also pursued advanced study in Paris, another major European center for philology and literary scholarship. The source gives no precise institution or date, but places Paris alongside Berlin in the period when he expanded his education after his Italian university formation. The experience reinforced the international character of his intellectual development and his engagement with the comparative study of Romance languages and literatures.
Paris was especially significant within the broader scholarly geography of Levi’s career because his research depended on movement among national literary traditions. His early interests in medieval poetry, comparative fiction, and the literary…

Before his appointment at the naval school in Livorno, Levi taught in the liceo of Lucera, beginning his professional life as a teacher within the Italian secondary-school system. This period followed his university and European studies and translated his scholarly formation into classroom practice. Lucera, in Puglia, represents an early teaching appointment in the south of Italy before his more sustained academic posts.
The Lucera chapter is important because Levi’s career combined teaching with research throughout his life. His later work would address Italian medieval poetry, comparative literature, Maria de Francia, and eventually modern Spanish literature. Early school teaching provided…

From 1912 to 1918, Levi taught at the Scuola Navale di Livorno, now associated with the Accademia Navale. The appointment placed a literary scholar within an institution devoted to naval education, broadening the social and professional settings in which he practiced teaching. During these years he continued to develop the interests in Italian literature and comparative narrative that characterized his early scholarship.
Livorno also marks a sustained period in which Levi combined institutional teaching with research. His early scholarly interests included the juglaresque world, Duecento poetry, and the comparative study of narrative, including the theme of Don Carlos. The naval school…

Between 1918 and 1922, Levi taught at the Magistero in Florence. The return to the city reunited his professional teaching with the intellectual environment in which he had studied with Pio Rajna and Alessandro d’Ancona. Around 1920, his scholarly attention became especially focused on Maria de Francia, marking a significant development in his interests.
This Florence period sits at the intersection of teaching and the expansion of his research program. Levi was moving beyond his initial work on Duecento poetry and comparative novel studies toward wider questions in medieval and Romance literary history. His marriage to Flora Aghib in 1916 and the later adoption of the d’Ancona surname in…

From 1923 to 1925, Levi taught Romance philology in Palermo. This appointment reflects the increasing specialization of his career and his sustained engagement with the linguistic and literary traditions of the Romance world. By this stage, his scholarship was moving toward a wider comparative framework in which Italian, French, and Spanish literary cultures could be studied in relation to one another.
Palermo was also part of the southern Italian academic landscape through which Levi passed before establishing a long teaching period in Naples. His mature interests increasingly centered on Spain, especially contemporary Spanish literature and Romantic literature, while his earlier work…

In 1926, Levi moved to Naples, where he taught until the racial legislation of 1938 removed him from his chair. This was the longest academic phase described in the source and coincided with the maturation of his interests in Spain, especially contemporary Spanish literature and Romantic literature. His published work from this period included studies of Spanish literature and the relationship between Lope de Vega and Italy.
Naples became a major setting for Levi’s scholarly identity as an Italian Hispanist. His works Vite romantiche, Motivi Hispánicos, and later Lope de Vega e L’Italia reflect the broadening of his research toward Spain and its literary connections with Italy. His…

s.loc: University of Naples area, Naples, Italy
s.d:
Levi’s Naples career was abruptly interrupted by the Real Decreto Ley núm. 1728 of 17 November 1938, a racial measure that resulted in his expulsion from his academic chair. The event transformed a long period of teaching and research into forced professional displacement. For an Italian scholar of Sephardi Jewish origin, the legislation marked a decisive rupture between his established academic life and the increasingly exclusionary political environment of late Fascist Italy.
The loss of his chair came after more than a decade of work in Naples, during which his scholarship had concentrated increasingly on Spanish literature and its relation to Italian culture. The expulsion was followed…

After leaving Italy in 1940, Levi settled in the United States and taught at Wellesley College in Massachusetts. This appointment gave the displaced Hispanist a new institutional setting in which to continue teaching and scholarship after the loss of his Italian chair. The move extended a career already marked by international study in Berlin and Paris into a new transatlantic phase.
At Wellesley, Levi’s scholarly profile remained connected to Spanish literature, Romance studies, and the comparative literary interests developed over earlier decades. His American appointment should be understood in the context of the forced displacement created by the 1938 racial laws. The move did not erase…

s.loc: Old North Church, Boston, United States
s.d:
Levi died in Boston in 1941, aged 57, after the final stage of a career transformed by exile. His death followed his arrival in the United States and his teaching appointment at Wellesley College. The source records that he died after being consumed by a stomach ulcer, bringing to a close a scholarly life that had moved across Italian and European academic centers before ending in Massachusetts.
His legacy combines Italian philology, Hispanism, and the study of literary connections across national traditions. He published works including Motivi Hispánicos, Vite romantiche, and Lope de Vega e L’Italia, and was elected an academician of the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de Valladolid in 1934.…
s.cr: Historic American Buildings Survey, Library of Congress, photographer Frank Branzetti

s.d:
Françoise Giroud, born Léa France Gourdji on 21 September 1916, entered the world in Lausanne within a family shaped by the late Ottoman Jewish diaspora. Her father, Salih Gourdji, was a journalist from Turkey, while her mother, Elda Faraggi, came from a family associated with Thessaloniki. The family's mobility across the Ottoman Mediterranean, Switzerland, and France placed Giroud within a distinctly transnational Sephardi setting from birth.
The Lausanne birthplace also anticipates the multilingual and cosmopolitan environment that marked Giroud's later career. Although she became a major figure in French journalism and politics, her family background remained connected to Sephardi Jewish…

By 1932, Françoise Giroud was established in Paris, where she encountered the cinema world through Marc Allégret and began work as a scripte. The move from clerical work into film production gave her an early apprenticeship in the disciplined organization of stories, scenes, dialogue, and visual continuity. Her subsequent work included productions associated with Marcel Pagnol and Jean Renoir, including La Grande Illusion.
Paris became the central professional environment of Giroud's life, connecting her to French cinema, publishing, and eventually political journalism. Her early work as a script girl, later screenwriter, and dialogue writer helped establish the editorial skills that would…

The German invasion of France in 1940 altered Giroud's professional trajectory. During the wartime displacement from Paris, she joined the movement of civilians and journalists toward Lyon, where she worked for Paris-Soir, then one of France's major newspapers. She also contributed features and short pieces to smaller publications, continuing to develop a journalistic voice under the constraints of the Occupation.
Lyon therefore represents a decisive transition from cinema to political journalism. The city became a temporary professional base in a period when press work was deeply entangled with censorship, displacement, and the reorganization of French public life. Giroud's wartime…

In 1943, Giroud's wartime activity moved from journalism into direct participation in the French Resistance. Working as a liaison agent alongside her sister Douce, she became involved in clandestine communications during the German Occupation. The Gestapo arrested her, and she was taken to Fresnes Prison near Paris. Her detention placed her within the machinery of political repression that confronted French resistance networks.
Giroud was released in 1944 and avoided deportation, while her sister was deported and later died after the war. The Fresnes episode became a formative part of Giroud's understanding of political violence, liberty, and civic responsibility. It also illuminates the…
s.cr: Scanné par Like tears in rain, Wikimedia Commons

s.d:
After the Liberation, Giroud returned to Paris and entered the editorial world of Elle, the women's magazine launched by Hélène Gordon-Lazareff in 1945. Giroud joined the publication in its formative period and became its editorial director, a position she held through 1953. The magazine provided a major platform for her development as a journalist, editor, interviewer, and cultural commentator.
At Elle, Giroud participated in the reconstruction of French media culture after the war while helping shape a modern vocabulary for women's public and private lives. Her work connected journalism, gender, culture, and popular publishing. The period established her as a senior editor before her…
s.cr: Gallica, Bibliothèque nationale de France, via Wikimedia Commons

s.d:
In 1953, Giroud founded L'Express with Jean-Jacques Servan-Schreiber. The first issue appeared on 16 May 1953, initially as a Saturday supplement associated with Les Échos. Giroud's editorial experience at Elle was transformed into a new model of political journalism centered on current affairs, public argument, and the relationship between journalism and government. The magazine quickly became an influential forum for French political debate.
Through L'Express, Giroud supported the political ideas associated with Pierre Mendès France and published forceful interventions on Indochina, the Algerian War, and the responsibilities of the press. Her role as editor-in-chief helped define the…

In 1974, Giroud left the direction of L'Express and entered national government as Secretary of State for the Condition of Women under Prime Minister Jacques Chirac and President Valéry Giscard d'Estaing. Her appointment marked a significant shift from editorial influence to direct institutional action. She brought to public office the concerns about women's rights, social equality, and civic participation that had developed across her journalistic career.
Her governmental work addressed the legal and social position of women, including questions of employment, childcare, and the inherited framework of the Napoleonic Code. Giroud's move into government demonstrates how postwar French…

In 1976, Giroud moved from the women's affairs portfolio to become Secretary of State for Culture in the government of Raymond Barre. The appointment extended her public role from social policy into the broader field of French cultural policy. Her earlier career in cinema, journalism, and publishing gave the portfolio a practical connection to the institutions and media worlds in which she had worked for decades.
The culture ministry chapter is important because it brings together several strands of Giroud's career: the film industry of her youth, the editorial authority developed at Elle and L'Express, and the institutional responsibilities of government. She served in the culture portfolio…

After leaving government, Giroud resumed the work that had defined much of her public identity. From 1983, she contributed a regular column to Le Nouvel Observateur, returning to journalism while maintaining a broad engagement with literature, television, culture, and public affairs. The return demonstrates the continuity of her editorial vocation across several decades of institutional and political change.
Her later journalism extended the concise and pointed style associated with L'Express, while her interests broadened through literary criticism, television commentary, and cultural debate. The Nouvel Observateur years also place Giroud within a mature phase of French intellectual…

s.loc: American Hospital of Paris, Neuilly-sur-Seine, France
s.d:
Giroud's life ended in Neuilly-sur-Seine on 19 January 2003, where she died at the American Hospital of Paris. Her final years remained connected to journalism and cultural commentary, preserving the professional identity she had developed across cinema, women's publishing, political news, and government service. Her death closed a career spanning the major transformations of French public life from the interwar period to the early twenty-first century.
The final chapter returns the map to the Paris metropolitan region that had become Giroud's principal professional and cultural environment. From her birth in Lausanne and her family's Ottoman Sephardi origins, through Resistance, journalism,…

Isaac de Matatías Aboab was born in 1632 within the flourishing Sephardi community of Amsterdam, a major center of Spanish and Portuguese Jewish culture in the Dutch Republic. The available source identifies him as a Sephardi poet and dramatist whose literary work developed in both Spanish and Portuguese.
His later activity places him in an intellectual environment where Jewish communal life, multilingual expression, and the preservation of inherited Iberian traditions intersected. Rather than treating Amsterdam simply as a place of residence, his career shows how the city's Sephardi literary culture could sustain poetry, dramatic writing, and the collection of works by fellow community…

s.t: Amsterdam: Spanish and Portuguese Literary Culture
s.d:
During the seventeenth century, Isaac de Matatías Aboab developed as a versatile writer in Spanish and Portuguese. The source characterizes him as a kind of self-taught philologist, a skilled versifier, and a collector determined to preserve poetry produced by his Sephardi contemporaries.
His literary practice joined creative composition with cultural preservation. He gathered poems and other texts that might otherwise disappear, including material associated with Sephardi women and with the everyday social life of the community. This combination of authorship and collecting is central to understanding his place in Dutch Sephardi letters. The supplied source does not provide a precise year…

By the later seventeenth century, Matatías Aboab was engaged with the varied voices of the Amsterdam Sephardi community. His collections preserve poems, dialogues, songs, and satirical material, demonstrating an interest in literary forms that reflected ordinary social experience as well as learned culture.
Particularly notable is his attention to female voices. The source describes a verse dialogue between Rica, a wife, and Sara, a domestic servant, as well as poems attributed to Blanca Rodríguez, presented as a prominent woman in the community. These texts illuminate marriage, household life, advice to newly married women, and communal support for a widow and her daughter. Aboab's…

In 1683, Isaac de Matatías Aboab produced Relagóes, cantigas, adevinhagóes e outras corizidades, a collection that exemplifies his work as a compiler, poet, and cultural archivist. The title itself signals a broad interest in songs, riddles, narratives, and other forms of literary curiosity.
